These three verses are Medinan, as Muqatil said, though the first one resembles the Meccan style.

If you intend "Hud" as the name of the surah, it is not declined (diptote), just as you do when you name a woman "'Amr" or "Zayd"; and if you intend the surah "Hud," you decline it.

His, Mighty and Majestic is He, saying:

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm, then detailed, from the presence of One Wise, All-Aware﴾ ﴿That you worship none but Allah. Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ ﴿And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will give you enjoyment, a good enjoyment, until a specified term, and will give every person of virtue his virtue. But if you turn away, then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ ﴿To Allah is your return, and He is over all things competent﴾

The discussion of the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'a) at the beginnings of surahs has already been comprehensively covered. This case is distinctive in that it has been said that the letters of "al-Rahman" are separated within it, as well as in "Ha Mim" and in "Nun, wal-Qalam."

Whoever says, "the letters are an indication of the letters of the alphabet (al-mu'jam)," then the letters are the subject; and whoever interprets the letters otherwise, then the subject is: "This is a Book," and by "the Book" is meant the Qur'an.

Then it was detailed by being divided and by varying its rulings and commands upon Muhammad ﷺ at different times. So "thumma" (then) retains its proper sense. This is the method of firmness (ihkam) and detail (tafsil), for firmness is an essential attribute, while detail is only according to the one to whom it is detailed. The whole Book is both firm and detailed. The firmness that is the opposite of abrogation (naskh), and the detail that is the opposite of generality (ijmal), are only used together with what we have mentioned, by way of shared meaning. Al-Tabari related from some interpreters: "Uhkimat" means with commands and prohibitions, and "futtilat" means with reward and punishment; and from others: "Uhkimat" means protected from falsehood, and "futtilat" means with the lawful and the unlawful. Such specifications are correct in meaning, but the wording does not necessarily imply them. Some said: "Futtilat" means "fussirat" (explained). Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Kathir, as related from him, read "thumma fasalat" with a fatha on the fa, sad, and lam. This may bear two meanings: the first: "fasalat," meaning it descended to the people, as one says, "fasala fulan" for his journey and similar meaning. The second: it distinguished between the true and the false among people.

"Min ladun" means: from the point where the endpoint begins, so said Sibawayh, and it has several dialectal forms. It is said "ladn" and "ludn" with the dal sukun, and both have been read as "min ladun"; it is also said "lad" with fatha on the lam and damma on the dal without nun; it is said "ladan" with a tanwin on a dal with maqsura; and it is said "lad" with a kasra on the dal with tanwin. Abu 'Ubayda related these forms.

"Hakim" means muhkim (one who makes firm), and "Khabir" means one who has complete experience of all affairs.

﴿Alla ta'budu﴾: "an" is in a position of nasb, either by implying a verb, or by assuming "bi-an" with the removal of the preposition. It was said: it is in apposition (badal) to the place of "al-ayat," but this is a weak objection, because "al-ayat" has no place; and if the position of the clause is considered, it is in the nominative. It may also be in the nominative position, with the estimate: "its detailing is that you not worship," and it was said: it is in apposition to the wording of "al-ayat."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾, meaning: from His punishment and with His reward. When these two words are used without qualification, warning pertains to what is disliked and good tidings to what is loved. "Warner" is placed first because warning against the Fire is the more important. "An" is conjoined to the one before it. The meaning of the verse: "Seek forgiveness of your Lord," that is, seek His forgiveness for you, and this is by seeking to enter Islam; "then repent," that is, shed disbelief and regret its past. "Thumma" indicates sequence, because the disbeliever first turns back, seeking the forgiveness of his Lord; when he repents and is stripped of disbelief, his faith is complete. The majority read "yumatti'kum" with a doubled ta; Ibn Muhaysin read "yumti'kum" with a sukun on the mim and a light ta. In Abu Hatim's book it is said: "These readings are with nun," and this requires examination. "Mata'an" is a verbal noun (masdar) of a form other than the preceding verb, like: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. It was also said: it is put in the accusative by the transitivity of "yumatti'kum," because you say: "mattatu Zaydan thawban" (I gave Zayd a garment). Describing the enjoyment as good pertains only to the believer's pleasant life through his hope in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in His reward, his joy in drawing near to Him through His obligations, and his delight in His promises; the disbeliever has no share in any of this. As for one who says that the good enjoyment is the benefits of this world and its adornment, this is weak, because the disbelievers share in that to the greatest degree. The specified term is the term of death, meaning: until a specified term for each one of you. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, and on this view the "great term" is the Day of Resurrection. The verse may also mean that the threat is of hastening punishment if they disbelieve, and the promise is of enjoyment if they believe, which resembles what Nuh, peace be upon him, said. On this view, "the great day" is like the Day of Badr or similar. The uncertainty as to which of the two matters will occur is only in relation to humans; the matter with Allah, exalted is He, is known and determined, and the term is one.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, meaning every person of goodness by his speech, his deed, his strength, his wealth, or other things by which one may draw near. "Fadlahu" may refer back to "dhi," meaning the reward of his virtue and its recompense. It may also refer back to Allah, meaning: Allah gives His bounty to every person of virtue and righteous deed among the believers. Similar to this meaning is what Allah, blessed and exalted, promised regarding the multiplication of a good deed to ten times its like, and multiplication beyond counting for whomever He wills. Ibn Mas'ud interpreted it this way and said: "Woe to him whose single units overcome his tens." It may also be that Ibn Mas'ud's statement agrees with the first meaning.

(p-٥٣٩)The majority read "wa in tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta and lam. Some said its meaning is the third person: "so say to them: indeed I fear for you"; others said its meaning is "fa in tatawallaw," with the ta removed, and the whole verse is addressed to those present. Al-Yamani and Isa ibn 'Umar read "wa in tuwallu" with a damma on the ta and lam and a fatha on the waw.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ is a threat of the Day of Resurrection, and it may also mean a day of this world, like Badr or another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ is a threat, and it supports the view that the great day is the Day of Resurrection, since he threatened with it, then mentioned the way to it, which is return to Allah. The meaning: your return is to His punishment and recompense. He is the Capable, whom nothing harms, whom no protector can shelter against Him, and whose decree no shield can avert. His saying: ﴿over all things﴾ is a general expression intended in a restricted sense, excluding what Allah is not described as capable of, such as impossibilities and other things which are not things. In language, "shay'" (thing) means what exists, and what is certain to exist, such as the quaking of the Hour and others.

(p-٥٣٦)In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The firmness that is the opposite of abrogation (naskh), and the detail that is the opposite of generality (ijmal), are only used together with what we have mentioned, by way of shared meaning. Al-Tabari related from some interpreters: "Uhkimat" means with commands and prohibitions, and "futtilat" means with reward and punishment; and from others: "Uhkimat" means protected from falsehood, and "futtilat" means with the lawful and the unlawful. Such specifications are correct in meaning, but the wording does not necessarily imply them. Some said: "Futtilat" means "fussirat" (explained). Ikrimah, al-Dahhak, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Kathir, as related from him, read "thumma fasalat" with a fatha on the fa, sad, and lam. This may bear two meanings: the first: "fasalat," meaning it descended to the people, as one says, "fasala fulan" for his journey and similar meaning. The second: it distinguished between the true and the false among people.

"Min ladun" means: from the point where the endpoint begins, so said Sibawayh, and it has several dialectal forms. It is said "ladn" and "ludn" with the dal sukun, and both have been read as "min ladun"; it is also said "lad" with fatha on the lam and damma on the dal without nun; it is said "ladan" with a tanwin on a dal with maqsura; and it is said "lad" with a kasra on the dal with tanwin. Abu 'Ubayda related these forms.

"Hakim" means muhkim (one who makes firm), and "Khabir" means one who has complete experience of all affairs.

﴿Alla ta'budu﴾: "an" is in a position of nasb, either by implying a verb, or by assuming "bi-an" with the removal of the preposition. It was said: it is in apposition (badal) to the place of "al-ayat," but this is a weak objection, because "al-ayat" has no place; and if the position of the clause is considered, it is in the nominative. It may also be in the nominative position, with the estimate: "its detailing is that you not worship," and it was said: it is in apposition to the wording of "al-ayat."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾, meaning: from His punishment and with His reward. When these two words are used without qualification, warning pertains to what is disliked and good tidings to what is loved. "Warner" is placed first because warning against the Fire is the more important. "An" is conjoined to the one before it. The meaning of the verse: "Seek forgiveness of your Lord," that is, seek His forgiveness for you, and this is by seeking to enter Islam; "then repent," that is, shed disbelief and regret its past. "Thumma" indicates sequence, because the disbeliever first turns back, seeking the forgiveness of his Lord; when he repents and is stripped of disbelief, his faith is complete. The majority read "yumatti'kum" with a doubled ta; Ibn Muhaysin read "yumti'kum" with a sukun on the mim and a light ta. In Abu Hatim's book it is said: "These readings are with nun," and this requires examination. "Mata'an" is a verbal noun (masdar) of a form other than the preceding verb, like: ﴿And Allah has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾ [Nuh: 17]. It was also said: it is put in the accusative by the transitivity of "yumatti'kum," because you say: "mattatu Zaydan thawban" (I gave Zayd a garment). Describing the enjoyment as good pertains only to the believer's pleasant life through his hope in Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and in His reward, his joy in drawing near to Him through His obligations, and his delight in His promises; the disbeliever has no share in any of this. As for one who says that the good enjoyment is the benefits of this world and its adornment, this is weak, because the disbelievers share in that to the greatest degree. The specified term is the term of death, meaning: until a specified term for each one of you. This is the apparent meaning of the verse, and on this view the "great term" is the Day of Resurrection. The verse may also mean that the threat is of hastening punishment if they disbelieve, and the promise is of enjoyment if they believe, which resembles what Nuh, peace be upon him, said. On this view, "the great day" is like the Day of Badr or similar. The uncertainty as to which of the two matters will occur is only in relation to humans; the matter with Allah, exalted is He, is known and determined, and the term is one.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and will give every person of virtue his virtue﴾, meaning every person of goodness by his speech, his deed, his strength, his wealth, or other things by which one may draw near. "Fadlahu" may refer back to "dhi," meaning the reward of his virtue and its recompense. It may also refer back to Allah, meaning: Allah gives His bounty to every person of virtue and righteous deed among the believers. Similar to this meaning is what Allah, blessed and exalted, promised regarding the multiplication of a good deed to ten times its like, and multiplication beyond counting for whomever He wills. Ibn Mas'ud interpreted it this way and said: "Woe to him whose single units overcome his tens." It may also be that Ibn Mas'ud's statement agrees with the first meaning.

(p-٥٣٩)The majority read "wa in tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta and lam. Some said its meaning is the third person: "so say to them: indeed I fear for you"; others said its meaning is "fa in tatawallaw," with the ta removed, and the whole verse is addressed to those present. Al-Yamani and Isa ibn 'Umar read "wa in tuwallu" with a damma on the ta and lam and a fatha on the waw.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great day﴾ is a threat of the Day of Resurrection, and it may also mean a day of this world, like Badr or another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah is your return﴾ is a threat, and it supports the view that the great day is the Day of Resurrection, since he threatened with it, then mentioned the way to it, which is return to Allah. The meaning: your return is to His punishment and recompense. He is the Capable, whom nothing harms, whom no protector can shelter against Him, and whose decree no shield can avert. His saying: ﴿over all things﴾ is a general expression intended in a restricted sense, excluding what Allah is not described as capable of, such as impossibilities and other things which are not things. In language, "shay'" (thing) means what exists, and what is certain to exist, such as the quaking of the Hour and others.

[p. 540] The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿Behold, they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Behold, even when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Indeed, He is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts.﴾ ﴿There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon God. He knows its resting place and its repository. All is in a Clear Book.﴾

It has been said: This verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers who, when they met the Messenger of God (ﷺ), would lower themselves and fold their breasts as if concealing themselves, turn their backs to him, and cover their faces with their garments, out of aversion and distance from him and dislike of meeting him. They thought this would be hidden from him and from God, the Exalted and Majestic, so the verse was revealed about that. According to this view, "صُدُورَهم" (ṣudūrahum, "their breasts") is in the accusative, governed by "يَثْنُونَ" (yathnūna, "they fold").

It has also been said: It is a metaphor for the rancor and hatred they harbored within. As one says: "So-and-so folds his side over his enmity and bends his chest over it." The meaning of the verse is: Behold, they conceal enmity and hide it, so that it may be hidden, in their assumption, from God. He, the Exalted, knows what they conceal, even when they cover themselves and go to great lengths to conceal.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "يُثْنُونَ" (yuthnūna) with a dammah on the yā' and nūn, from athnā (to fold). Ibn 'Abbas read "لَيَثْنُونَ" (layathnūna). Ibn 'Abbas also read, as did Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, Ibn Abza, Nasr ibn 'Asim, al-Jahdari, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Razin, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali, Yazid ibn 'Ali, Ja'far ibn Muhammad, Abu al-Aswad, and al-Dahhak: "تَثْنَوِي" ... rather, "تَثْنَوِيْ" was read with "صُدُورُهُمْ" in the nominative (تَثْنَوِي صُدُورُهُمْ, with the breasts as subject). This reading admits the two meanings mentioned above for "يَثْنُونَ." Its form is تَفْعَوْعِلُ (tafa'wa'il), a pattern of intensification indicating repetition of the action, as one says: "اعْشَوْشَبَتِ الأرْضُ" (i'shawshabat al-ardu, "the land became thickly grassed") and "احْلَوْلَتِ الدُنْيا" (ihlawlatal-dunya, "the world became sweet"), and similar forms.

Al-Tabari reported from Ibn 'Abbas, on this reading, that the verse was revealed concerning some people who, whenever they had intercourse with their wives or relieved themselves, would cover their garments, out of dislike of exposing their private parts to the sky.

Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with him and his father), as transmitted by Ibn 'Uyayna, read "تَثْنَوِي" with the thā' placed before the nūn and without a nūn after the wāw. Abu Hatim said: This reading is an error and is not acceptable. Nasr ibn 'Asim, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "تَثْنَوِي" with the nūn placed before the thā'. 'Urwa, Ibn Abi Abza, and al-A'sha read "تَثْنَوِنِّ" with a thā' (unpointed as a triangle in the original text) followed by a fatha-marked nūn, then a kasra-marked wāw. They, and Mujahid as reported from him, also read "تَثْنَئِنُّ" with a hamzah replacing the wāw. Both of these are derived from "الثِنِّ" (ath-thinn), which is the grass that bends easily. The breasts are likened to it, since they are inclined to this folding over of deceit and trickery.

The underlying form of "تَثْنَوِنَّ" is "تَثْنَوْنِنْ": the kasra-marked nūn was made quiescent, its vowel was transferred to the wāw before it, and it was assimilated into the following nūn. As for "تَثْنَئِنُّ", its origin is "تَثْنانَّ", like "تَحْمارَّ", and then they said "اثْنَأنَّ", just as they said "احْمَأرَّ" and "ابْيَأضَّ".

The pronoun in "مِنهُ" (minhu, "from Him") refers to God, the Exalted. This is the most eloquent and fitting interpretation in meaning. Under some interpretations it may refer to Muhammad (ﷺ).

"يَسْتَغْشُونَ" (yastaghshūna) means: they make them coverings and wrappings. From this usage is the saying of al-Khansa':

I graze the stars, though I was not charged with their pasturing,
and at times I wrap myself in the surplus of my worn garments.

Ibn 'Abbas read "عَلى حِينَ يَسْتَغْشُونَ" (ʿalā ḥīna yastaghshūna). From this usage is the saying of al-Nabigha:

When I rebuked gray hair for youth,
and I said: "Enough, let me awaken, though gray hair restrains me."

"ذاتُ الصُدُورِ" (dhāt al-ṣudūr, "that which is in the breasts"): this means what is in them. The word "ذات" (dhāt) is used in speech in several ways, of which this is one. Like the saying of the Arabs: "الذِئْبُ مَغْبُوطٌ بِذِي بَطْنِهِ" (al-dhi'b maghbūṭun bidhī baṭnihi, "the wolf is envied for the one in its belly"), meaning for what is in it of fullness. And like the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him): "إنَّما هو ذُو بَطْنٍ خارِجَةٍ" (innamā huwa dhū baṭnin khārijah, "he is only one with a belly of Kharijah"). The meaning of "dhāt" as the essence and self of a thing is unsuitable in this context. It may be distinguished between "ذِي بَطْنِهِ" and "الذاتِ," and what connects them is only the general meaning.

God's words: ﴿And there is no creature...﴾ ... this verse continues the description of God, blessed and exalted, in a manner similar to His words: ﴿He knows what they conceal and what they reveal﴾. "الدابَّةُ" (al-dābba, "creature") means whatever crawls among living beings. The intended meaning is all living beings that need provision, and this includes birds, insects, and others. All of these are called "دَوابّ" (dawābb, "creatures"). Al-A'sha said:

Slender like a branch of the ban tree, she quivers when she walks,
with the gait of the sand-grouse of the valley floor at every watering place.

'Alqama ibn 'Ubayda said of birds:

...... to their birds there is a gait (dabīb).

In the hadith of Abu 'Ubayda: "فَإذا دابَّةٌ مِثْلَ الظَرْبِ" (fa-idhā dābbatun mithla al-ẓarb, "there was a creature like the ẓarb"), he means a creature of the sea. Its restriction by "فِي الأرْضِ" (fī al-arḍ, "on the earth") is only because it is closest to their perception. Birds and swimmers are also on the earth. Any living thing that dies before it has fed has, in a certain way, been nourished in its mother's womb.

This verse indicates that provision is anything from which benefit can be validly derived, contrary to the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), who said that it is only lawful property that one owns.

God's words: ﴿upon God﴾ are an expression of grace (ījāb tafaḍḍul), since nothing is obligatory upon Him by reason. "المُسْتَقَرُّ" (al-mustaqarr, "resting place") is the loins of the father. "المُسْتَوْدَعُ" (al-mustawda', "repository") is the womb of the mother. It has also been said that al-mustaqarr is the dwelling place, and al-mustawda' is the grave. According to this view, both are locative nouns. It has also been said that al-mustaqarr is what has come into existence as a living thing, and al-mustawda' is what will be found later.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

According to this last view, al-mustaqarr is a verbal noun from istaqarra, and it is not a passive participle like al-mustawda', because istaqarra is intransitive. God's words: ﴿in a Book﴾ refer to the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Some people said: This is a metaphor, and it refers to God's knowledge.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This view is weak, and taking it in its apparent sense is more fitting.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 11, verses 7–8:**

[Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:]

﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed. But if you say, "Indeed, you will be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ ﴿And if We delay the punishment from them for a counted nation, they will surely say, "What is it that restrains it?" Unquestionably, on the day it comes to them, it will not be turned away from them, and what they used to mock will surround them.﴾

Most of the people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) said: the "days" are days of this world. A group said: they are days of the Hereafter, each day being a thousand years. This was said by Ka'b al-Aḥbār, but the first view is more likely. The mention of "the heavens" suffices to include all that is in them, since everything was created within those six days.

The ḥadīths (prophetic reports) differed concerning the day on which creation began. Abū Hurayrah reported, in what al-Ṭabarī transmitted, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took his hand and said: "Allah created the clay on Saturday, the mountains on Sunday, the trees on Monday, the disliked things on Tuesday, light on Wednesday, He spread the creatures on Thursday, and He created Adam after 'Aṣr on Friday." A similar report, that the beginning was on Saturday, is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim. In the Dalā'il of Thābit it is said: "The creation of Adam was on Friday, but it is not counted, since he was a human like all his descendants; and if it were counted, the days would be seven, contrary to what is in the Book of Allah." It is narrated from Ka'b al-Aḥbār that he said: "Allah began the creation of the heavens and the earth on Sunday, finished on Friday, and created Adam in the last hour of it." Similar reports are found in most of the collections (dawāwīn), that the beginning was on Sunday. Others said: Allah created these creatures in six days, although He is able to create them in an instant, as a method of deliberation and patience in actions, so that human beings may perfect their deeds. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The Throne was upon the water, and the water was upon the wind."

As for His saying, ﴿that He might test you﴾, it is connected to "created": the meaning is that His creating them was for this purpose. Some people said it is connected to a verb whose implied sense is: "He informed of that in order to test you." The aim of this speaker is that these created things were not made for the sake of human beings.

ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read "wa-la-in qultu" with a ḍammah on the tā' (qultu, "I said"), while the majority read "qulta" with a fatḥah on the tā' (qulta, "you said").

The meaning of the verse is: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has these attributes, and these people, in their disbelief, are in a state where, if you tell them, "Indeed, they will be resurrected," they deny it and say, "This is magic." That is, this is a contradiction on your part, since every person of sound nature (mafṭūr) acknowledges that Allah is the Creator of the heavens and the earth. They are among those who affirm this, yet they deny what is far easier than it, namely resurrection from the graves, since originating creation is more difficult than restoring it, and creating the heavens and the earth is greater than creating people.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 11, verses 7–8:**

[Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says:]

﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days, and His Throne was upon the water, that He might test you as to which of you is best in deed. This was said by Ka'b al-Aḥbār, but the first view is more likely. The mention of "the heavens" suffices to include all that is in them, since everything was created within those six days.

The ḥadīths (prophetic reports) differed concerning the day on which creation began. Abū Hurayrah reported, in what al-Ṭabarī transmitted, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took his hand and said: "Allah created the clay on Saturday, the mountains on Sunday, the trees on Monday, the disliked things on Tuesday, light on Wednesday, He spread the creatures on Thursday, and He created Adam after 'Aṣr on Friday." Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 9–11:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us, then withdraw it from him, indeed he is despairing and ungrateful.﴾ ﴿And if We let him taste bounty after adversity has touched him, he will surely say, "The evils have gone away from me." Indeed, he is exultant and boastful.﴾ ﴿Except those who are patient and do righteous deeds; those will have forgiveness and a great reward.﴾

"Adhaqna" (We let taste) here is a metaphor (musta'ara), because "al-rahma" (mercy) here encompasses everything that is benefited from: food, clothing, status, and other things. And "al-insan" (man) here is a generic noun (ism al-jins), and the meaning is: this creation has the disposition of people. Then He made an exception from them of those whom the sharia and faith have guided to patience and righteous action. "Ya'us" (despairing) and "kafur" (ungrateful) are both forms of intensification (mubalagha). "Kafur" here is from kufr al-ni'ma (ungratefulness for blessings), and the meaning is: he despairs, becomes distressed, and becomes resentful, whereas if he looked at God's blessings remaining upon him in his intellect, his senses, and other things, and did not deny them, that would not occur. If this happens to be in a disbeliever as well, according to the sharia, that is valid, but it is not from the wording of the verse.

Some people said regarding this verse: "al-insan" is meant only as the disbeliever, and the word "kafur" led them to this. In my view this is rejected, because the attribute of disbelief is not applied to all people, as the word "insan" implies.

"Al-na'ma" (bounty) includes health, wealth, and the like, and "al-darra'" (adversity) is from "al-darr" (harm), and it too is comprehensive. The use of "al-darra'" is often applied to what concerns the body. The phrase "The evils have gone away from me" implies, out of insolence and ignorance, that this is by a favor from God, the Exalted, and the belief that it happened by chance or by some corrupt belief. Otherwise, if one who believes that its going away is by a favor and grace from God were to say it, that would not occur. "Al-sayyi'at" (evils) here means: everything that causes harm in this world.

One group read "lafarih" with a kasra on the ra', and another group read "lafaruh" with a damma on it. This joy is unrestricted, and for this reason it is blamed, since joy is the outpouring of the soul. Joy is not praised in the Qur'an except when it is qualified as being in something good.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Except those who are patient﴾ and the rest of the verse. This exception is connected (muttasil), according to what we have presented, that "al-insan" is general and intended as the genus. But whoever said "it is specific to the disbeliever" said here that the exception is disconnected (munqati'), and this is a weak view in terms of meaning; as for wording, it is sound, and some grammarians have said so. God excepted from those who follow the disposition of man those who have been driven by their religions to patience in the face of hardships and persistence in worshipping God. None of that is in the natural disposition of humans; rather, what drives them to it is love of God, fear of the Hereafter. Patience and righteous action benefit only together with guidance and faith. Then He, blessed and exalted, promised the people of this quality—as encouragement and incitement to it—forgiveness of sins and bestowal of reward and bliss.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 12–13:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Perhaps you would leave out part of what is revealed to you, and your breast would be constrained by it, because they say, "Why has a treasure not been sent down to him, or an angel not come with him?" You are only a warner, and Allah is Guardian over everything.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "Then bring ten surahs like it, invented, and call upon whomever you can besides Allah, if you are truthful."﴾

The occasion of this verse was that the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, if you would stop reviling our gods and foolishing our fathers, we would sit with you and follow you." They also said: "Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it," and similar statements. So Allah addressed His Prophet (ﷺ) in this manner of address, and placed him in that position as a means of answering their statements and nullifying them. The meaning is not that he (ﷺ) intended something of that kind and was then restrained from it, for he never at all wished to leave aside anything of what was revealed to him, nor did his breast become constrained. Rather, his breast would become constrained by their statements, their actions, and their distance from faith.

"Perhaps" (la'alla) here carries the sense of reproach and affirmation (taqrir). "What is revealed to you" is the Qur'an, the Shari'ah, and the call to Allah the Exalted. That included the reviling of their gods, the foolishing of their fathers, or other things. It is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) found the hardship he encountered very grave, and so inclined toward there being a permission from Allah the Exalted to show some leniency toward the disbelievers, and similar beliefs that befit him (ﷺ), as the verses of mutual truce came. He expressed with "constrained" (ḍā'iq) rather than "tight" (ḍayyiq) for the sake of consistency in wording with "leaving" (tārik). Although "ḍayyiq" is more commonly used, since it denotes a permanent attribute, "ḍā'iq" denotes a passing attribute, and it is the one suited here. The pronoun in "by it" refers to "part" (al-ba'ḍ), and it is possible that it refers to "what" (mā).

"Lest" (an) is in the place of the accusative, under the presumption of "out of dislike that". "Treasure" (kanz) here means wealth. This was their request for a sign that would compel faith. Allah, blessed and exalted, did not send the prophets with signs of compulsion; rather He sent them with signs of reflection and reasoning. He did not make the sign of compulsion except for the nations whose punishment He had decreed for their disbelief after a sign of compulsion, like the she-camel for Thamud.

Then Allah consoled him with His saying: ﴿You are only a warner﴾, that is: this measure is what has been entrusted to you, and Allah the Exalted after that is the Guardian who executes the faith of whomever He wills and the disbelief of whomever He wills.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Or do they say﴾ and the verse that follows: this "or" (am) is, according to Sibawayh, in the sense of "rather, and the interrogative alif", as if he had turned away from the first statement and asked in the second, in the sense of affirmation, like their saying: "Is it camels, or sheep?" Iftira' (invention) is more specific than kadhib (lying). It is not used except for what a person fabricates with brazenness and obstinacy, bringing a great and denounced matter. The challenge in this verse was with ten surahs because He qualified them with "invented." He thus widened the measure for them so that the proof would be established to its utmost. For He had already rendered them incapable in another verse with a surah like it, without qualification. So this is a complete equivalence in the hidden matters of the Qur'an, its meanings, its composition, its promise, and its threat. In this verse they were rendered incapable; rather, it was said to them: "Match a measure of it with ten like it in quantity, while the purpose is one, and make it invented; nothing will remain for you except its composition." This is the furthest extent of the widening. The meaning is not: "Match ten surahs with ten," because that would have been the matching of an invented surah with an invented surah without regard to the order of their revelation. This view is supported by the fact that the obligation in the verse of al-Baqara arises from doubt, and only knowledge that they cannot produce a complete equivalent removes doubt. In this verse, the obligation arises from their saying "he has invented it," so they were obligated to produce something like what they said. This does not apply consistently to the verse of Yunus.

Some people said: this (Hud) precedes that (Yunus) in revelation, and it is not valid that they be rendered incapable in one and then obligated to ten, while the two obligations are equal, and it is not valid that a single surah be anything other than invented. The verse of the surah of Yunus concerns the obligation to produce a surah composed upon their saying "he has invented it," and likewise the verse of al-Baqara; their doubt is only that the Qur'an is invented.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The one who says this has not noticed the difference between the two obligations: the complete equivalence in one case, and their being confined to the composition in the other.

As for "whomever" (man) in His saying ﴿whomever you can﴾, it is intended to refer to the gods, the idols, the devils, and everything they used to venerate. His saying ﴿if you are truthful﴾ means: in the claim that the Qur'an is invented.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 14–16:

The Most High said:

﴿And if they do not answer you, then know that it has been sent down with the knowledge of God, and that there is no god but Him. Will you then submit?﴾ ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire; what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾

This verse has two interpretations:

The first: the address is from the Prophet ﷺ to the disbelievers, meaning: if those whom you call upon do not respond with any opposition, and all of you are unable to produce it, then submit at that point and know that it is from God. The statement ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ comes as a firm establishment (of the proof).

The second: the address is from God Most High to the believers, meaning: if the disbelievers do not respond to what they were called to of opposition, then know that this is from God. This is in the sense of: remain upon your knowledge, for they were already aware of that. Mujahid said: the words of the Most High ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ are addressed to the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ.

The words of the Most High ﴿with the knowledge of God﴾ may carry two meanings: first, that it was sent down by His permission and with His knowledge; second, that it was sent down with what God Most High knows of the unseen, as though He meant: "the things known to Him." The statement ﴿Will you then submit?﴾ is an affirmation.

(p-550) The words of the Most High ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world﴾ and the verse that follows: a group said: its outward meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific to the disbelievers. This is the view of Qatada and al-Dahhak. Mujahid said: it refers to the disbelievers and to the people of showing-off (riya') among the believers. ﴿And if they do not answer you, then know that it has been sent down with the knowledge of God, and that there is no god but Him. Will you then submit?﴾ ﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein, and they will not be deprived therein.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones for whom there is nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire; what they did therein will come to nothing, and what they used to do is void.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 17:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is one who has a clear proof from his Lord, and a witness from Him recites it, and before it the Book of Moses was a guide and a mercy? Those believe in it. And whoever of the factions disbelieves in it, the Fire is his promised place. So do not be in doubt about it. Indeed, it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe.﴾

The interpreters (al-mutaʾawwilun) have differed concerning the intended meaning of His saying "Afa-man" (Is one who). One group said: what is meant is the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). Another group said: what is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ) specifically. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Ibn ʿAbbas said: what is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ) and the believers all together.

Likewise, they differed concerning the intended meaning of "al-bayyinah" (the clear proof). One group said: what is meant is the Qur'an, that is, upon clarity by means of the Qur'an. Another group said: what is meant is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the ha' in "al-bayyinah" is for emphasis (mubalaghah), like the ha' in ʿallamah (very learned) and nassabah (very knowledgeable in genealogies).

Likewise, they differed concerning the intended meaning of "al-shahid" (the witness). Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Abu Salih and ʿIkrimah said: it is Jibril (Gabriel).

Al-Husayn ibn ʿAli said: it is Muhammad (ﷺ). Mujahid also said: it is an angel whom Allah appointed to preserve the Qur'an.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that by these expressions He intends Jibril.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: it is the tongue of the Prophet (ﷺ). One group said: it is ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and this was narrated from him. One group said: it is the Injil (Gospel). One group said: it is the Qur'an. One group said: it is the inimitability of the Qur'an (iʿjaz al-Qur'an).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The word "yatluhu" (recites it / follows it) admits of two meanings: in the sense of "yaqra'u" (reads), and in the sense of "yatba'uhu" (follows it). Its usage depends on the difference of opinion mentioned concerning "al-shahid." Let us now arrange the consistency of each view and what it admits.

If we say that "Afa-man" refers to the believers, and then "al-bayyinah" is taken to be Muhammad (ﷺ), it is valid for "al-shahid" to be the Injil, and "yatluhu" then means "yaqra'uhu" (reads it), because the Injil reads of the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also valid for "al-shahid" to be Jibril (peace be upon him), and then "yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu," that is, in conveying the Shariʿah and assisting in it. It is also valid for "al-shahid" to be an angel, and then the pronoun in "minhu" refers to "al-bayyinah," which we have taken to be Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also valid for "al-shahid" to be the Qur'an, and then "yatluhu" means "yatba'uhu," and the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Lord.

If we take "al-bayyinah" to be the Qur'an, on the basis that "Afa-man" refers to the believers, then it is valid for "al-shahid" to be Muhammad (ﷺ), and valid for it to be the Injil, and valid for it to be Jibril and the angel, with "yatluhu" meaning "yaqra'uhu" (reads it). It is also valid for "al-shahid" to be the inimitability (iʿjaz), with "yatluhu" meaning "yatba'uhu," and the pronoun in "minhu" referring to the Qur'an.

If we take "Afa-man" to refer to the Prophet (ﷺ), then "al-bayyinah" is the Qur'an, and "al-shahid" may be the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), or the Injil, or Jibril and the angel, or ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, or the inimitability. "Yatluhu" is then interpreted according to "al-shahid," as we have said. However, this view is weakened by His saying "ulaʾika" (those). For if we take His saying "Afa-man" to refer to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, we do not find in the verse any mentioned people to whom this refers, and we would need to resort to a figurative usage and comparison in the verse, like His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ [al-Talaq: 1], and this is an analogy that is not strong.

The more correct view regarding the verse is that "Afa-man" refers to the believers, or to the believers together with the Prophet (ﷺ) among them, such that "al-shahid" afterwards is not intended to be the Prophet, if we have taken him to be included in "Afa-man." What we have omitted of expanding on this order, careful reflection will quickly reveal, so reflect upon it.

The majority of people read "kitabun" with a nominative (raf') ending, while al-Kalbi and others read "kitaban" with an accusative (nasb) ending. Whoever reads it in the nominative takes "al-shahid" to be the Injil, meaning: it reads the Qur'an, or Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the difference of opinion, and "the Injil" and "from before it" [govern] "the Book of Moses," since in both books there is mention of the Qur'an and mention of Muhammad (ﷺ).

It is also valid to take the nominative subject "al-shahid" to be the Qur'an, and the words then follow consistently. Whoever reads "kitaban" in the accusative takes "al-shahid" to be Jibril (peace be upon him), meaning: Jibril recites the Qur'an, and before the Qur'an was the Book of Moses.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Here an objection is raised: when He said "min qablihi kitabu Musa" or "kitaban" in the accusative according to the two readings, the pronoun in "qablihi" refers to the Qur'an. Why did He not mention the Injil, which is before it, between it and the Book of Moses? The answer: He singled out the Torah for mention because both communities agree that they are from Allah, and the Injil is not so. Therefore, citing what establishes the proof against both groups is more fitting. This accords with the saying of the jinn: ﴿Indeed, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾, and with the saying of the Negus: ﴿Indeed, this and what Moses brought came out of one niche﴾. As for omitting the Injil, it is because their position regarding it contradicts the state of the Qur'an and the Torah. The accusative "imaman" is a circumstantial state (hal) relating to "kitabu Musa." "Al-ahzab" here is intended to mean all the nations. Saʿid ibn Jubayr narrated from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "No one from this community, nor from the Jews and Christians, hears of me and then does not believe in me, except that he enters the Fire." I said: where is the confirmation of this in the Book of Allah? Until I found it in this verse. And whenever I heard a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ), I sought its confirmation in the Book of Allah.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The preferred view among the views on this verse, in my opinion, is that "Afa-man" refers to the believers, or to them together with the Prophet (ﷺ), since the mention of those who have nothing in the Hereafter but the Fire has already preceded, so He followed their mention with mention of others. "Al-bayyinah" is the Qur'an and what it contains. "Al-shahid" is Muhammad (ﷺ) or Jibril, if the Prophet is included in His saying "Afa-man," or the Injil. The pronoun in "yatluhu" refers to "al-bayyinah," the pronoun in "minhu" refers to the Lord, Exalted is He, and the pronoun in "qablihi" refers to "al-bayyinah." Other meanings I have mentioned just now remain possible.

Both the majority and the reading of "fi miryah" (in doubt) have the kasra on the mim, while al-Sulami, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Khattab al-Sadusi read "fi muryah" with a damma on the mim. Both are dialectal forms meaning doubt. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to the state of the disbelievers, whose promised place is the Fire. The rest of the verse is clear.

In this verse there is an implied contrast (muʿadalah mahdhufah), which the apparent wording requires, its estimated form being: "Is one who is upon a clear proof from his Lord like one who disbelieves in Allah and denies His prophets?" and similar to this in the sense of omission is His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which mountains were moved, or by which the earth was split, or by which the dead were made to speak...﴾ [al-Ra'd: 31], meaning: this Qur'an would be [this one]. And of this is the saying of the poet:

"By Allah, if anything other than you had come to us from His Messenger, we would have rejected it, but we found no way to repel you."

The estimated sense: we would have rejected it and not paid attention to it.

The commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 18–20:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God? Those will be presented before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Ah, the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers,"﴾ ﴿those who bar [others] from the way of God and seek to make it crooked, and they are, of the Hereafter, disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Those will not be able to escape in the earth, and they had no protectors other than God. Their punishment will be doubled. They were not able to hear, and they did not see.﴾

His saying, "And who": it is an interrogative (istifham) with the meaning of affirmation (taqrir), as if He said: no one is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie. By "who" is meant the disbelievers who call upon another god along with God and invent falsehoods without any basis. His saying, "Those will be presented before their Lord," is an expression for publicly exposing them and disgracing them for their humiliation; otherwise, every human being is presented before God on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, "and the witnesses will say": one group said: it means the martyrs (shuhada') from among the prophets and the angels, so His saying, "These are the ones who lied against their Lord," comes as information about them and as testimony against them. Another group said: "the witnesses" (al-ashhad) means those who bear witness, and it means all of creation, and in this is a public exposure of them. A hadith has been related in this sense: "Indeed, no one will be disgraced on the Day of Resurrection except that all who attended the gathering will know that." In this case, His saying, "These," according to this interpretation, is an interrogative about them and a confirmation concerning them, as you say when you see a criminal who has been punished: "This is the one who did such-and-such," even if you already knew that. It is also possible that it is information about them. His saying, "Ah" (ala) is an opening of speech (istiftah kalam). "Curse" (al-la'na) is distancing (al-ib'ad). "Who" (alladhina) is an attribute (na't) of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimin). It is also possible to read it in the nominative, with the implied meaning "they are those who." As for "they bar" (yasuddun), it may be taken as transitive, in the sense: they bar people and prevent them from the way of God; and it may be taken as intransitive, in the sense: they themselves turn away (ya'ridun). "The way of God" is His law (shari'ah). "And they seek it" (wa yabghunaha) means: they seek for it, as you say, "I sought for you good or evil," meaning I sought for you. "Crooked" ('iwajan), according to this, is an object. It is also possible that the meaning is: "and they seek the way with crookedness," meaning they will never be guided; and so "crooked," according to this, is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). "Crookedness" (al-'iwaj) is deviation and inclination that leads to corruption. He repeated His saying, "they are," for emphasis (ta'kid), and it is a clause in the position of the predicate of the first subject (khabar al-ibtida' al-awwal). This is not the place of separation (fasl), because separation occurs only between two definites, or between a definite and an indefinite that approximates a definite, since it distinguishes between what follows being an attribute or a predicate and makes it purely a predicate. "Unable to escape" (mu'jizin) means: escapers who cannot be overtaken. The mention of "the earth" is specified because the human being's activity and enjoyment are only in it, and it is his limit; he cannot pass beyond it. His saying, "and they had no protectors other than God," may have two meanings:

One: that He negates that they have any protector or helper, whoever he may be.

The second: that He intends to describe the idols and gods as not being protectors in reality, even though they themselves believe that they are protectors.

Then He informed that their punishment will be doubled on the Day of Resurrection, meaning it will be intensified until it is twice what it was. "Will be doubled" (yudaʻafu) is a new independent verb and is not an attribute.

His saying, "They were not able to hear, and they did not see," may have five aspects:

One of them: that He describes these disbelievers with this attribute, in the sense that God has sealed upon them with this, so they do not hear in a way that benefits them, and they likewise do not see.

The second: that He described them with this because of their hatred toward the Prophet (ﷺ), so they are not able to force themselves to listen to him or look at him. This is supported by the case of Tufayl ibn 'Amr, who stuffed his ears with cotton, and by the refusal of the Quraysh at the time of al-Hudaybiyyah to hear what was conveyed to them of the words of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until their elders turned them back from that.

The third: that He described with this the idols and gods, which He negated, according to the earlier interpretation, from being protectors.

In these aspects, "ma" is a negation particle (nafiyah).

The fourth: that the reading is: "Their punishment will be doubled for what they were," with the preposition deleted, and "ma" is then a verbal particle (masdariyyah). This is an opinion that involves forcing (tahammul). It was stated by al-Farra', who linked it to the saying: "I will repay you for what you did to me."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 21–24:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿Those are the ones who have lost their souls, and what they used to fabricate has strayed away from them.﴾ ﴿Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds and humbled themselves before their Lord — those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever.﴾ ﴿The parable of the two groups is like the blind and the deaf versus the seeing and the hearing. Are they equal in likeness? Will you not then be reminded?﴾

﴿They have lost their souls﴾ by the obligation of punishment upon them, and there is no loss greater than the loss of the soul. And "wa-ḍalla" (and it strayed away) means: it perished, and they did not find it where they had hoped for it. And "lā jaram" is a compound expression made up of "lā" and "jaram," and the two were built together.

The meaning of "lā jaram": it is true (ḥaqq). This is the view of Sibawayh and al-Khalil. Some grammarians said: its meaning is: there is no doubt, there is no question, and there is no escape, and this has been narrated from al-Khalil. Al-Zajjaj said: "lā" is a rejection of them and of what preceded it of all that came before it, and "jaram" means: earned, i.e., their deed earned ﴿that they in the Hereafter are the greatest losers﴾. So the position of "anna" — according to Sibawayh's view — is in the nominative case; and its position according to al-Zajjaj's view is in the accusative case. Al-Kisa'i said its meaning is: no turning away and no prevention.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So "jaram," according to this, is from the meaning of cutting; you say: "jaramtu," i.e., I cut off. And according to al-Zajjaj's line of interpretation, it is from earning, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"The jarima (earned portion) of a hawk on the top of a cliff — you see for the bones what it has gathered, a carcass."

And the jarima of a people is their earner.

As for the saying of the poet:

"Indeed I stabbed Abu Umayma with a stab; Fazara, after it, earned that they would be angry."

It admits of both meanings, and the meaning of the verse differs accordingly.

There are dialectal variants of "lā jaram": some Arabs say: "lā dhā jaram," some say: "lā an dhā jaram," some say: "lā 'an dhā jaram," and some say: "lā jar," dropping the mīm due to its frequent use.

As for "akhbatū": it was said its meaning is: they humbled themselves (khasha'ū), said by Qatada; it was said: they turned penitently (anābū), said by Ibn 'Abbas; it was said: they became tranquil (ṭama'annū), said by Mujahid; it was said: they feared, also said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. These statements are close to one another in some respects. The root of the word is from "al-khabt," which is the open, bare, level wasteland of the earth. So the one who is "mukhbit" in the wasteland is as though he has been exposed, submitted, and remains without protection, and so the one who is humbled and humble is likened to that. It was also said: it is derived from it for its levelness and tranquility. And His saying "ilā rabbihim" — it was said: it carries the meaning of "li" (for), i.e., they humbled themselves for their Lord. It was also said: the meaning is that they made their aim, by their humbling, directed to their Lord. And "al-farīqān" (the two groups) are the disbelievers and the believers: the disbeliever is likened to the blind and the deaf, and the believer is likened to the seeing and the hearing; so it is, according to this, an illustration by two examples. Some interpreters said: the estimate is "like the blind-deaf and the seeing-hearing," and the conjunctive waw has entered, as you say: "Zayd the intelligent and the generous came to me," and you mean one and the same person; so it is, according to this, an illustration by one example.

"Mathalan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). It may also be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl).

﴿And We certainly sent Noah to his people: "Indeed I am to you a clear warner."﴾ ﴿"That you not worship except Allah. Indeed I fear for you the punishment of a painful day."﴾ ﴿So the eminent ones among those who disbelieved from his people said: "We do not see you except as a human being like ourselves, and we do not see those who follow you except the lowest of us, at first glance; and we do not see that you have any merit over us. Rather, we think you are liars."﴾

(p-561) This is a verse of narrative containing an illustration for Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs, and an informing of Muhammad ﷺ that he is not an innovation among the messengers.

It is narrated that Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger to the people. It is narrated that Idris was a prophet from the children of Adam, but he was not sent as a messenger. So the messengership of Noah was only to his people, like the other prophets; as for the universal messengership, it was not except for Muhammad ﷺ.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Hamza recited "Inni" with a kasra on the alif, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i recited "Anni" with a fatha on the alif. The kasra is on the basis of an implied verb of saying, and the meaning is: he said to them: ﴿Indeed I am to you a clear warner﴾; then his saying "that you not worship" (alla ta'budu) comes as an object of "We sent" (arsalna), meaning: We sent Noah with "that you not worship except Allah," and the statement "Indeed I am to you a clear warner" is interposed in the middle of the speech. The fatha is on the basis of "arsalna" governing "anni," meaning: with "that I am to you a clear warner." Abu 'Ali said: In this reading there is a shift from the third person (ghayba) to the second person (mukhatabah).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is open to question; rather, it is a relating of his address to them in speech, and this is not a true shift from the third person to the second person. Had the wording been "an andhirhum" (warn them) or similar, that would have been correct.

"Nadhir" (warner) is for guarding against what is disliked, by making it known and alerting to it; and "mubin" is from abana, yubinu (to make clear).

His saying, the Exalted: "that you not worship except Allah" is evident that they used to worship idols and the like, and that is clear in other than this verse. "Alim" means "mu'lim" (painful), and it is attributed to the day, while its proper attribution is to the punishment, by way of metonymy (tajawwuz), since the punishment occurs in the day; it is like their saying: "a fasting day" and "a standing night."

"Al-mala'" is the assembly, and most often of a tribe, a city and the like; and the nobles are called "mala'," since they are the pillars of the assembly and those who fill its place in opinions and affairs; and every large group is a "mala'."

When Noah said to them, "Indeed I am to you a warner," they said: "We do not see you except as a human being like ourselves," meaning: by Allah, God does not send a messenger from among mankind; so they denied what is permissible for Allah, the Exalted.

"Al-aradhil" is the plural of "aradhal" (lowest). It was said: it is the plural of "aradhul," and "aradhil" is the plural of "radhl." On this basis, the required form would be "aradhil," and when the yā' is retained in the plural of "sayraf," it is even more fitting that it not be removed in the place where it is deserved. They are the basest of people, those who have no morals, and who care not what they say or what is said to them.

The majority recited "badiya al-ra'y" with a yā' without a hamza, from "bada yabdu"; and it is possible that it is from "bada'a" with facilitation (tashil). Abu 'Amr and 'Isa al-Thaqafi recited "badi'a al-ra'y" with a hamza, from "bada'a yabda'u."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Between the two readings there is a difference in meaning that reflection yields, and I have left off lengthening it by elaborating it. The Arabs say: "Amma badi'a bad'in fa-inni ahmadu Allah" and "wa-amma badiya badiyin," without a hamza in both, and the rajiz said:

"It has become for my uncle that my resemblance is 'badiya badi' (at first sight), and my tongue and hand have become for the stallion camel."

And another said:

"And a sudden affliction has overtaken me, 'badi badi'."

The majority recited "al-ra'y" with a hamza, and Abu 'Amr recited without the hamza. "Badiya" is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it is valid for the active participle to be an adverb as it is valid in "qarib" and similar, and "fa'il" and "fa'il" are always interchangeable with one meaning, and in the verbal noun as in your saying: "jahda nafsi uhibbu kadha wa kadha."

The connection of his saying "badiya al-ra'y" admits six aspects:

The first: that it connects with "naraka" (we see you), at first look and least reflection; and that is "badiya al-ra'y," meaning: none but those who follow you are our lowest.

The second: that it connects with his saying "ittaba'aka" (followed you), meaning: and we do not see that those who followed you followed you at first sight except the lowest. Then, on this basis, his saying "badiya al-ra'y" admits two meanings: One of them: that it intends: they followed you in the outward appearance of their matter, and perhaps their inner states are not with you.

The second: that they followed you at first look and by superficial opinion without reflection; had you examined them, they would not have followed you. And in this aspect there is a censure of opinion that is not based on transmission.

The third aspect of the connection of his saying "badiya al-ra'y" is that it connects with his saying "aradhilun" (our lowest), meaning: those who are our lowest at first look at them, and by "badiya al-ra'y" this is known of them.

It is possible that their saying "badiya al-ra'y" is a description from them of Noah, meaning: you claim greatness while your opinion is exposed, with no judgment (hasafa) for you; and its accusative is as a circumstantial (hal) and as an attribute (sifa).

It is possible that it is an interjection within the speech, addressed to Muhammad ﷺ. All of this yields six meanings, and it is permissible to connect it in this aspect with "qala" (he said).

And the meaning of: ﴿and we do not see that you have any merit over us﴾ is: there is nothing for which you deserve to be followed and obeyed. Then he said: ﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾. It is possible that they addressed Noah and those who believed with him among his people, meaning: you are liars in your affirming this liar, and your saying that he is a messenger prophet. And it is possible that they addressed Noah alone, in which case it is of the type of His saying: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce [women]﴾ [al-Talaq: 1].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 28–30:

The Exalted said:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, but it has been made obscure to you, shall we compel you to accept it while you are averse to it?"﴾ ﴿"And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it. My reward is only from Allah. And I will not drive away those who have believed; indeed, they will meet their Lord. But I see you as a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿"And O my people, who would help me against Allah if I drove them away? Will you not then take heed?"﴾

It is as if he said: "Tell me, if Allah has guided me and misguided you, shall I compel you to the guidance while you are averse to it and turn away from it?" His interrogation in this verse, both the first and the second, is for the purpose of affirmation (taqrir, establishing a fact by way of a question). The expression of Noah, peace be upon him, in his language, indicated the meaning that subsists in the self (al-ma'na al-qa'im bi-nafsihi). This is what is understood from this Arabic expression, and on this basis it is correct to say "such and such," since speech is that which conveys the meaning that subsists in the self.

His saying ﴿upon a clear proof﴾ means: upon a matter that is manifest and evident. The ha' in "bayyina" (bayyinah) is for emphasis (mubalaghah, intensification), as in 'allamah (very knowing) and nassabah (very skilled in genealogies). "His giving him mercy" is His guiding him to the clear proof. What is indicated by all of this is prophethood and the revealed law. His saying ﴿from Himself﴾ is an emphasis (ta'kid), as in His saying: ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. Its benefit is to remove the possibility of shared meaning, even if by way of metaphor (isti'arah, metaphor).

Most of the reciters read "fa-'ummiyat" (فَعُمِّيَتْ). For this there are two meanings:

The first: it was hidden. For this reason the clouds are called al-'ama', because they conceal what is in them, just as they are called al-ghamam, because they cover it. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah was before He created things in 'ama'." The second meaning: the intended sense is "fa-'amitum antum 'anha" (you became blind to it), but it has been inverted (qalb, transposition of the terms), as the Arabs say: "I put the cap on my head" (adkhaltu al-qalansuwata fi ra'si). From this is the saying of the poet:

"You see the bull in it putting his head into the shade, while the rest of him is exposed to the sun entirely."

Abu 'Ali said: This is among what is inverted, since there is no difficulty in it. And in the Qur'an: ﴿So do not think that Allah will fail His promise to His messengers﴾ [Ibrahim: 47].

Hafs, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "fa-'ummiyat" (فَعُمِّيَتْ) with a damma on the 'ain and a shaddah on the mim, in the passive form of the verb. This only occurs with concealment, and the inversion mentioned is also possible.

Al-A'mash and others read "fa-'ammaha 'alaykum" (فَعَمّاها عَلَيْكُمْ). Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash narrated from Ibn Wathhab "wa-'amiyat" (وَعَمِيَتْ) with a waw, with light (unshaddened) pronunciation.

His saying ﴿shall we compel you to accept it﴾ intends compulsion by force, such as fighting and the like. As for the obligation (ilzam al-ijab), it is established. Al-Nahhas said: its meaning is "we make it obligatory upon you," but his statement about this is an error. In the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, it is "shall we compel you to accept it from the side of ourselves" (min shatri anfusina), and its meaning is "of our own accord" (min talqa' anfusina). It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he recited it as "from the side of our hearts" (min shatri qulubina).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it﴾, the pronoun in "'alayhi" refers to the conveying of the message.

His saying: ﴿And I will not drive away those who have believed﴾ indicates that they asked him to drive away the weak who hastened to believe in him, similar to what the Quraysh proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), namely to drive away his followers in Makkah who were not from the Quraysh.

His saying: ﴿indeed, they will meet their Lord﴾ is an alert to the return to Allah and the meeting with His recompense. The meaning is: He will convey them to their right in My presence if I wrong them by driving them away. Then he described them as ignorant for making such a proposal and similar ones.

His saying: ﴿And O my people, who would help me against Allah﴾ is an interrogation in the sense of affirmation and reproach: that is, there is no helper who would repel from me the punishment of Allah if I wronged them by driving them away from the good that they accepted. Then he made them stand (before their own consciences) by his saying ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾, and he set before them the reflection that leads to the soundness of this argument.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 31–32:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And I do not say to you that with me are the treasures of Allah, nor do I know the unseen, nor do I say that I am an angel, nor do I say to those whom your eyes look down upon that Allah will never give them any good. Allah knows best what is in their souls. Indeed, I would then be among the wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us and you have multiplied your disputation with us, so bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful."﴾

His saying, ﴿And I do not say﴾, is a continuation of His saying, ﴿I do not ask you for wealth in return for it﴾ [Hud: 29]. The meaning of this verse is: I do not feign towards you, nor do I undertake anything other than what Allah has qualified me for. So I do not say, "With me are the treasures of Allah," meaning the power by which a thing comes into existence after it was non-existent. It is possible that some of the existing things, such as winds and water, and the like, are numerous by Allah's originating them, and if that is called, in a figurative sense, "stored," then it is apt. Do you not see what is related concerning the wind of 'Ad, that He released upon them from the wind only the amount of a ring's hoop, and had it been the size of a bull's nostril it would have destroyed the earth. It is also narrated that the wind rebelled against the angels entrusted with its measure, and therefore Allah described it with rebellion (ʿutuw). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: it rebelled against the treasurers. So this and similar reports imply that there are treasuries. Then he said, ﴿nor do I know the unseen﴾, then he descended from these two to say, ﴿nor do I say that I am an angel﴾. The apparent meaning of this verse is the superiority of the angel over the human being, and over the Prophet ﷺ, and this is a matter of difference of opinion. The apparent meanings of the Qur'an are in accordance with what we have said. Even if we take his saying, ﴿nor do I say that I am an angel﴾ in the sense that had he said, "nor do I say that I am a star or the like," the path of preference would vanish, but the apparent meaning is what we have mentioned.

"Tazdari" (تَزْدَرِي) its root is "tazta ri" (تَزْتَرِي), a form of "iftaʿala" from zara, yazri, and the meaning of "tazdari" is: you despise. "Al-khayr" (الخَيْر, good) here appears to be the good of the Hereafter, except that their looking down may be due to (p-567) poverty, in which case "al-khayr" would be wealth. Some exegetes have said: wherever Allah mentions "khayr" in the Qur'an, it means wealth. In this statement there is excess, and what seems more appropriate to say is that wherever "khayr" is mentioned, wealth is included in it.

His saying, ﴿Allah knows best what is in their souls﴾, is a submission to Allah, mighty and majestic, meaning: I do not judge them by any of this; rather Allah judges them by that, and His judgment comes into the realm of existence. Allah, who knows what is in their souls, recompenses them accordingly. Some interpreters said: it is a rebuttal of their saying, "Only our lowest-ranking people have followed you," based on what appears from them.

The shaykh, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As previously mentioned in some interpretations of that verse a moment ago, the meaning is: it is not I who judge them to have no good, based on your assumption about them that their inner selves are not like their outward appearances. Allah, mighty and majestic, knows best what is in their souls. Then he said, "Indeed, I would then," if I did that, "be among the wrongdoers," those who place a thing in other than its proper place.

His exalted saying, ﴿They said, "O Noah, you have disputed with us"﴾, the verse's meaning: this argument has gone on too long from you. It is the exchange of proofs, contention, and confrontation with statements until victory occurs. It is derived from "jadl," which is the intensity of twisting; from it comes "a twisted rope" (ḥablun majdūl), meaning tightly twisted, and from it it is said of the falcon "ajdal" because of the strength of its build and the twisting of its limbs. "Al-jidal" (الجِدال) is a form (fiʿāl), the verbal noun of "fāʿala," which occurs between two parties; the verbal noun of "fāʿala" comes in the patterns fiʿāl, fayʿāl and mufāʿala, so the yā' of fayʿāl was dropped and discarded. Among disputation is what is praiseworthy, namely when it is with a hostile unbeliever who is in his stronghold and one hopes through disputation that he will be guided, and from this is this verse, and from it His saying, ﴿And dispute with them in the way that is best﴾ [An-Nahl: 125], along with other examples. Among disputation is what is disliked, which is what occurs among Muslims, some against others, in seeking the reasons of the sharia and imagining what the Law reports of Allah's power; the Prophet ﷺ forbade this, and the scholars disliked it, and Allah is the One sought for help.

Ibn 'Abbas recited: "qad jadaltana fa-aktharta jadalana" (قَدْ جادَلْتَنا فَأكْثَرْتَ جَدَلَنا) without an alif and with a fatha on the jim, mentioned by Abu Hatim.

The intended meaning of their saying, ﴿so bring us what you threaten us with﴾, is the punishment and destruction. The second object of "taʿiduna" (تَعِدُنا) is implied, its estimated form being: "bima taʿiduna-hu" (what you promise us). And since the context implies punishment, it is permissible to use the word "promise" (waʿd) for it.

That is because they said: "The Qur'an is an invention, and he invented this story about Nūḥ." So the verse was revealed concerning that.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, if it were authentic with a chain of narration, must be stopped at. Otherwise, it is possible that it refers to the matter of Nūḥ, peace be upon him, and the coherence of the verse remains consistent. The pronoun in *iftarāhu* would then return to the punishment with which he threatened them, or to all of his reports. The fabrication (*iftirā'*) is attributed to the punishment because it occurs through reporting it. The meaning: "Or do these disbelievers say: Nūḥ invented this threat of punishment and wanted to terrify us with it?" Then the rest of the verse continues in this manner.

*Am* here is the one that means *bal* (rather). *Al-ijrām* is the verbal noun of *ajrama yujrimu*, when he committed (a wrong). It is said *jarama* and *ajrama* have the same meaning. From this is the saying of the poet:

*An outcast of his tribe and a hostage to a sin,*
*for what my hand has committed and my tongue has wrought.*

**The saying of the Most High:** ﴿He said: "Only Allah will bring it to you, if He wills, and you cannot escape."﴾ ﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wish to counsel you, if Allah intends to lead you astray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: "If I have invented it, then upon me is my crime, and I am innocent of what you commit as crime."﴾

**The meaning:** That is not in my hand, nor is its bringing about up to me. Rather, it is in the hand of Allah, and He is the One who brings it, if He wills and when He wills. You are not, in your strength, in the position of one who escapes or takes refuge with one who can save him. Rather, you are in the grip of power and under the subjugation of the one who holds dominion. My counsel does not benefit, and my wish for good for you does not suffice, if Allah, the Exalted, has willed for you misguidance (*ighwa'*), error (*ḍalāl*) and destruction (*ihlāk*). The second condition is a parenthetical interjection within the speech, and in it there is eloquence in the combination of the two wills, and that the will of human beings is not sufficient. The attachment of this condition is to "my counsel," and the attachment of the other is to "will not benefit." Counsel (*nuṣḥ*) is closing the gap in the opinion of the one counselled and mending it. It is derived from *naṣaḥa al-thawb*, meaning he sewed the garment. The *minṣaḥ* is the needle, and the sewn garment is called *minṣaḥ* and *naṣṣāḥ*.

A group said: the meaning of His saying *yughwiyakum* is *yuḍillakum* (lead you astray), from their saying *ghawā al-rajul yaghwā* (the man went astray). From it is the saying of the poet:

*Whoever meets good, people praise his affair,*
*and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error.*

If this is the meaning of the word, then in the verse there is a proof against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who say that misguidance comes only from the servant.

Another group said: the meaning of His saying *yughwiyakum* is *yuhlikukum* (destroy you). *Al-ghawā* is sickness and destruction. In the dialect of Ṭayyi', it is said: "So-and-so became *ghawiyan*," meaning sick. *Al-ghawā* is also the bloating of the suckling calf (*bashm al-faṣīl*), as stated by Ya'qūb in *al-Iṣlāḥ*. It was said: it is its lack of milk until it dies of hunger, as stated by al-Farrā' and related by al-Ṭabarī. It is said *ghawā yaghwā*. Al-Zahrāwī related that it is the one whose milk has been cut off until he almost perishes, but has not yet perished. If this is the meaning of the word, the point of dispute between Ahl al-Sunna (the people of the Sunna) and the Mu'tazila disappears, and the argument against them remains by what is clearer than this verse, such as His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide, He expands his breast to Islam﴾ [al-An'ām: 125], and similar verses.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I believe that Makkī (Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib) thought the Mu'tazila have a connection and a compelling argument with this interpretation, so he refuted it and went to excess, to the point that he denied that *ghawā* in the sense of destruction exists in the language of the Arabs.
