Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 36–37:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not grieve over what they have been doing."﴾ ﴿And construct the ship under Our eyes and Our inspiration, and do not address Me concerning those who have wronged; indeed, they are to be drowned.﴾

Abu al-Barahsam recited "wa-ūḥiya" (and it was revealed) with a fatḥa on the hamza, attributing the verb to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and "innahu" with a kasra on the hamza. It was said that this (revelation) to Noah came after the disbelief of the generations following one another had prolonged its hold over him. A man would bring his son to him and say: "My son, do not believe this old man; so my father and my grandfather bequeathed him to me as a liar and a madman." This was related by ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and others. This verse is the one that despaired Noah, peace be upon him, of his people. It is narrated that when this was revealed to him, he supplicated, saying: ﴿My Lord, leave not upon the earth from among the disbelievers a single dweller﴾ [Nuh: 26].

"Tabtaʾis" derives from "al-bu's" (distress), in the form taftaʿila, and its meaning is: do not grieve yourself. From this is the saying of the poet, who is Labid ibn Rabiʿa:

In a gathering like the ewes of Ṣāra, / they grieve over what we have suffered.

Ṣāra: a place name.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Regarding the matter of Noah, peace be upon him, there is an apparent contradiction between the verses and the hadiths, and we ought to resolve the discussion concerning it. The apparent sense of his affair is that he, peace be upon him, supplicated against the disbelievers in general from all nations, and did not single out his own people to the exclusion of others. The narrations and the books of tafsir are unanimous that the drowning reached all the inhabitants of the earth and the water covered all of it, as Ibn ʿAbbas and others said. This entails the command to Noah to carry pairs of animals, and had it not been for fear of the extinction of their species from all the earth, that would not have been. Therefore it is not consistent for us to say that there was no one on earth at that time other than the people of Noah, because Noah must have been sent to all people. It is firmly established that this distinction is specific to Muhammad ﷺ, by his saying: "I have been given five things that none before me was given." So we must affirm that many nations existed at that time. If that is so, how did they deserve punishment in their totality, when Noah was not sent to all of them? Here we would estimate that Allah, Exalted, sent messengers to them before Noah, and they disbelieved them and their disbelief persisted; but we find the hadith stating that Noah is the first of the messengers to the people of the earth. Nor can we say that they were punished without a messenger, while we find in the Qur'an: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15].

The resolving interpretation that frees us from all of this is to say: Noah, peace be upon him, was the first messenger sent to disbelievers among the people of the earth, to reform creation, to exert himself in conveying the message, and to bear hardship from people, according to what is established in the hadith. Then we say: he was sent specifically to his own people, for conveyance, supplication and warning; and nations remained on earth to whom he was not charged to speak. Thus the specificity for Muhammad ﷺ is sound. Then we say: the nations to whom he was not sent to address, if they were in a state of disbelief and worship of idols, while the proofs of Allah, Exalted, were set up and exposed to reflection, and they were able to reflect by means of their perception, and the Shariʿa, through the sending of Noah, was present and established, then reflection became obligatory for them, and by abandoning it they became in the position of those who deserve punishment. For this is a messenger who was sent, even if he was not sent to them specifically. Do you not see that the wording of the verse is: ﴿And We would not punish until We send a messenger﴾ [al-Isra: 15], that is, until We bring him into existence? Because the sending of prophets to specific peoples is in the sense of fighting and severity, whereas in terms of offering counsel and accepting those who believe, people are all equal in that. Noah remained for a thousand years less fifty years calling to Allah, so it is impossible that his prophethood did not reach the near and the far, and the punishment of all by drowning came after the sending of a messenger, namely Noah, peace be upon him. And nothing from the hadith or the verses contradicts us along with these interpretations, and Allah is the Granter of success to what is correct.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And construct the ship﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿so do not grieve﴾. Al-Fulk is the ship, and its plural is also fulk. It is not a word that is used for both singular and plural; rather it is the form fuʿl, which was pluralized on the pattern fuʿl. Just as faʿal may be pluralized on fuʿl, like asad and usd, so fuʿl may be pluralized on fuʿl. Thus the apparent form of the plural in it is like the apparent form of a singular, yet it is not that; this is shown by the degree of the dual between them, for you say: fulk, fulkān, and fulk. The vowel in the plural is like the ḍamma of the ṣād when you call "yā manṣū" meaning "yā manṣūr," elided on the dialect of one who says "yā ḥār" with a ḍamma; for the ḍamma of the ṣād is in pronunciation like the ḍamma of the original, but it is not so in ruling.

His saying: ﴿under Our eyes﴾ may, as far as interpretation goes, mean in Our sight and within Our perception; so it is an expression for perception, care and protection. The plural of "eyes" here is for magnification, not for multiplicity, as Exalted is He said: ﴿So excellent are the Able Ones﴾ [al-Mursalat: 23]. Thus the meaning of "eyes" in this and in other places returns to the meaning of "eye" in His saying: ﴿and so that you may be raised under My eye﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39]. All of this is an expression for perception and its encompassing of what is perceived. He, blessed and exalted, is far above senses, likeness and modality; there is no lord other than Him. It is also possible that His saying "under Our eyes" means by Our angels, whom We made as eyes over the places of your protection and aid, in which case the plural is for multiplicity. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif recited "bi-aʿyunnā" with assimilation.

His saying "and Our inspiration" means: and Our teaching you the form of the work through inspiration. It was narrated about this that when Noah, peace be upon him, did not know how to build the ship, Allah revealed to him: build it on the model of the breast of a bird, and other things that Noah knew of its making. It was also narrated that it was square in shape, long in height, narrow at the top, and that its purpose was preservation, not speed of movement. The hadith that states it was like the breast of a bird is sounder, and its meaning is clearer, for if it were square it would not be a ship but merely a container; and Allah, Exalted, described it as running upon the sea. In the hadith: "The one who steered Noah's ship, peace be upon him, was Jibril, peace be upon him," and the rāzz is the one in charge of the operation of ships. As for whoever interpreted "and Our inspiration" as "by Our command to you," that is weak, because His saying "construct the ship" suffices without it.

And ﴿those who have wronged﴾ are his people who turned away from guidance until the retribution overtook them. Ibn Jurayj said: in this verse Allah forbade Noah in advance from interceding on their behalf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 38–40:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿And he began building the ark, and whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him. He said: If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock.﴾ ﴿Soon you will know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and upon whom will descend a lasting punishment.﴾ ﴿Until when Our command came and the oven boiled over, We said: Load into it two of each kind, and your family, except for those against whom the word has already gone forth, and those who believe.﴾ And none believed with him except a few.

The estimate: he began to build (fa-shara'a yasna'u), so the present tense of the future is related (ḥukiyat ḥāl al-istiqbāl), since their passing by him occurred during it. Ibn 'Abbas said: Nuh built the ark in the land of Damascus, and took its wood from Lebanon and its wood from al-Shamshad, which is al-Baqs. It is also narrated that its wood was teak (al-sāj), and that Nuh planted it until it grew up over forty years. It is narrated that the length of the ship was one thousand two hundred cubits and its width six hundred cubits; this was mentioned by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. It was also said: its length was three hundred cubits and its width fifty cubits, and its height in the sky was thirty cubits; this was mentioned by Qatadah. Other things were narrated that are not established, so I have omitted mention of them. Al-Tabari mentioned the narration of the revival of 'Isa ibn Maryam for Sam ibn Nuh and his asking him about the matter of the ship, and he mentioned that it had three decks: a deck for people, a deck for animals, and a deck for birds, along with other things in a long narration.

"Al-mala'" here means the group. "Sakhiru" means: they considered him ignorant (istajhalūhu). This considering him ignorant, if the matter was as mentioned, that they had not previously seen a ship and none existed, then the reason for considering him ignorant is clear, and the commentaries are unanimous on this. Even if ships were known at that time, they considered him ignorant in that he was building it in a place not near the sea. It is narrated that they used to say to him: "Have you become a carpenter after prophethood?"

As for His words: ﴿then we mock you﴾, al-Tabari said: he means: in the Hereafter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The words may also bear—indeed, this is more probable—the meaning: we mock you now, that is, we consider you ignorant, because of our knowledge of your state of deception regarding Allah, the Exalted, and your being on the verge of His punishment. Then His words ﴿Soon you will know﴾ came as a threat. Al-sukhr means considering someone ignorant together with ridicule, and its verbal noun is sukhra with a dammah on the sin; the verbal noun of al-sukhrah and al-taskhir is sikhra with a kasrah.

"The disgracing punishment" is drowning, and "the lasting punishment" is the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Zahrawi reported that he read "wa-yaḥullu" with a dammah on the ha', and "wa-yaḥillu" with a kasrah on it, meaning "and it is obligatory." "Man" is in the accusative position governed by "ta'lamūna." It is permissible for "ta'lamūna" to be like "ta'rifūna" in transitivity to one object, and it is also permissible that the transitivity be to two objects with only one being mentioned.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Until when Our command came﴾ and the verse. "Al-amr" here may be the singular of "al-umūr" (matters), and it may be the verbal noun of amara, so its meaning is: Our command to the water to gush forth, or to the clouds to be sent, or to the angels to act accordingly, and similar things that are determined in the event. "Fāra" means: gushed forth with force. The people differed about "al-tannūr." One group—and they are the majority—including Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and others, said: it is the bread oven in which fire is kindled. Another group said: this was a sign which Allah made for Nuh, meaning: when the oven boils over, board the ship. It is likely that the aspect of the sign is that if the place where fire is kindled boils over with water, then elsewhere it would boil over even more strongly and more so. It is narrated that the oven was that of Adam, peace be upon him, which reached Nuh, and he used to kindle fire in it. Al-Naqqash said: the name of the place where fire is kindled is tannur in every language. Ibn Qutaybah in al-Adab mentioned something similar from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched.

It was also said: the place of Nuh's oven was in India; it was said: it was at the site of the mosque of Kufa; it was said: it was in the region of Kufa, as said by al-Sha'bi and Mujahid; it was said: it was on the western side of the qibla of the mosque in Kufa. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and 'Ikrimah said: al-tannur is the surface of the earth, and it is called the oven of the earth. Qatadah said: al-tannur is the high parts of the earth. Another group said: al-tannur is a spring in the region of al-Jazira. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: al-tannur is the gathering place of the water of the ship, from which water gushed while it was still dry. Another group said: al-tannur is the dawn; the meaning: when dawn breaks, board the ship. This is an opinion narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, except that morphology weakens it, since it would have required "al-tannur" to be... Another group said: the speech is metaphorical, and he intended only the overwhelming of the water and the manifestation of the punishment, as the Prophet ﷺ said regarding the intensity of battle: "Ḥamiya al-waṭīs" (the fight has become hot). Al-waṭīs is also the place where fire is kindled, so there is no difference between ḥamiya and fāra, since both are used of fire. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They hear from it a roaring while it boils over﴾ [al-Mulk: 7]. So there is no difference between al-waṭīs and al-tannur.

Hafs, from 'Asim, read: "min kullin zawjayni ithnayni" with tanwin on "kullin," and the others read: "man kulli zawjayni" with "kulli" in construct with "zawjayni." Whoever reads with tanwin omits the genitive noun; the estimate is: "from every animal or the like," and "al-ḥaml" (carrying) governs "zawjayn," and His words "ithnayn" came as emphasis, as in: "ilāhayn ithnayn." Whoever reads with the construct makes "al-ḥaml" govern "ithnayn," and His words "zawjayn" are in the sense of generality, that is, of everything that has a mate. This is the meaning of His words ﴿min kulli zawjayn﴾, as said by Abu 'Ali and others. If we estimate the meaning as: "carry from every two existing pairs, two," it would necessitate carrying four of each kind. The word "zawj" is used in the well-known speech of the Arabs for one of a pair, so it is said: "this is the zawj of this," and "they two are zawjan." **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 41–42:**

Allah the Exalted said:

﴿And he said: "Embark in it; in the name of Allah is its course and its mooring. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful."﴾ ﴿And it sailed with them through waves like mountains, and Noah called out to his son, who was apart: "O my son, embark with us and do not be with the disbelievers."﴾

The meaning: Noah said, when he was commanded to carry (the believers) on the ship, to those who believed with him: ﴿Embark in it﴾. He used the feminine pronoun because it is a ship (safina), whereas the ark (al-fulk) mentioned is masculine. In Ubayy's codex it reads "ʿalā ismi Allāh" (upon the name of Allah). His words "bismi Allāh" (in the name of Allah) may be in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject) referring to the pronoun in "embark," as when you say: "Zayd went out with his clothes and his weapons," meaning: embark seeking blessing through Allah the Exalted. His words ﴿its course and its mooring﴾ would then be two ẓarf (adverbial expressions of time or place), meaning: at the time of its sailing and its anchoring, as the Arabs say: "Praise be to Allah for your night-travel, your new moon, the setting of the star, and the arrival of the pilgrim," where this is an adverb of time, and the element governing this adverb is the sense of the verb contained in "bismi Allāh." It is also possible that his words "bismi Allāh" are in the position of a khabar (predicate) and "its course and its mooring" are two mubtada' (subjects) being verbal nouns, as if he had said: "Embark in it, for by the blessing of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring." In this case this sentence is in the position of a ḥāl from the pronoun in His words "fīhā" (in it). It cannot be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "embark," because there is no returning pronoun in the sentence referring back to it. On this interpretation al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: when Noah wished the ship to move, he said "bismi Allāh" and it moved, and when he wished it to stop, he said "bismi Allāh" and it stopped.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim (in the narration of Abu Bakr), and Ibn 'Amir read "mujrāhā wa-mursāhā" with a ḍamma on both mīms, meaning: its sailing and its anchoring. This is the reading of Mujahid, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Shayba, and the majority of people. From this is the verse of Labid:

*"I have lived long before the racing of Dahis, had the stubborn soul been granted eternity."*

It is narrated that the sky poured down rain in its entirety, so that there was no part of the air without rain, and the whole earth gushed forth with springs, and thus was the meeting of the waters. It is also narrated that the water rose above the mountains and exceeded the earth by forty cubits, and it was said: fifteen cubits. Al-Zajjaj and others indicated that the water of the earth and the water of the sky joined together, so that the whole became like a sea.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is weak. Where was the wave like mountains on this view? And how could the lives of those in the ship remain intact on this view?

A group read "ibnahu" (his son) as an idāfa (construct) of "the son" to Noah, and this is the view of those who say he was his son by his own loins. Some people said he was the son of a relative of his, and he called him "son" out of tenderness and affection. *"...my two legs, longing for him, sleepless."*

On this reading the interpretation of those who said "she was a betrayer" enters it, and this will be mentioned later. *"Are you not leading him with a sheep so that you may eat it, or to sell him in some of the markets?"*

Ibn al-A'rabi recited as evidence for this:

*"So I shall not overtake what has passed from me by lamenting, nor will I be worn out, nor will I be blamed."*

He means: "bilahfa" (by lament).

Al-Nahhas faulted Abu Hatim for dropping this alif, and it is not as he said. Wakī' ibn al-Jarrāh read "wa-nādā Nūḥun ibnahu" with a ḍamma on the tanwīn, and Abu Hatim said: this is an evil dialect that is not known.

His words: ﴿and he was apart﴾, meaning: in a side. It is possible that it means: apart in religion, and it is possible that it means: apart in his distance from the ship. The wording encompasses both. Makki said in al-Mushkil: whoever said "ma'zil" (with a kasra on the zāy) meant the place, and whoever said "ma'zal" (with a fatḥa on it) meant the verbal noun. He did not state explicitly that these are readings, but his wording implies it.

The Seven (readers) read "yā bunayya" with a kasra on the doubled yā'. These are three yā's: the first is the yā' of diminutive, and its proper form is sukūn; the second is the verb's radical lām, and it should take a kasra according to the yā' of possession, since what precedes the yā' of possession is kasra; the third is the yā' of possession, which was dropped. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 43–44:

(p-583) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water." He said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for He on whom He has mercy." And the wave came between them, and he was among the drowned.﴾ ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold," and the water subsided and the matter was concluded, and it came to rest upon al-Judi. And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾

The son of Noah thought that this rain and water were in the usual way. As for His saying, ﴿there is no protector﴾, it has been said that it is in the form of the active participle (fa'il). As for His saying, ﴿except for him on whom He has mercy﴾, it means: except Allah, the Merciful. So "man" (who) is a metonym for the name of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. The meaning is: there is no protector today except He who had mercy on us, so "man" is in the nominative position. It has also been said that His saying, ﴿except for him on whom He has mercy﴾, is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'), as if He had said: there is no protector today existing, but whoever Allah has mercy upon exists. This is made acceptable in terms of meaning, in that the negation of a protector requires the negation of the one protected, and so it is achieved in meaning. As for the wording, "man" is in the accusative position, on the pattern of the verse of al-Nabigha:

؎ Except the remnants... ∗∗∗ ...........

It cannot be in the nominative position on the pattern of the poet's verse:

؎ And a land in which there is no companion ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ except the wild oxen and the she-camels

For these two are the companions of that barren place, and the protected one here is not a protector in any way. It has also been said that "ʿāṣim" means "one who seeks protection" (dhu i'tisam), so "ʿāṣim" in this sense carries the meaning of "maʿṣūm" (one protected), and the exception is sound, and "man" is in the nominative position, and "al-yawm" is an adverbial of time, and it is connected to His saying (p-584) ﴿from the command of Allah﴾, or to a predicate that is implied: "existing today." It is not valid for it to be connected to "ʿāṣim," because it would then have come with tanwin: "lā ʿāṣiman al-yawma," which returns to the original state of the accusative, so that three things do not become one. The rule is that the two things be one: "lā" and what it governs. The grammarians' example for this issue is: "lā amran yawma al-jumʿati lak" (no command on Friday for you). If you make "yawm" governed by "lak," you say: "lā amr."

And "baynahumā" means: between Noah and his son, so the son was among those who drowned.

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water"﴾, and the verse, the passive construction of the verb is more emphatic in magnificence and majesty, and likewise the construction of the verbs after that throughout the verse. It is narrated that a Bedouin heard this verse and said: "This is the speech of those who are capable." "Al-bal'" is the swallowing and gulping down of a thing, so the earth's seizing of the water and its seeping into it was likened to that, and it was commanded to do the likening. He attributed the water to it, since it is upon it and present within it. As for "al-sama'" in this verse, it is either the enveloping sky or the clouds. "Al-iqla'" from a thing is leaving it, and the meaning is: cease from pouring rain. "Ghiḍa" means: decreased, and it most often occurs in the sense of drying up, as in His saying: ﴿and the water subsided﴾, and as in His saying: ﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. Most of the exegetes hold that this refers to menstruation, and likewise the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

؎ ......................... ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ what was diminished of my sight and my limbs

(p-585) This is because an aged person's decline occurs through drying up and emaciation.

As for His saying: ﴿And the matter was concluded﴾, it is an indication of the whole story: the sending forth of the water, the destruction of the nations, and the rescue of the people of the ark. It is narrated that Noah, peace be upon him, boarded the ark from the spring of Warda in al-Sham on the first day of Rajab; it was said: on the tenth of it; it was said: on the fifteenth; it was said: on the seventeenth. The ark came to rest in Dhu al-Hijjah, and it remained upon al-Judi for a month. It was said to him: "Descend," on the day of ʿAshura', so he fasted it, and those with him of people and animals fasted it. Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn Ishaq what implies that he remained upon the water for about a year. He also mentioned a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Noah boarded the ark on the first day of Rajab, and fasted the entire month, and the ark sailed with them until the day of ʿAshura', and on it it settled upon al-Judi, so Noah and those with him fasted it."

It is narrated that when Noah's stay upon the water was prolonged, he sent the raven to bring him news of the complete subsidence of the flood, but it found a floating carcass and remained upon it, and did not return with news. So Noah cursed it, its color turned black, and it became feared by people, and therefore it is wary of them. Then Noah sent the dove, and it came to him with an olive leaf in its beak, and it found no earth on which to set its feet. So it stayed forty days, then he sent it again, and it found that the water had receded from the place of the Ka'ba, which was the first patch of ground the water receded from; so it touched the mud with its feet and came to him, and he knew that the water had begun to ebb. He prayed for it, and so it was given a collar and made tame. Therefore it is for this reason that it is fond of people. Then Allah revealed to the mountains that the ark would settle upon one of them, so all of them grew tall, but al-Judi remained — and it is a mountain in al-Mawsil in the region of al-Jazira — it did not grow tall, out of humility before Allah. So the ark came to rest upon it by the command of Allah, and its timbers remained upon it. In a hadith: "The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Some of it remains, which the earliest of this Ummah reached.'" And al-Zajjaj said: al-Judi is in the region of Amid.

(p-586) Others said: it is near Baqirdi. It is narrated that when the ark set out from the spring of Warda, it sailed until it came to the Ka'ba, and found that it had risen from the earth, so no drowning reached it; it circled it seven times, then went on to Yemen, and returned to al-Judi.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The narratives on these meanings are many and difficult to exhaust, so I have pointed out some excerpts from them; and differences enter into them, as you see in the matter of the Ka'ba, and Allah knows best how it was. "Istawat" in its meaning: it became firmly established and settled. Most of the people read: "ʿalā al-Jūdiyyi" with a kasra on the yā' and its shadda; al-A'mash and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read: "ʿalā al-Jūdī" with the yā' sukūn, and both are dialects. As for His saying: ﴿And it was said, "Away"﴾, it may be from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, coordinated with the first "wa-qīla," and it may be from the saying of Noah and the believers; the first is more apparent and more eloquent.

He attributed the water to it, since it is upon it and present within it. As for "al-sama'" in this verse, it is either the enveloping sky or the clouds. "Al-iqla'" from a thing is leaving it, and the meaning is: cease from pouring rain. "Ghiḍa" means: decreased, and it most often occurs in the sense of drying up, as in His saying: ﴿and the water subsided﴾, and as in His saying: ﴿And what the wombs diminish and what they increase﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8]. Most of the exegetes hold that this refers to menstruation, and likewise the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

؎ ......................... ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ what was diminished of my sight and my limbs

(p-585) This is because an aged person's decline occurs through drying up and emaciation.

As for His saying: ﴿And the matter was concluded﴾, it is an indication of the whole story: the sending forth of the water, the destruction of the nations, and the rescue of the people of the ark. It is narrated that Noah, peace be upon him, boarded the ark from the spring of Warda in al-Sham on the first day of Rajab; it was said: on the tenth of it; it was said: on the fifteenth; it was said: on the seventeenth. The ark came to rest in Dhu al-Hijjah, and it remained upon al-Judi for a month. It was said to him: "Descend," on the day of ʿAshura', so he fasted it, and those with him of people and animals fasted it. Al-Tabari mentioned from Ibn Ishaq what implies that he remained upon the water for about a year. He also mentioned a hadith from the Prophet ﷺ: "Noah boarded the ark on the first day of Rajab, and fasted the entire month, and the ark sailed with them until the day of ʿAshura', and on it it settled upon al-Judi, so Noah and those with him fasted it."

It is narrated that when Noah's stay upon the water was prolonged, he sent the raven to bring him news of the complete subsidence of the flood, but it found a floating carcass and remained upon it, and did not return with news. So Noah cursed it, its color turned black, and it became feared by people, and therefore it is wary of them. Then Noah sent the dove, and it came to him with an olive leaf in its beak, and it found no earth on which to set its feet. So it stayed forty days, then he sent it again, and it found that the water had receded from the place of the Ka'ba, which was the first patch of ground the water receded from; so it touched the mud with its feet and came to him, and he knew that the water had begun to ebb. He prayed for it, and so it was given a collar and made tame. Therefore it is for this reason that it is fond of people. Then Allah revealed to the mountains that the ark would settle upon one of them, so all of them grew tall, but al-Judi remained — and it is a mountain in al-Mawsil in the region of al-Jazira — it did not grow tall, out of humility before Allah. So the ark came to rest upon it by the command of Allah, and its timbers remained upon it. In a hadith: "The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Some of it remains, which the earliest of this Ummah reached.'" And al-Zajjaj said: al-Judi is in the region of Amid.

(p-586) Others said: it is near Baqirdi. It is narrated that when the ark set out from the spring of Warda, it sailed until it came to the Ka'ba, and found that it had risen from the earth, so no drowning reached it; it circled it seven times, then went on to Yemen, and returned to al-Judi.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The narratives on these meanings are many and difficult to exhaust, so I have pointed out some excerpts from them; and differences enter into them, as you see in the matter of the Ka'ba, and Allah knows best how it was. "Istawat" in its meaning: it became firmly established and settled. Most of the people read: "ʿalā al-Jūdiyyi" with a kasra on the yā' and its shadda; al-A'mash and Ibn Abi ʿAbla read: "ʿalā al-Jūdī" with the yā' sukūn, and both are dialects. As for His saying: ﴿And it was said, "Away"﴾, it may be from the saying of Allah, the Exalted, coordinated with the first "wa-qīla," and it may be from the saying of Noah and the believers; the first is more apparent and more eloquent.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 45–46:**

The Exalted said:

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord and said, "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family, and indeed Your promise is true, and You are the most just of judges."﴾ ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, his is unrighteous work. So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge. I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant."﴾

This sentence is joined to the one before it without strict chronological order (*ma'tuf 'ala al-lati qablaha dunna tartib*). This story occurred at the very beginning of Noah's boarding of the ship. From the words of al-Tabari it appears that it took place after the son had drowned, which is possible, but the first view (that it occurred before the drowning) is more fitting.

This verse is an argument presented by Noah, peace be upon him. Allah had commanded him to carry his family aboard, and his son was of his family, so it seemed that he should be carried. Allah then showed him that what was intended was those of the family who believed. Then he (Noah) made his address graceful with his words, "And indeed Your promise is true," and with his words, "And You are the most just of judges." These statements support his argument (*mu'ina fi hujjatihi*). {p-587} This verse indicates that Noah, peace be upon him, thought his son was a believer, and that is the stronger of the two possibilities.

As for the Exalted's words, "He said, 'O Noah...'" and the rest of the verse, the meaning is: Allah the Exalted said, "O Noah." A group said that what is meant by His words, "indeed he is not of your family," is: "he is not your son by birth." They claimed that he was the product of an illegitimate union (*ghayya*), and that his unbelieving wife had been unfaithful to him in this matter. This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Sirin, and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr. Ibn Abza said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) only ruled that the child belongs to the marriage bed (*li'l-firash*) because of the son of Noah." Al-Hasan swore that he was not his son, while 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak swore that he was his son.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Al-Hasan relied on the Exalted's words, "Indeed he is not of your family," while al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima relied on the Exalted's words, "And Noah called out to his son" [Hud: 42].

Al-Hasan and those who interpreted his view read, "indeed he is [the doer of] unrighteous work" (*innahu 'amalun ghayru salih*) according to this meaning. This is the reading of the Seven, except al-Kisa'i, and the reading of the majority of people. Those who disagreed with al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning is: "He is not of your family, those whom the promise encompassed, because he is not upon your religion, even if he is your son by [legal] affiliation (*bi'l-wala'*)." Whoever among this group read, "indeed he is [the doer of] unrighteous work," made it a description of him by means of the verbal noun (*al-masdar*) as an intensification, describing him thus, just as al-Khansa said describing a she-camel whose offspring had gone from her:

*She grazes whatever she is unaware of, until when she remembers, then she is only coming and going.*

That is, "possessing coming and going."

Some of this group read, "indeed he did unrighteous work" (*innahu 'amila ghayra salih*), which is the reading of al-Kisa'i. Umm Salama and 'A'isha narrated this reading from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); Abu Hatim mentioned it. Al-Tabari weakened this reading and criticized the hadith, saying it comes through the chain of Shahr ibn Hawshab. It is the reading of 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'isha, and Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with them. Abu Hatim preferred it. Some read, "indeed he did an unrighteous deed" (*innahu 'amila 'amalan ghayra salih*).

A group said: the pronoun in His words, "indeed it is unrighteous work," according to the reading of the majority of the Seven, refers to the request of Noah which the speech implies, and the end of the verse explains it. What strengthens this interpretation is that in the codex (*mushaf*) of Ibn Mas'ud it reads, "indeed it is unrighteous work that you ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge." Another group said: the pronoun refers to the boarding of Noah's son with them, which Noah's request implies. The meaning is: that the boarding of the unbeliever with the believers is unrighteous work. Abu 'Ali said: It is also possible that the intended meaning is that your being with the unbelievers and your abandoning boarding with us is unrighteous work.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation that does not hold up in terms of meaning.

All these groups said that the claim that the son was the product of an illegitimate union and of the marriage bed is pure error. They said: it has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that "no wife of a prophet ever committed adultery."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This hadith is not well known. It is actually a statement of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and the nobility of prophethood supports it. Regarding the Exalted's words, "but they betrayed them" [al-Tahrim: 10], they said: one of the two wives used to tell people, "He is insane," while the other used to alert [the enemies] to the guests. As for other than this, no. These are the arguments and proofs of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and his statement, and the view of the majority of people.

Ibn Abi Malika read, "fa-la tasalni" (so do not ask Me), with the nun lightened, the ya' affirmed, the lam sukun, and without hamza. A group read with the nun lightened, the ya' dropped, and with hamza, "fa-la tas'alni." Abu Ja'far and Shayba read with the nun kasra and doubled, with hamza and the ya' affirmed, "fa-la tas'alanni." Nafi' read the same without the ya', "fa-la tas'alnn." Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "fa-la tas'alanna," with the doubled nun fatha, which is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas. Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "fa-la tasalni," with the nun lightened and the lam sakin. Abu 'Amr used to affirm the ya' in continuous speech (*al-wasl*), while 'Asim and Hamza omitted it both in continuous speech and at pause (*al-waqf*).

The meaning of His words, "So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge," is: since I have promised you, know with certainty that there is no breaking of the promise. So when you see that your son was not carried, it was obligatory upon you to pause and to know that this is a matter that is necessary and true before Allah.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

But Noah, peace be upon him, was moved by the compassion of prophethood and the disposition of a human being to seek the breaths of mercy and to remind. It is upon this degree that his rebuke occurred. For this reason it came with gentleness and elevation in His words, "I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant." Allah, blessed and exalted, said to Muhammad (ﷺ), "So do not be" (*fa-la takunanna*), and that here is in accordance with the matter for which he was rebuked and its gravity, for it was due to the constriction of his breast by the burdens of prophethood. Otherwise, it is established that Muhammad (ﷺ) is the best of mankind and the most deserving of gentle address. But this is in accordance with the two matters, not in accordance with the prophets. Some said: Noah was treated with respect only because of his age. Others said: the words were directed to Muhammad (ﷺ) as a person addresses the one particularly beloved to him.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak.

It is possible that His words, "So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge," mean: do not request from Me a matter whose benefit you do not know with certain knowledge. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi inclined to this view and said that "bihi" (about it) may be connected to the word "'ilm" (knowledge), as the poet said:

*My recompense was that I be beaten with the staff.*

It is also possible that "bihi" has the position of "fihi" (in it), so that the preposition (*ba'*) is connected to the implied predicate (*al-mustaqarr*).

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The difference between these two views is only verbal, and the meaning in the verse is one. It is also narrated that this son was his stepson (*rabibahu*), but this is weak. Al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd that the meaning of His words, "I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant," is: lest you believe that I do not fulfill a promise I made to you.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an ugly interpretation. Nothing in the wording requires that Noah believed this, and we seek refuge in Allah. The most that happened to Noah, peace be upon him, was that he saw the leaving behind of his son as conflicting with the promise, so he reminded of it and supplicated out of compassion, in order to reveal to him the reason that made his son deserve being left among the drowned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 47–49:

(p-591) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of. And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾ ﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you. And there will be nations We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew it before this. So be patient; indeed, the final outcome is for the righteous.﴾

In this verse is Noah's turning back (to God, inabah) and his submission to the command of God, Exalted is He, and his seeking forgiveness. The question that was forbidden is the question accompanied by determination (al-'azm, a firm and insistent resolve), with argument and urgent insistence, about a matter whose wisdom has been concealed. As for asking about matters in the manner of seeking knowledge and guidance, this is not included in this.

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of﴾ [Hud: 46] covers both kinds of asking. Therefore I have pointed out that the intended one is one of them and not the other. And "the losers" (al-khasirun) are those who have been cheated of their share of good.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace"﴾ was at his descent from the ship with his companions to spread out on the earth. "Peace" (al-salam) here means safety, security, and the like. "Blessings" (al-barakat) means good and growth in all directions. This promise encompasses all believers until the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

His saying: ﴿from those with you﴾ means: from the descendants of those who are with you and from their offspring. So "min" (from), according to this, is for the beginning of the end point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: these nations will come from them. And "man" (those who) is a relative pronoun whose clause is "ma'aka" (with you) and what is implied along with it, like your saying: "mimman istaqarra ma'aka" (from those who settled with you) and the like. Then his saying "wa-umam" (and nations) is cut off to begin a new sentence, since their matter is separate from the first matter. These are the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen﴾: the verse refers to the story, meaning: this is from the unseen matters whose time has long passed and whose knowledge remains only with God, Blessed and Exalted. Its knowledge, or the knowledge of its like, was not with you nor with your people. We reveal it to you so that it may be for you guidance and a model regarding what other prophets encountered, and so that it may be for your people an example and a warning, lest there befall them, if they deny you, the like of what befell these and others of the punishing matters.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

On this meaning the eloquence of His saying becomes apparent: ﴿So be patient; indeed, the final outcome is for the righteous.﴾ That is: strive in conveying the message, be earnest in the mission, be patient through hardships, and know that the outcome will be yours just as it was for Noah in this story. In the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "from before this Qur'an."

And unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be among the losers."﴾ ﴿It was said: "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations from those with you. And there will be nations We will grant enjoyment, then a painful punishment from Us will touch them."﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. In this verse is Noah's turning back (to God, inabah) and his submission to the command of God, Exalted is He, and his seeking forgiveness. The question that was forbidden is the question accompanied by determination (al-'azm, a firm and insistent resolve), with argument and urgent insistence, about a matter whose wisdom has been concealed. As for asking about matters in the manner of seeking knowledge and guidance, this is not included in this.

The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of﴾ [Hud: 46] covers both kinds of asking. Therefore I have pointed out that the intended one is one of them and not the other. And "the losers" (al-khasirun) are those who have been cheated of their share of good.

This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

His saying: ﴿from those with you﴾ means: from the descendants of those who are with you and from their offspring. So "min" (from), according to this, is for the beginning of the end point (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), meaning: these nations will come from them. And "man" (those who) is a relative pronoun whose clause is "ma'aka" (with you) and what is implied along with it, like your saying: "mimman istaqarra ma'aka" (from those who settled with you) and the like. Then his saying "wa-umam" (and nations) is cut off to begin a new sentence, since their matter is separate from the first matter. These are the disbelievers until the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 50–52:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And to 'Ad [We sent] their brother Hud. He said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. You are but inventing falsehood."﴾ ﴿"O my people, I do not ask you for any reward for it. My reward is only from the One who originated me. Will you not then use reason?"﴾ ﴿"And O my people, seek forgiveness from your Lord and then turn back to Him; He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength. And do not turn away as criminals."﴾

"And to 'Ad" is conjoined with His saying "to his people" in the story of Nuh. "'Ad" is a tribe, and they were Arabs, as has been mentioned, and Hud (peace be upon him) was from among them. He called him "their brother" according to lineage and kinship. If we suppose he was not from among them, then the brotherhood is according to upbringing, language and neighbourhood. As for the saying of one who said, "It is a brotherhood according to the Adamic lineage," it is weak.

The majority of readers read "O my people" (yā qawmi) with a kasra on the mim. Ibn Muhaysin read "yā qawmu" with a damma on the mim, and this is a dialect related by Sibawayh. The majority of readers read "ghayruhu" with a raf' (nominative), as an adjective (na't) or an apposition (badal) to the position of "min ilāhin." Al-Kisa'i alone read it with a kasra on the ra', taking it according to the wording of "ilāhin"; this too is as an adjective or apposition. "Ghayrahu" with a nasb (accusative) as an exception (istithna') is also permissible.

"Muftarun" means: liars, in the most shameful lie, in your making divinity belong to other than Allah, the Exalted. The pronoun in His saying "'alayhi" refers to the call to Allah, blessed and exalted be He, and the meaning is: "My reward and recompense are only from Allah, the Exalted." Then He described Him by His saying, "who originated me," making it an attribute that refutes them in their worship of idols and their belief that they act. The description with this was placed within the flow of his speech, alerting to the acts of Allah the Exalted, and that He is the One who deserves worship. "Fatara" means: invented and produced. His saying, "Will you not then use reason?" is a rebuke regarding the ground for the claim that other than the Originator is a god. It may also be meant: "Will you not then use reason, since I do not seek any worldly gain? I only desire benefit for you and the Hereafter." The first is more apparent.

"Istighfar" is the seeking of forgiveness. It may be by the tongue, and it may be by the turning of the heart in repentance, seeking guidance, and eagerness for the presence of a clear path. These are states that may occur from the disbelievers. It is as if he said to them: "Seek the forgiveness of Allah by turning in repentance, and by seeking proof of my prophethood. Then turn back in faith from your disbelief." The ordering, according to this, is coherent; otherwise, considerable contrivance is needed to order repentance after seeking forgiveness. Either "turn back" (tubu) is a command to persistence, and "istighfar" is the seeking of forgiveness through faith; and this is the view of al-Tabari. Abu al-Ma'ali said in al-Irshad: "Tawba" in the terminology of the theologians is regret, after he said that linguistically it is return. Then he built on this, saying that when the disbeliever believes, his faith is not repentance; rather his repentance is his regret afterwards.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"What I say is: repentance is a resolve to abandon what one repents of, preceded by knowledge of the corruption of what is repented of and the goodness of what one returns to, accompanied by regret over what has passed of what is repented of, which does not separate from it, and it is one of its conditions." So I say: the faith of the disbeliever is his repentance from his disbelief, because it is itself his return.

"Taba" in the speech of the Arabs means: he returned to obedience and to the best of matters. The use of the word in the Qur'an with "ila" requires that it is return, not regret. Regret is a necessary right of repentance, as we have said. The reality of repentance is abandoning the like of what one repents of, with a firm, sincere resolve, as we have explained. And Allah is the One sought for help.

"Midrāran" is a broken plural pattern, and its original form would have required a ta' marbuta, but it was dropped with the intention of the nisba and on the basis that "the sky" is the rain itself. It derives from "darra yadurru," and the pattern mif'al may come from the active participle of a triliteral root and from the active participle of a quadriliteral root. The saying of one who said, "It is more characteristic of the quadriliteral," is not necessarily so.

It is related that Allah the Exalted had withheld rain from 'Ad for three years. They were people of tillage, gardens and fruits, and their lands were east of the Arabian Peninsula. Therefore He promised them rain. From this came their joy when they saw the cloud, and their saying: ﴿This is a cloud bringing us rain﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24], and their urging one another to draw down rain through faith and turning back. That is Allah's custom with His servants. From this is the saying of Nuh (peace be upon him): ﴿Seek forgiveness of your Lord, indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ [Nuh: 10] ﴿He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Nuh: 11]. From this too is the action of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), when he made all of his speech in seeking rain and his supplication consist of istighfar, and rain fell. When he was asked about that, he said: "I have indeed drawn down rain by the constellations of the sky."

His saying, ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾, its apparent meaning is general over everything in which Allah the Exalted bestows goodness upon the servants. A group said: Allah the Exalted had withheld their offspring, so the meaning of His saying ﴿and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ is: children. It may also be that He specifically mentioned strength because they were the strongest of peoples, so they were promised an increase in that in which they excelled. Then He forbade them from turning away from the truth and from turning aside from the command of Allah. "Mujrimin" is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "tatawallaw."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 57–60:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿And if they turn away, then I have certainly conveyed to you that with which I was sent to you. And my Lord will replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. Indeed, my Lord is Guardian over all things.﴾ ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and We saved them from a harsh punishment.﴾ ﴿And that was 'Ad; they denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every obstinate tyrant.﴾ ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, 'Ad disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with 'Ad, the people of Hud!﴾

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "tawallaw" with a fatha on the lam and the ta, meaning "tatawallaw" (you turn away). 'Isa al-Thaqafi and al-A'raj read "tuwallu" with a damma on the ta and the lam. "In" (if) is a conditional particle, and the answer (jawab) is in the fa' and what follows it in His saying: ﴿then I have certainly conveyed to you﴾. The meaning is: I have no great concern for you if you turn away; my innocence is established through the conveying (al-tabligh), while you are the ones who bear the sin of turning away from faith.

It is also possible that "tawallaw" is a past-tense verb, and that there is a shift in the speech from third person (ghayba) to second person (khitab), meaning: say, "I have certainly conveyed to you."

The majority read "wa-yastakhlifu" with a damma on the fa', as a report of that. 'Asim, as transmitted by Hubayra from Hafs from him, read "wa-yastakhlif" with a jazm, coordinating it with the position of the fa' in His saying "fa-qad" (then indeed).

His saying "wa-la tadurrunahu shay'an" (and you will not harm Him at all) can carry two meanings:

The first: you will not harm Him by your departure and your destruction at all, meaning His dominion will not be diminished and His affair will not be disturbed. According to this meaning, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud read: "wa-la tanqusunahu shay'an" (and you will not diminish Him at all).

The other meaning: "wa-la tadurrunahu" means that when He destroys you, you will not be able to harm Him in any way, nor to avenge yourselves against Him, nor will you oppose His action toward you with anything that harms Him.

Then He informed them that their Lord is Guardian over all things, knowing of them. The repetition of these attributes and their like serves as an admonition and a reminder.

"Al-amr" is the singular of "al-umur" (affairs/commands). It may also be the verbal noun of "amara, ya'muru" (to command), meaning: Our command to the wind, or to its keepers, and the like. His saying "bi-rahmah" (by mercy) may either be a plain report of a mercy from God that reached them, or it may be intended to inform that salvation was completed only by the mere mercy of God, not by their deeds. In this case the verse carries the meaning of the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "No one enters Paradise by his deed." They said: "Not even you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Not even I, unless God covers me with His grace and mercy."

His saying "wa-najjaynahum min 'adhabin ghalizin" (and We saved them from a harsh punishment) may mean the punishment of the Hereafter. It may also mean that the salvation previously mentioned was from a harsh punishment, meaning the wind. In this case the purpose is to enumerate the blessing. The well-known manner of their punishment by the wind is that it would lift them up, demolish their dwellings, uproot them, and carry off the litter (al-za'ina) as it was. Al-Zajjaj reported that it would enter their bodies, exit from their posteriors, and cut them apart limb by limb.

"Jahadu" is transitive with a preposition (harf jarr) when it is treated as equivalent to "kafaru" (disbelieved), and this is reversed in the verse after this. His saying "wa-'asaw rusulahu" (and disobeyed His messengers) is a reproach against them, because in denying one messenger there is denial of all the messengers and disobedience to them, since all prophethood is united upon belief in God and affirmation of His lordship. It may be that what is intended is Hud, Adam, and Noah, peace be upon them.

"Al-'Anid" is the form fa'il from "anada" when one is obstinate (ata). From it is the poet's saying:

Indeed I am old, unable to bear the stubborn (al-'anada),

meaning the difficult camels. The arrogance and obstinacy were among the character traits of 'Ad because of their strength.

His exalted saying: "wa-utbi'u fi hadhihi al-dunya la'nah" (and they were followed in this world by a curse) — the verse: they were judged with this judgment because of their disbelief and persistence, until the punishment descended upon them. "Al-la'nah" is distance (from mercy) and disgrace. It is certain that these people died upon disbelief, and so the disbelieving person who dies upon his disbelief is cursed; but a specific living individual is not cursed, neither a disbeliever, nor a sinner, nor an animal; all of that is disliked according to the hadiths. "Yawm" is an adverbial noun of time (zarf), its meaning being that the curse upon them is in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Then the cause that necessitates this was mentioned, which is their disbelief in their Lord. "Kafara" is transitive without a preposition here, since it has the meaning of "jahadu," as you say "shakartu laka" and "shakartuka," and "kafara ni'matahu" and "kafara bi-ni'matihi." "Bu'dan" is in the accusative governed by a verb understood, and it occupies the position of that verb.

Indeed I am old, unable to bear the stubborn (al-'anada),

meaning the difficult camels. The arrogance and obstinacy were among the character traits of 'Ad because of their strength.

His exalted saying: "wa-utbi'u fi hadhihi al-dunya la'nah" (and they were followed in this world by a curse) — the verse: they were judged with this judgment because of their disbelief and persistence, until the punishment descended upon them. "Al-la'nah" is distance (from mercy) and disgrace. It is certain that these people died upon disbelief, and so the disbelieving person who dies upon his disbelief is cursed; but a specific living individual is not cursed, neither a disbeliever, nor a sinner, nor an animal; all of that is disliked according to the hadiths. "Yawm" is an adverbial noun of time (zarf), its meaning being that the curse upon them is in this world and on the Day of Resurrection. Then the cause that necessitates this was mentioned, which is their disbelief in their Lord. "Kafara" is transitive without a preposition here, since it has the meaning of "jahadu," as you say "shakartu laka" and "shakartuka," and "kafara ni'matahu" and "kafara bi-ni'matihi." "Bu'dan" is in the accusative governed by a verb understood, and it occupies the position of that verb.

He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. He produced you from the earth and made you its inhabitants, so seek His forgiveness and then turn to Him in repentance. (p-599) The estimated sense: "And We sent [to] Thamud." This has already been mentioned in similar wording, and the meaning of brotherhood was discussed in the story of Hud.

"... when Tamim drank from it and drank again"

And another said:

"Tamim ibn Marr and its partisans"

And there are names in which both forms are common, such as Thamud and Saba', so both readings here are eloquent and in use. A group read "غَيْرُهُ" with a raised ra' (ghayruhu, as a nominative), which has been mentioned just above.

"اسْتَعْمَرَكُمْ" means: He made you inhabitants (ʿummār), as one says "istakṭaba" and "istaʿmala" (he made him a scribe, he made him an employee). Some people held that it derives from ʿumr (life span), meaning "He let you live long in it (ʿammarakum)". A similar expression to His words ﴿فاسْتَغْفِرُوهُ ثُمَّ تُوبُوا إلَيْهِ﴾ has been mentioned before. ﴿إنَّ رَبِّي قَرِيبٌ مُجِيبٌ﴾ means: His answering and His forgiveness are near to those who believe and turn back to Him. "مُجِيبٌ" means: with the condition of His will.

The apparent meaning, which the majority of exegetes relate, is that His words "مَرْجُوًّا" mean "esteemed" (musawwadan): "we hoped that you would become a leader who fills the place of the great." Then they affirmed this, in a rebuking manner according to their claim, by saying "أتَنْهانا". Al-Naqqash related from some of them that he said its meaning is "insignificant" (ḥaqīran).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for the word "مَرْجُوًّا" meaning "insignificant," this is not in the speech of the Arabs. It is only tenable as an explanation of the sense. The intention behind their words "مَرْجُوًّا" would be: "You were easy to deal with among us, your affair was easily refuted, of one who is not thought to grow strong in such a matter." So the meaning of "مَرْجُوٍّ" is: one whose rejection and defeat are expected, and the like. This is then in the manner of contempt, which is why it was explained as "insignificant." A similar meaning is found in the saying of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb: "Indeed the affair of the son of Abu Kabsha has been made prominent..." [the hadith continues]. Then their words "أتَنْهانا" come in the manner of threat and of showing disapproval of this statement from him.

By "ما يَعْبُدُ آباؤُنا" they mean the idols and images. Then they asserted that they were in doubt about his matter and his sayings, and that they were doubting with a doubt increasing beyond its level.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is no difference between this state and the state of firm resolve upon disbelief. "مُرِيبٍ" means: causing confusion, accused. From it is the saying of the poet:

"O people, what is wrong with Abu Dhu'ayb,
that whenever I came to him from his absence,
he sniffs the edge of my garment and touches my clothing,
as if I had caused him doubt by a doubt."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 63–65:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord, and He has given me mercy from Himself, then who will help me against Allah if I disobey Him? You would only add to me loss.﴾ ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you, so leave her to eat in Allah's earth, and do not touch her with harm, lest a near punishment seize you.﴾ ﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said, "Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That is a promise not to be denied."﴾

His saying "a'ra'aytum" (tell me) is from the seeing of the heart, meaning: "Have you considered?" The conditional clause that follows it and its answer take the place of the two objects of "a'ra'aytum." "Bayyina" means proof and certainty, and the "ha'" in "bayyina" is for intensification (mubalagha), though it may also be the feminine ta' (ha' al-ta'nith). "Rahma" (mercy) in this verse means prophethood and what is attached to it. In the speech there is an omitted element, whose estimate is: "Will your doubt harm me, or will your obedience be possible for me?" and similar to this, of what fits the meaning of the verse.

As for his saying, ﴿So you would only add to me loss﴾, its meaning is: "So you give me nothing, regarding what I require from you of faith and what I ask of you of repentance, except loss for your own selves." It is from "khasara" (loss). The "loss" in this verse applies only to them and to their situation. He attributed the increase to himself because, insofar as he is one who requires their words and is entrusted with their faith, it is as when you say to one you advise: "I want good for you, and you want evil for me." The clear form would be "and you want evil," but since you are one who wants good and requires that, it is fine to attribute the increase to yourself.

As for His, the Exalted, saying, ﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah﴾ and so on, the mention of the beginning of the matter of the she-camel is abbreviated in this verse. It is narrated that his people asked him for a sign that would compel them to faith, so Allah, His power be exalted, brought forth the she-camel for them from the mountain. It is also narrated that they proposed that the she-camel come out from that particular rock. (p-602) It is narrated that the mountain shook like a pregnant woman, the rock split, and a she-camel came out of it with her young. It is narrated that she came out heavily pregnant and gave birth after emerging. Then Salih made them stand and said to them: ﴿This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾. "Aya" (sign) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

A group read "ta'kul" with a jussive (ta'kul), as the answer to the imperative. Another group read "ta'kulu" (with a damma), as a resumed new clause (istinaf) or as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "dharuha." His saying ﴿and do not touch her with harm﴾ is general, covering hamstringing and other things. His saying ﴿lest a near punishment seize you﴾ is by revelation from Allah to him that when your people hamstring the she-camel, a punishment will come to them, near in time from the moment of disobedience. These are the three days that Salih, peace be upon him, understood from the cry of the young camel upon the mountain of al-Qarra. He attributed the hamstringing to all of them because the one who hamstrung her was one of them, and it was by their consent and collective agreement. Her hamstringer was Qudar. It is narrated in the report about this that Allah revealed to Salih that his people would hamstring the she-camel and the punishment would descend upon them at that time, so he informed them of that. They said: "We seek refuge in Allah from doing that." He said: "If you do not do it yourselves, soon there will be born among you one who will do it." He also told them that the description of her hamstringer is: red-faced, blue-eyed, and fair-haired. So they made the condition known to the midwives and ordered them to inspect the infants; whoever had this description would be killed. In the city there were two noble, honored elders, and one had a son while the other had a daughter. They intermarried, and between the couple was born Qudar, with the aforementioned description. The guards resolved to kill him, but his two grandfathers prevented them from doing so until he grew up. He was the one who hamstrung her with a sword at her hind legs. It was said that he struck her udder with an arrow. Her young fled from that and climbed a mountain called al-Qarra, and it cried out three times. Salih said: "This is the appointed time of three days for the punishment." Before the cry of the young camel, he had ordered them to seek it, perhaps they might reach it and thereby the punishment would be averted from them. They attempted to climb the mountain, but the mountain rose into the sky until the birds could not reach it. At that moment the young camel cried out.

His saying ﴿in your homes﴾ (fi darikum) is the plural of "darah," as you say "sahah," "sah," "suh." From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"For him there is a caller in Mecca, rising in sound, and another calling near his dwelling."

(p-603) It is possible to call the whole dwelling-place of a tribe a "dar." The three days is a limit of time which people have analogized to giving respite to one who has been sentenced, and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is different, because respite for one under judgment, a debtor in pre-emption cases, and the like is an expansion, whereas here it is a fixing of humiliation and punishment. Qatada narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If you had climbed up to al-Qarra, you would have seen the bones of the young camel."

They said: "We seek refuge in Allah from doing that." He said: "If you do not do it yourselves, soon there will be born among you one who will do it." He also told them that the description of her hamstringer is: red-faced, blue-eyed, and fair-haired. So they made the condition known to the midwives and ordered them to inspect the infants; whoever had this description would be killed. In the city there were two noble, honored elders, and one had a son while the other had a daughter. They intermarried, and between the couple was born Qudar, with the aforementioned description. The guards resolved to kill him, but his two grandfathers prevented them from doing so until he grew up. He was the one who hamstrung her with a sword at her hind legs. It was said that he struck her udder with an arrow. Her young fled from that and climbed a mountain called al-Qarra, and it cried out three times. Salih said: "This is the appointed time of three days for the punishment." Before the cry of the young camel, he had ordered them to seek it, perhaps they might reach it and thereby the punishment would be averted from them. They attempted to climb the mountain, but the mountain rose into the sky until the birds could not reach it. At that moment the young camel cried out.

His saying ﴿in your homes﴾ (fi darikum) is the plural of "darah," as you say "sahah," "sah," "suh." From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

"For him there is a caller in Mecca, rising in sound, and another calling near his dwelling."

(p-603) It is possible to call the whole dwelling-place of a tribe a "dar." The three days is a limit of time which people have analogized to giving respite to one who has been sentenced, and the like.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view this is different, because respite for one under judgment, a debtor in pre-emption cases, and the like is an expansion, whereas here it is a fixing of humiliation and punishment. Qatada narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "If you had climbed up to al-Qarra, you would have seen the bones of the young camel."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 66–68:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us and from the disgrace of that day. Indeed, your Lord is the Strong, the Mighty.﴾ ﴿And the blast seized those who had wronged, and they were found lying prostrate in their homes,﴾ ﴿as if they had never dwelt there. Unquestionably, Thamud disbelieved in their Lord. Unquestionably, away with Thamud!﴾

The word *al-amr* (the command) may mean the verbal noun of *amara* (to command), and it may also mean a single matter among affairs (*umur*). His saying ﴿by mercy from Us﴾ allows two readings: that the rescue came solely through mercy, or that it is a description of circumstance only, informing that He showed them mercy at the time of the rescue. His saying "*min-na*" (from Us) apparently relates to "mercy," and it may also relate to his saying "*najjayna*" (We saved).

A group recited "*wa-min khizyin yawma'idhin*" with tanwin (nunation) on *khizy* and a fatha on the *mim* of *yawma'idhin*. This reading permits the fatha on the *mim* to be an *i'rab* (grammatical inflection, the case-ending marking of a word's grammatical function), and it also permits the adverbial expression to be *mabni* (indeclinable, fixed in form) because it was attached to a non-declinable word (*ghayr mutamakkin*). Thus you have the choice between the two readings. The two transmissions also apply to the words of the poet:

﻿*ʿalā ḥīna ʿātabtu al-mashība ʿalā al-ṣibā* ∗∗∗ *wa-qultu alammā aṣḥu wa-al-shaybu wāziʿu*

[Translation of the verse: "At the time I rebuked grey hair for youth, and I said: 'Would that I were awake, while the grey hair is a restrainer!'"]

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir recited "*wa-min khizyin yawmi'idhin*," with *khizy* in the genitive construct and a kasra on the *mim* of *yawmi'idhin*. This is an expansion in attaching a verbal noun to an adverbial expression, as in the saying "*makru al-layli wa-al-nahari*" (the scheming of the night and the day) and similar constructions. The analogous form of this reading would be to say "*sira ʿalayhi yawmu'idhin*" with a damma on the *mim*. This is also their recitation in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from the punishment of that day﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 11], and ﴿from the terror of that day﴾ [al-Naml: 89]. ʿĀsim and Hamza recited likewise, except in His saying "*min fazaʿin yawmaʾidhin*," where both of them made the *ʿayn* carry tanwin and put a fatha on the *mim*. Their transmission differed from Nafi' on the kasra and fatha of the *mim*, and he uses the idafa (construct) in both readings. Al-Kisa'i recited "*min khizyi yawma'idhin*" without tanwin and with a fatha on the *mim* of *yawma'idhin*, which combines the idafa with the indeclinability of the adverbial expression. He recited "*wa-min fazaʿin*" like ʿĀsim and Hamza.

As for *idh*, its original form should have been *idhin* with sukun, but it is supposed to be followed by full clauses. When a clause is omitted here, the tanwin is given as compensation for it. The reference in His saying "*yawma'idhin*" is to the day of punishment.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the blast seized those who had wronged﴾, and so on. It is related that Salih, peace be upon him, said to them when the she-camel bellowed: "Your faces will turn yellow on the first day, will turn red on the second, and will turn black on the third." When it was so, they wrapped themselves in shrouds made of leather and prepared for destruction. A blast seized them, containing every kind of terrifying sound, which split their hearts and struck everyone of them in the east and west of the earth, except a man who was in the Sacred Sanctuary, and the Sanctuary protected him from that, but he died after that. In the Musannaf of Abu Dawud: "It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, who is that man?' They said: 'Abu Raghal.'"

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is room for scrutiny in this, and the opposing view is found in the biographies (*siyar*). He masculinized the verb attributed to *al-sayha* (the blast) because it carries the meaning of *al-siyah* (the cry), and its feminine gender is not real (*ghayr haqiqi*). It was also said that this was permissible even though it is feminine, since a separation was made between the verb and it, as they said: "A woman attended the judge today." The first view is more correct. *Al-sayha* is only used in mention of punishment, because it is a *fa'la* form indicating a single occurrence of an unusual kind, whereas *al-siyah* indicates a lengthy verbal noun. In their speech it is anomalous to say "*laqitahu liqa'atan wahidatan*" (I met him one meeting), and the analogical form would be *laqyatun*.

"*Jathimin*" means kneeling, meaning that they were struck down with them (their bodies) lying prone. It is a comparison with the crouching of birds, and in that sense it resembles the crouching of hearthstones and the crouching of ashes.

"*Yaghnaw*" is the imperfect of *ghaniya* in the place, when one dwells there in comfortable living, and *al-maghani* (the dwellings) derives from it. Hamza alone recited "*alā inna thamūda*" (without tanwin), and likewise in al-Furqan, al-ʿAnkabut and al-Najm. Al-Kisa'i inflected all of them (with tanwin). As for His saying "*alā buʿdan li-thamūda*" (away with Thamud), the transmission from ʿĀsim differed: Hafs related from him leaving it uninflected as Hamza does, while Abu Bakr related from him the inflection of all four, and leaving it uninflected in His saying "*alā buʿdan li-thamūda*." The rest recited "*alā inna thamūdan*," inflected, and "*alā buʿdan li-thamūdа*," uninflected. Both recitations are eloquent, and likewise they inflected in al-Furqan, al-ʿAnkabut and al-Najm.
