(p-606) The Exalted said:

﴿And certainly Our messengers came to Abraham with glad tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and he did not delay before bringing a roasted calf.﴾ ﴿But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt a fear of them. They said, "Do not fear; we have been sent to the people of Lot."﴾ ﴿And his wife was standing, so she laughed. Then We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob.﴾

"The messengers" are the angels: Jibril, Mika'il and Israfil. A group said that instead of Israfil it was 'Izra'il, the Angel of Death. It is narrated that Jibril among them was specifically charged with destroying the town of Lot, Mika'il specifically with giving Abraham the good news of Isaac, and Israfil specifically with saving Lot and those with him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This verse requires that they all shared in the good news of Isaac. A group, which is the majority, said: "the glad tidings" was of Isaac. Another group said: "the glad tidings" was of the destruction of the people of Lot.

As for His saying "salaman" (peace), it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), its governing verb being an implied verb of the same root, as if he said: "I greet you with peace (usallimu salaman)." It is also possible that "salaman" is a quotation expressing the meaning of what they said, not their exact words; this was said by Mujahid and al-Suddi, and therefore the verb "qala" (they said) governs it, as when you say, "The man said: 'There is no god but Allah,'" and you reply, "You spoke the truth, or sincerely." If you were to quote their exact words, it would not be correct for the verb "qala" to govern it. His saying, may He be blessed and exalted, "He said, 'Peace (salam)'" is a quotation of his exact words, and "salam" is in the nominative either as the subject (mubtada'), with the predicate omitted, its estimated form being "upon you," or as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being "my affair is peace." This is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so patience is beautiful﴾ [Yusuf: 18], which may be read as "so my affair is beautiful patience," or as "so patience is more beautiful."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited "qalu salaman, qala salamun." Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "qalu salaman, qala salmun," and their difference is similar in Surat adh-Dhariyat. This has two possible readings. It may mean the same word "salam" itself, as they say "hill" (halal) and "harm" (haram) and in the verse of the poet:

"We passed by and said, 'Ayh, salm (peace),' and she greeted back,
as the clouds, sweeping, are crowned with lightning."

"Iktalla" means: took a crown or something similar. Al-Tabari said: it is also related as "kama nkalla."

Or it may mean "salm" in the sense opposed to war, as one says, "We are at peace with you (salm lakum)." The greeting of the angels was a hoped-for supplication, which is why it was in the accusative; but the Friend (Abraham) greeted them with something better than what they gave, namely that which is firm and established, which is why it came in the nominative.

His saying, "fa-ma labitha an ja'a" (he did not delay before bringing), may be read with "ma" as a negation, with the subject of "labitha" being Abraham, and "an ja'a" in the accusative position, meaning "in that he came." It is also possible that "ma" is a negation and "an ja'a" is, by interpretation, a verbal noun in the nominative position as the subject of "labitha," meaning "his coming did not delay," and in this case "labitha" does not have Abraham as its subject. It is also possible that "ma" means "that which," with "labitha" having Abraham as its subject and "an ja'a" as the predicate of "ma," meaning: "Abraham delayed his coming with a roasted calf." It is part of the etiquette of hospitality that the host should make his hospitality follow this verse.

"Al-hanidh" means "mahnudh," i.e., a roasted calf, well done, whose juice drips. This dripping distinguishes the hanidh from other roasted meats. But the state of the mahnudh in the language is that it is covered with stones or heated sand, or with a barrier between it and the fire, by which it is covered; and the "mu'arrad" of roasted meat is that which is laid on the embers, while "muhaddab" is roasted meat that has a barrier between it and the fire, with the meat placed on it and not buried in it. And "tahnidh" in the training of horses means covering the horse with one blanket over another so that its sweat pours out.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But when he saw their hands﴾ and the verse: it is related that they used to dip arrows (in the manner of divination) into the meat, while their hands did not reach it. In this verse there is also an etiquette of eating: the host should observe whether his guest eats or not.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This should be done with a sidelong glance and discreetly, not with a fixed stare. It is related that a Bedouin ate with Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, and Sulayman saw a hair in the Bedouin's morsel and said to him, "Remove the hair from your morsel." He replied, "Do you look at me with the gaze of one who sees hair in my morsel? By Allah, I will not eat with you again."

As for "nakirahum" (he regarded them with suspicion), according to what many people have said, its meaning is "ankarahum" (he disliked/disowned them), and they cited in support of this the verse which Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' attributed to al-A'sha:

"She disowned me, and what she disowned was not any of the events except white hair and baldness."

Some people said: "nakira" is used of what is seen with the eye, so it is recognized as strange, while "ankara" is used of matters not established in meaning. So it is as if al-A'sha said: "You disowned my affection and my companionship," and so on; then he used "nakira" for white hair and baldness, which are visible to the eye. From this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"They saw him and shied away, and a swift, fast-running she-camel and a long-legged mount grappled with him."

What Abraham (peace be upon him) feared is indicated by their refusal to eat; for the custom of one who brings evil is that he does not eat the food of the one he visits. "Awjasa" means: he felt within himself fear of them. "Al-wajis" is what affects the soul at the time of caution and the beginnings of alarm. So they reassured him by saying, "Do not fear," and he knew that they were angels.

Then the verse turns to mention the woman and her good news. A group said its meaning is: she was standing behind a screen, listening to Abraham's conversation with his guests. Another group said its meaning is: she was standing in prayer. Al-Suddi said its meaning is: she was standing serving the people. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "and she was standing while he was sitting."

His saying, "fa-dahikat" (so she laughed): Mujahid said its meaning is: she menstruated. The lexicographers cited in support the verse:

"The laughing of hares upon the rock is like the blood of the belly on the day of encounter."

This view is weak and of little firmness. Some lexicographers denied that "dahikat" in the sense of "menstruated" occurs in Arabic speech, while others affirmed it. It is said "dahika" when something is full and overflows. Al-Zajjaj rejected the saying of Mujahid. The majority said it is the well-known laughter. They differed over what she laughed at. A group said: she laughed at their assurance to Abraham with their words, "Do not fear." Some made it conjoined to "Isaac," but it is not declined; the one who held this considered it easy to separate the conjunction from the conjoined by a prepositional phrase, whereas Sibawayh does not permit this except by repeating the preposition. It is as when you say: "I passed by Zayd today and yesterday 'Amr," where in his view the correct form is "and yesterday by 'Amr"; and if the preposition is not repeated, there is great awkwardness. The better way to read its accusative is that it is governed by an implied verb indicated by the glad tidings, the estimate being: "and from behind Isaac We granted Ya'qub"; this was preferred by Abu 'Ali.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It is related that at the time of this glad tidings Sarah was ninety-nine years old, and Abraham was a hundred years old.

This verse indicates that the one offered in sacrifice was Isma'il, and that he was older than Isaac. That is because Sarah, at the time when the tyrannical king had given her service (to Hajar), was a young, beautiful woman, as in the hadith; Abraham (peace be upon him) took her as an umm walad (mother of a child), and Sarah became jealous of her. He took her and her son Isma'il out from Sham upon the Buraq, and arrived in Makkah the same day, leaving them there (as is in the biographies), and returned to Sham the same day. Then came the glad tidings of Isaac, when Sarah was an old woman past childbearing. As for the way the verse indicates that Isaac was not the one offered: Sarah and Abraham were given glad tidings of Isaac, and that Ya'qub would be born to him; then he was commanded to sacrifice when his son reached the age of striving with him. How then could he be commanded to sacrifice a son who had already been given glad tidings that a son would be born to that son? Also, there is no report at all that Isaac entered the Hijaz, and there is consensus that the command of sacrifice took place at Mina. This purpose is supported by the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones" (ibn al-dhabihayn), meaning his father 'Abd Allah and his forefather Isma'il. It is also supported by what Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) drew as evidence from the sequence of Surat as-Saffat, for after the completion of the matter of the sacrificed one, He said: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾ [As-Saffat: 112].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In all of this there is a place for objections from the one who holds the other view, that the sacrificed one was Isaac; but what we have mentioned is the more preponderant, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 72–73:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿She said, "Woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is an astonishing thing!"﴾ ﴿They said, "Are you amazed at the decree of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the household. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious."﴾

People differed concerning the alif in His saying "yā waylatā" (woe to me). The most apparent view regarding it is that it substitutes for the ya' of possession (ya' al-idafah). Its original form is "yā waylatī," just as you say "yā ghulāman" (O boy) and "yā ghawthan" (O help). This alif may be followed by a ha' in speech, though it was not read that way. ʿĀṣim, al-Aʿmash and Abū ʿAmr inclined this alif (imālah).

The meaning of "yā waylatā" in this context is an expression of what overcame the soul of wonder at the birth of an old woman. The origin of this invocation of woe and the like is in lamentation for severe hardship or a distressing matter that troubles the soul; then it was afterward used for a wonder that overtakes the soul. Some said: she only said "yā waylatā" when the pain and severity of childbirth passed through her thoughts, then she returned in her thoughts to amazement and uttered her words, "Shall I give birth while I am an old woman?" — the verse.

A group read "a-ʾalidu" (ﺃﺄﻟِﺪُ) with both hamzas made clear (tahqiq). Another group read it with the first lightened and the second made clear, and pronouncing this is difficult. Another group read it with the first made clear and the second lightened, and the lightening here is its prolongation (madd). Another group read "ʾa-ʾalidu" with both hamzas made clear and a prolongation between them.

"Al-ʿajūz" is the aged woman, and some people have related that the Arabs say "al-ʿajūzah." "Al-baʿl" is the husband. "Shaykhan" is put in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and it is a state of a pointed-to subject (mushār ilayhi) that cannot be dispensed with, because it is the intended point of the statement. This is valid only if the speaker does not intend to define the bearer of the state, such as when the addressee already knows him. But if the speaker intends to define him, it is necessary that the definition be in the predicate before the state, and the state comes in its proper place, dispensable. An example of this is your saying, "This is Zayd standing," if you wish to define Zayd, or if he was known and you wished to define his standing. But if the speaker intends that Zayd's being Zayd is only while he is standing, then the statement is not permissible.

Al-Aʿmash read "hādhā baʿlī shaykhun" (this, my husband, is an old man). Abū Ḥātim said, "It is likewise in the codex of Ibn Masʿūd." Its nominative case has several aspects:

Among them: it is a predicate following a predicate, as you say, "This is sweet, sour." Among them: it is the predicate of an implied subject, its estimate being: "He is an old man." It is related that some people read it, "Wa hādhā baʿlī hādhā shaykhun," and this reading resembles this interpretation. Among them: it is an apposition (badal) to "baʿlī." Among them: her saying "baʿlī" is an apposition to "hādhā" or an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān) upon it, and "shaykhun" is the predicate of "hādhā."

It is said "shaykh" and "shaykhah," though some Arabs use "shaykh" for both masculine and feminine. It is related that Sarah was at the time of this utterance ninety-nine years old. It was said: ninety, said by Ibn Isḥāq. It was said: eighty. Likewise it was said about the age of Ibrahim, that he was one hundred and twenty years old; it was said: one hundred years; and other figures that need a sound chain of transmission.

The pronoun in His saying "qālū" (they said) refers to the angels, and His saying "min amr Allah" (at the decree of Allah) may mean one of the matters, i.e., of giving birth at this age, and it may mean the verbal noun of "amara" (to command), i.e., of what Allah commanded in this event.

His saying "raḥmatu Allāh wa barakātuhu ʿalaykum ahla al-bayt" (the mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the household): the wording may be a supplication or a statement of fact, and its being a statement is more noble, because that requires the mercy and blessing to have been realized for them, whereas its being a supplication only requires that it is something hoped for and not yet attained. The accusative of "ahla al-bayt" is in the mode of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ). This is the view of Sibawayh, and for this reason this and the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ) were placed in two chapters, as if he distinguished the accusative of praise by the word in the accusative itself containing praise in its essence, as you say, "This is Zayd, wise of his people." Specification was assigned when the word does not contain that, as in his saying, "Indeed we, the company of the prophets," and "Indeed we, the sons of Nahshal."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Specification is only with praise or blame, but this is not in the accusative word itself.

This verse indicates that a man's wife is among his household, since she was addressed with this. Thus the view regarding the wives of the Prophet ﷺ is strengthened, that they are among his household, whom Allah removed uncleanness from, contrary to what the Shiʿah hold. Some scholars also said this. They said: "the household of his" are those who were forbidden the charity. The first view is stronger and is clear and evident from Surat al-Aḥzāb, because He addressed them with His saying, ﴿O wives of the Prophet﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 30], then with His saying, "ahla al-bayt."

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In al-Bukhārī there occurs, from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "The household of his are those who were forbidden the charity after him." Ibn ʿAbbās intended the household of lineage, concerning whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed, charity is not lawful for the household of mine; it is only the filth of people."

The "bayt" (house) in this verse and in Surat al-Aḥzāb is the house of dwelling, so in the word there is a shared meaning (ishtirāk) that should be examined. Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, is among the household of Muhammad ﷺ in both senses, and ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, in one sense, and his wives in the other. As for the Shiʿah, they exclude the wives out of hatred for ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her. "Ḥamīd" means His actions require that He be praised; "Majīd" means He is characterized by attributes of elevation, and "majada" is said of a thing when its attributes are good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 74–76:

The Exalted and Majestic said:

﴿So when fear had left Abraham and the glad tidings had come to him, he began to argue with Us concerning the people of Lot.﴾ ﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing, compassionate, and repentant.﴾ ﴿"O Abraham, turn away from this. Indeed, the command of your Lord has come, and indeed there will reach them a punishment that cannot be turned back."﴾

Al-ra'w (ar-rawʿ): the fright and fear that was mentioned earlier, and its departure was by their informing him that they were angels. Al-bushra (al-bushrā): 

It may mean the child, and it may mean other glad tidings, the intended meaning being something other than that; the first is clearer. His saying "yujadiluna" (he argues with Us) is a present-tense verb, which may stand in the place of the past tense that would suit the answer of "lamma" (when), especially since the difficulty is removed by the passing of the time of the matter and the listeners' knowledge of it. It may also be that the estimate is "zalla" or "akhadha" or the like, so that "yujadiluna" means "he began to argue," and it was omitted for brevity because the apparent speech points to it. It may also be that his saying "yujadiluna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from Abraham, or from the pronoun in his saying "jā'athu" (came to him), and the answer of "lamma" in the second verse would be: "We said: O Abraham, turn away from this." Abu 'Ali chose this view. Al-mujadala (argument) means the exchange of speech and proofs, and it seems more general than al-mukhasama (contention), for one may argue with someone without contending with him, as Abraham did.

In this incident Abraham was described as "ḥalīm" (forbearing). It was said: he never became angry for his own sake, except that he became angry for the sake of God.

Al-ḥilm (ḥilm): intellect, unless it is joined by patience (anāh) and forbearance (iḥtimāl). Al-awwāh (awwāh) means: one who is fearful and often moans (ta'awwuh) out of fear of God the Exalted. It is related that Abraham, peace be upon him, used to hear the pounding of his heart out of awe; it was said: like the hearing of the wings of vultures. The commentators have various expressions concerning "al-awwāh," all of which return to what I have mentioned and necessarily include it. Al-munīb (munīb): one who returns to God the Exalted in all his affairs.

The form of Abraham's argument, peace be upon him, was that he said: "If there are one hundred believers among them, will you punish them?" They said: "No." He said: "Then ninety?" They said: "No." He said: "Then eighty?" He continued thus until he reached five, and he stopped at that point, having counted in Lot's house his wife, and he found six of them there, so he hoped for their salvation and did not perceive that she was among the disbelievers. This was from Abraham out of eagerness for the faith and salvation of that nation. The narrators among the commentators have varied greatly regarding these numbers in the speech of Abraham, peace be upon him, and the meaning of all of them is close to what I have mentioned. Likewise they mentioned that the people of Lot were four hundred thousand in five villages. A group said: the intended meaning is "He argues with Us concerning the believers among the people of Lot," but this is weak; and His command to him to turn away from the argument requires that the argument was concerning the disbelievers out of eagerness for them. The meaning: "We said: O Abraham, turn away from arguing about these people and from pleading on their behalf, for the decree has been executed upon them, and the command of your Lord has come." The "amr" here means: a singular matter, by the context of its being described as having "come"; if we make it the verbal noun of "amara," we estimate an omitted modifier, i.e., "the requirement of the command of your Lord has come," and similar. His saying "ātīhim ʿadhāb" is an inchoative and predicate, a clause in the position of the predicate of "inna." It was said: "ātīhim" is the predicate of "inna," being an active participle dependent on what precedes it, and "ʿadhāb" is its subject (fā'il) with "ātīhim."

This verse indicates that supplication is only that God enables the one who supplicates to seek what is within His decree; as for supplication seeking what is not decreed, it is futile and of no benefit.

It is said that they found Lot in his field, and it is said that they found his daughter drawing water from the river of Sodom, which was the largest of the cities of Lot's people. They asked her to direct them to someone who would host them. She saw their appearance and feared for them from Lot's people, and said to them, "Wait here," and she went to her father and informed him. He went out to them, and they said to him:

"We want you to host us tonight." He said to them, "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said, "And what are their deeds?" He said, "I testify before God that they are the worst people on earth." God, Mighty and Majestic, had said to the angels, "Do not punish them until Lot has testified against them four times." When Lot said this, Gabriel said to his companions, "This is one." The statement went back and forth among them until Lot repeated the testimony four times. Then Lot brought them into the city, and at that time he was "distressed on their account," meaning that harm had befallen him.

"Distressed" (sī'a) is a verb in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ūl). "Al-dhar'" (felt helplessness) is a verbal noun derived from "al-dhirā'" (the forearm). Since the forearm is the seat of a person's strength, it was said of a matter that one cannot bear: "This matter has constricted the forearm of so-and-so" (ḍāqa bihi dhirā'u fulān) and "the dhar' of so-and-so," meaning his resourcefulness with his forearm. They extended this usage until they reversed it, saying "so-and-so is broad of forearm" (raḥb al-dhirā') when they described him with breadth of capability. From this is the saying of the poet:

"O lord, you are not a lord of the kind who is ... trodden-shouldered, broad of forearm."

His saying, "This is a trying day" (yawm 'aṣīb), indicates what he feared of his people's aggression against his guests, and his need to repel them while he was too weak to do so. "'Aṣīb" is an active participle form (ism fā'il) meaning one who "afflicts people with evil," just as one who beats a sallama tree (a thorny acacia) to shake off its leaves afflicts it. From this is al-Hajjaj's saying in his sermon: "I will certainly beat you as one beats the sallama tree." It derives from "al-'iṣāba" (binding). Then the description "'aṣīb" came to be applied to days. From this is the saying of the poet, who is 'Adī ibn Zayd:

"I was the fierce opponent of your enemy and did not flee, and they confronted you on a trying day."

From this is the saying of another:

"If you do not accept Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a trying day in Iraq."

So "'aṣīb," in general, is in the place of something severe and hard to bear, and its derivation is as we have mentioned.

As for His saying, "His people came to him" (wa-jā'ahu qawmuhu), it is related that the unbelieving wife of Lot, when she saw the guests and saw their beauty and appearance, went out until she came to the gatherings of her people and said to them, "Lot has hosted tonight young men the like of whom has never been seen for beauty, and such and such." Then they came rushing toward him. "Yuhra'ūn" means "they hasten." "Al-ih'rā'" is that a matter drives a person to hasten until he moves between a trot and a run; it is the gait of a captive who is rushed along, or of a greedy person who hurries toward a matter he fears losing. Similarly it is said: "The man was driven (hari'a) and it made him hasten (ahra'ahu), whether by greed, enemy, fear, or the like."

The well-known reading is "yuhra'ūn" with a dammah on the yā', meaning greed drives them on (yuhri'uhumu al-ṭama'). A group read "yahra'ūn" with a fatḥah on the yā', from hara'a. From this word is the saying of Muhalhil:

"They came rushing, while they were captives, led against their will."

His saying, "and before this they had been doing evil deeds" means that their custom was to commit the abomination with men. So they came to the guests for that purpose, and Lot stood up to them in defence and said, "These are my daughters." One group said that he pointed to his own daughters and urged them in this statement toward marriage. This would be on the basis that their custom permitted marrying a believing woman to an unbeliever, or on the basis that his words implied that they should believe. Another group said that his words were only a means of repelling them and he did not intend their fulfilment. This view was narrated from Abu 'Ubayda, and it is weak. It is like saying to someone who forbids the property of another: "The pig is more lawful for you than this." This kind of hair-splitting is not the speech of the prophets (peace be upon them). Another group said that by his saying "my daughters" he referred to the women in general, since the prophet of a people is a father to them. This is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is their father." Lot also, under this interpretation, pointed to marriage.

One group, which is the majority (al-jumhūr), read "hunna aṭhar" with a ḍammah on the rā', as the predicate of the inchoative (khabar al-ibtidā'). Al-Hasan, 'Isa ibn 'Umar, Muhammad ibn Marwan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read "aṭhara" with a fatḥah. Sibawayh said: "This is a grammatical error (laḥn)." Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: "Ibn Marwan persisted in his error (iḥtabā fīhi... fī laḥnihi)." The way of reading it with the accusative, according to those who recited it so, is that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl): "my daughters" is the inchoative subject, "hunna" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "these" (hā'ulā').

This is a grammatical analysis (i'rāb) narrated from al-Mubarrad, and Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) mentioned it, but it is an error regarding the meaning of the verse. He corrected only the wording, while the meaning is in His saying "aṭhar," and this is the point to be stated. So it is a circumstantial clause that cannot be dispensed with, as was mentioned in His saying, "and this is my husband, an old man" (hādhā ba'lī shaykhan). The correct analysis is to say: "hā'ulā' banātī" is an inchoative and predicate, "hunna" is a separator (faṣl, pronoun of separation), and "aṭhar" is a circumstantial clause. Although the condition for a separator is that it should come between two definites, so that the speech is separated from the description and goes on to the predicate, nevertheless, since the predicate here is "aṭhar," the separator was permissible. Since Abu 'Amr and Sibawayh did not accept this, they judged Ibn Marwan's reading to be an error. Abu 'Amr and Sibawayh would not have overlooked what Abu al-Fath mentioned.

Their custom was that whoever was refused in a marriage proposal to a woman would never be lawful to her again. Therefore they said, "You know that we have no right to your daughters."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is far-fetched that this was their special custom. The meaning of the speech is: we have no connection to your daughters, nor is that our intention, nor is there a custom we seek in that matter. Their saying, "and you know well what we want," refers to the guests. When he saw their persistence in their error and their dominance and his weakness before them, he said, in a tone of grief and humiliation, "If only I had strength against you." This is a regular feature of "anna" that follows "law" (if only). The response to "law" is omitted, and omitting such a response is more eloquent, because it leaves the hearer to reach the furthest of his imaginings. The meaning is: "I would have done such and such."

The majority read "aw āwī" with the yā' silent. Shayba and Abu Ja'far read "aw āwiya" with the accusative, the estimate being "aw an āwiya," so that "an" with "āwī" is understood as a verbal noun, as Maysun bint Bahdal said:

"And wearing a cloak, and my eye being comforted..."

The arrangement of the speech would then be: "If only I had strength against you, or a refuge." "Āwā" means: to seek refuge and join. Lot's intention, peace be upon him, by "al-rukn" (mighty support) is the clan and the protection of numbers. The ugliness of their deeds drove him to this, despite his knowledge of what is with God, Exalted is He. It is related that the angels were displeased with him when he said these words, and they said, "Indeed your support is mighty." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on Lot; he used to take refuge in a mighty support." So what is strange is that he showed weakness.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a criticism, because Lot uttered these words. Otherwise, the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) at the time of the placing of the entrails of the slaughtered camel, with the people of Ta'if, and on other occasions, would call for the statement of Lot. But Muhammad (ﷺ) did not utter anything of that kind, out of steadfastness and courage. Lot only feared that God would give respite to those wicked people so that they would disobey him concerning the guests, as He had given them respite before that for their sins. So he wished for a human support that would overtake them with it, while he knew that God, Exalted is He, is behind their punishment. It is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, Exalted is He, did not send a prophet after Lot except among a people of abundance," meaning in protection and might.

This is a regular feature of "anna" that follows "law" (if only). The majority read "aw āwī" with the yā' silent. Shayba and Abu Ja'far read "aw āwiya" with the accusative, the estimate being "aw an āwiya," so that "an" with "āwī" is understood as a verbal noun, as Maysun bint Bahdal said:

"And wearing a cloak, and my eye being comforted..."

The arrangement of the speech would then be: "If only I had strength against you, or a refuge." "Āwā" means: to seek refuge and join. Lot's intention, peace be upon him, by "al-rukn" (mighty support) is the clan and the protection of numbers. The ugliness of their deeds drove him to this, despite his knowledge of what is with God, Exalted is He. It is related that the angels were displeased with him when he said these words, and they said, "Indeed your support is mighty." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on Lot; he used to take refuge in a mighty support." So what is strange is that he showed weakness.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is a criticism, because Lot uttered these words. Otherwise, the state of the Prophet (ﷺ) at the time of the placing of the entrails of the slaughtered camel, with the people of Ta'if, and on other occasions, would call for the statement of Lot. But Muhammad (ﷺ) did not utter anything of that kind, out of steadfastness and courage. Lot only feared that God would give respite to those wicked people so that they would disobey him concerning the guests, as He had given them respite before that for their sins. So he wished for a human support that would overtake them with it, while he knew that God, Exalted is He, is behind their punishment. It is related that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God, Exalted is He, did not send a prophet after Lot except among a people of abundance," meaning in protection and might.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 11, verses 77–80:**

The Almighty's saying:

﴿When Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed on their account and felt helpless for them, and said, "This is a trying day."﴾ ﴿His people came rushing toward him, and before this they had been doing evil deeds. He said, "O my people, these are my daughters; they are purer for you. So fear God and do not disgrace me concerning my guests. Is there not among you one right-minded man?"﴾ ﴿They said, "You know that we have no right to your daughters, and you know well what we want."﴾ ﴿He said, "If only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in a mighty support."﴾

"The messengers" here are the angels who were the guests of Abraham (peace be upon him). When they went out to the town of Lot, which was eight miles from the village of Abraham, they reached it. It is said that they found Lot in his field, and it is said that they found his daughter drawing water from the river of Sodom, which was the largest of the cities of Lot's people. They asked her to direct them to someone who would host them. She saw their appearance and feared for them from Lot's people, and said to them, "Wait here," and she went to her father and informed him. He went out to them, and they said to him:

"We want you to host us tonight." He said to them, "Have you not heard of the deeds of these people?" They said, "And what are their deeds?" He said, "I testify before God that they are the worst people on earth." God, Mighty and Majestic, had said to the angels, "Do not punish them until Lot has testified against them four times." When Lot said this, Gabriel said to his companions, "This is one." The statement went back and forth among them until Lot repeated the testimony four times. Then Lot brought them into the city, and at that time he was "distressed on their account," meaning that harm had befallen him.

"Distressed" (sī'a) is a verb in the passive voice (mabni li-l-maf'ūl). "Al-dhar'" (felt helplessness) is a verbal noun derived from "al-dhirā'" (the forearm). Since the forearm is the seat of a person's strength, it was said of a matter that one cannot bear: "This matter has constricted the forearm of so-and-so" (ḍāqa bihi dhirā'u fulān) and "the dhar' of so-and-so," meaning his resourcefulness with his forearm. They extended this usage until they reversed it, saying "so-and-so is broad of forearm" (raḥb al-dhirā') when they described him with breadth of capability. From this is the saying of the poet:

"O lord, you are not a lord of the kind who is ... trodden-shouldered, broad of forearm."

His saying, "This is a trying day" (yawm 'aṣīb), indicates what he feared of his people's aggression against his guests, and his need to repel them while he was too weak to do so. "'Aṣīb" is an active participle form (ism fā'il) meaning one who "afflicts people with evil," just as one who beats a sallama tree (a thorny acacia) to shake off its leaves afflicts it. From this is al-Hajjaj's saying in his sermon: "I will certainly beat you as one beats the sallama tree." It derives from "al-'iṣāba" (binding). Then the description "'aṣīb" came to be applied to days. From this is the saying of the poet, who is 'Adī ibn Zayd:

"I was the fierce opponent of your enemy and did not flee, and they confronted you on a trying day."

From this is the saying of another:

"If you do not accept Bakr ibn Wa'il, there will be for you a trying day in Iraq."

So "'aṣīb," in general, is in the place of something severe and hard to bear, and its derivation is as we have mentioned.

As for His saying, "His people came to him" (wa-jā'ahu qawmuhu), it is related that the unbelieving wife of Lot, when she saw the guests and saw their beauty and appearance, went out until she came to the gatherings of her people and said to them, "Lot has hosted tonight young men the like of whom has never been seen for beauty, and such and such." Then they came rushing toward him. "Yuhra'ūn" means "they hasten." "Al-ih'rā'" is that a matter drives a person to hasten until he moves between a trot and a run; it is the gait of a captive who is rushed along, or of a greedy person who hurries toward a matter he fears losing. Similarly it is said: "The man was driven (hari'a) and it made him hasten (ahra'ahu), whether by greed, enemy, fear, or the like."

The well-known reading is "yuhra'ūn" with a dammah on the yā', meaning greed drives them on (yuhri'uhumu al-ṭama'). A group read "yahra'ūn" with a fatḥah on the yā', from hara'a. From this word is the saying of Muhalhil:

"They came rushing, while they were captives, led against their will."

His saying, "and before this they had been doing evil deeds" means that their custom was to commit the abomination with men. So they came to the guests for that purpose, and Lot stood up to them in defence and said, "These are my daughters." One group said that he pointed to his own daughters and urged them in this statement toward marriage. This would be on the basis that their custom permitted marrying a believing woman to an unbeliever, or on the basis that his words implied that they should believe. Another group said that his words were only a means of repelling them and he did not intend their fulfilment. This view was narrated from Abu 'Ubayda, and it is weak. It is like saying to someone who forbids the property of another: "The pig is more lawful for you than this." This kind of hair-splitting is not the speech of the prophets (peace be upon them). Another group said that by his saying "my daughters" he referred to the women in general, since the prophet of a people is a father to them. This is strengthened by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is their father." Lot also, under this interpretation, pointed to marriage.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 81:

The phrase of the Most High:

﴿They said, "O Lut, indeed we are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you. So travel with your family during a part of the night, and let not anyone among you look back, except your wife. Indeed, she will be struck by what strikes them. Indeed, their appointed time is the morning. Is not the morning near?"﴾

The pronoun in "qalu" (they said) refers to the angels. It is narrated that when the people overpowered Lut and attempted to break down the door while he was holding it shut, the messengers said to him, "Step away from the door." He stepped aside, the door was flung open, and Jibril (peace be upon him) struck them with his wing, blinding their eyes, and they were made blind. They turned back on their heels, saying, "Escape! Escape!" "There are sorcerers with Lut," and they threatened Lut. Lut was then frightened by their threat, and at that point they said to him, "Indeed we are messengers of your Lord," and he was reassured. This is what al-Naqqash mentioned, but the tafsir of others implies that their saying "Indeed we are messengers of your Lord" came before the blinding of the eyes. Then they commanded him to travel by night and informed him that the punishment was descending upon the people. Lut said to them, "Then punish them now." They said to him, "Indeed their appointed time is the morning," meaning that this is what God has commanded. Then they comforted him in his anxiety with their words:

"Is not the morning near?"

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "fa-sri" (from sara, which means to travel during part of the night), while the rest read "fa-asri" (from asra, which means to travel at the beginning of the night). "Al-qit'" means a portion of the night. It is possible that Lut traveled with his family from the beginning of the night until he passed the town that was uprooted, and his deliverance occurred at dawn. Thus this verse is reconciled with His saying: "Except the family of Lut; We delivered them at dawn." The line of al-Nabigha combined the two verbs in his saying:

﻿؎ Asrat 'alayhi min al-Jawza'i sariyatun ∗∗∗ tuzjī al-shamālu 'alayhi jāmida al-barad

Some people held that sara and asra have one meaning, and they used this line as evidence.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I say that the line may bear both meanings, and that is more apparent to me, because he intended to describe this rainstorm, that it began at the beginning of the night at the time of the rising of al-Jawza' in winter.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "illa imra'atuka" with the nominative (raf'), as a substitute (badal) for "ahad," and this is the more correct reading when the exception is from a negated statement, as in your saying: "No one came to me except Zayd." This is the exception from those who turn back. The rest read "illa imra'ataka" with the accusative (nasb). A group of grammarians considered the accusative to be the preferred form in exception from a negated statement, since a negated statement in this sense is independent in itself, like an affirmative one, and therefore its ruling is like its ruling regarding the accusative of the exception. Some of those who read "illa imra'ataka" with the accusative interpreted the exception as coming from "al-ahl" (the family), as if he had said: "So travel with your family except your wife." On this interpretation, only the accusative is possible.

Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam said: If the statement were "wa la yaltafit" with the nominative, the nominative in His saying "illa imra'atuka" would be correct; but it is a prohibition, so when "the woman" is excepted from "ahad," "the woman" must be one for whom turning back was permitted, and thus the meaning of the verse would be corrupted.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This objection is sound. It applies to the exception from "ahad" whether you read the ta' with a damma or a fatha. Its resolution is found in a statement related from al-Mubarrad, which is that the prohibition was directed at Lut alone, and "turning back" is negated for them in meaning, i.e., do not let any one of them turn back. This is like your saying to a man: "None of these should stand up except Zayd," while those people have not heard you; the meaning is: do not let any one of these stand up, and standing is negated in meaning for those referred to.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The summary of this is that the wording of the verse is the wording of our saying: "None should stand except Zayd," and we need its meaning to be the meaning of our saying: "None should stand except Zayd." That wording does not return to this meaning except by the supposition that al-Mubarrad related, so reflect upon it. It appears from the position of Abu 'Ubayd that the exception is only from "the family." In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "So travel with your family during a part of the night, except your wife," and the words "and let not anyone among you look back" are omitted.

The apparent meaning of "yaltafit" is that it derives from looking back (iltifat al-basar). A group said it derives from lafata al-shay' yalfituhu, meaning to twist or turn something, so its meaning would be: "and let him not hesitate." This is anomalous despite being sound. In the book of al-Zahrawi, the meaning is: "and let no one look back at what was left behind, but rather let him leave hastily with Lut, peace be upon him." It is narrated that when the wife of Lut heard the crash, she turned her gaze back and said, "Alas, my people!" A stone struck her and killed her.

A group read "al-Subuh" with a damma on the ba'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 82–83:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿So when Our command came, We turned it upside down and rained upon it stones of hardened clay (sijjil), layered one upon another,﴾ ﴿marked from your Lord. And it is not far from the wrongdoers.﴾

It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, inserted his wing beneath the cities of the people of Lut, uprooted them, and raised them until the people of the lowest heaven heard the crowing of roosters and the barking of dogs. Then he sent them down upside down, and the stones followed them from the sky. It is also narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, seized them with the outer feathers of his wing. And it is related that one city among them was spared, one that was specific to Lut, peace be upon him, called Zughar.

As for "Our command" (amrunā) in this verse, it may be a verbal noun from amara, and the speech would then contain an omitted modifier, its estimated form being: "the requirement of Our command." It may also be the singular of "affairs" (umur). The pronoun in His saying "its highest part its lowest" refers to the cities. The verb "rained upon it" is used in the same way, and what is meant is "upon its people." It is also related that the stones overtook those among them who were outside their cities, until they killed them all. And it is related that among them there was a man in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram) whose stone remained suspended in the air until he left the Haram, and then the stone killed him. "Amtara" (to rain upon) is always used for what is disliked, whereas "matara" (to rain) is used for what is loved. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not so, and His saying, may He be exalted: "This is a cloud bringing us rain" (46:24) refutes this view, because they only thought it was a cloud of the usual mercy. As for His saying "of sijjil," there is disagreement about it. Ibn Zayd said: "Sijjil is the name of the lowest heaven."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, and its description as "layered" (mandud) refutes it. Another group said: it is derived from the word al-sijill, meaning that it is from a matter written against them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched. Another group said: it is derived from al-sajl, when a thing is released as the bucket (sajl) is released, and as you say: "He said it as a released (musajjala) utterance."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Another group said: "min sijjil" means: from Jahannam, because it is said: sijjil and sijjin, with a lam placed in it instead of a nun, as they said: uṣaylāl and uṣaylān. Another group said: sijjil means: hard. Al-Tabari cited in this regard:

؎ "A blow which the warriors have enjoined upon one another as sijjil"

The verse is from a rhyming ode (qasida nuniyya), where the word is sijjīnan. Another group said: sijjil is a word whose origin is non-Arabic (ghayr muʿarraba); its origin is "sanj" and "jil." It has also been said that its origin is other than this. Its meaning is water and clay. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and others. This group holds that the stones with which they were pelted were like baked brick, made of clay that had turned to stone (this was explicitly stated by al-Hasan).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is plausible, and it is the correct one upon which the majority agree. Another group said: the meaning of sijjil is a stone mixed with clay, that is, stone and clay. The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This could be referred back to the view before it, since baked brick and what resembles it may be described as stone and clay, for it has taken a share of each of the two. It is clay in terms of its origin, and stone in terms of having been hardened.

"Mandud" means: one part upon another, that is, successive. It is an adjective of sijjil. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said, regarding "nadduhu": that it is in the heaven, arranged, one part upon another.

"Musawwama" means: marked with a sign. 'Ikrima and Qatada said: there were white and red marks on them. It is related that each stone bore the name of its owner. This word is from sawwama, meaning to make known. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." It may also be that "musawwama" here means "sent down," and its marking is from its descent.

His saying "and it is not far" refers to the stones. "The wrongdoers" was said to mean the Quraysh. It was also said that it means the general category of everyone characterized by wrongdoing, and this is the more correct view, because it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will occur in my community sinking, transformation, and being pelted with stones." There is also a hadith: "Indeed this community is safe from that." It was said that by "it" (hiya) is meant the cities, and the meaning would be an informing that these lands were near Makkah. The first is clearer. It is related that these lands were between Madina and Syria. Al-Tabari, in naming these cities, mentioned: Say'a, Sa'ada, 'Amaza, Duma, and Sadum, which is the greatest of the villages.

This is weak, and its description as "layered" (mandud) refutes it. Another group said: it is derived from the word al-sijill, meaning that it is from a matter written against them.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched. Another group said: it is derived from al-sajl, when a thing is released as the bucket (sajl) is released, and as you say: "He said it as a released (musajjala) utterance."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Another group said: "min sijjil" means: from Jahannam, because it is said: sijjil and sijjin, with a lam placed in it instead of a nun, as they said: uṣaylāl and uṣaylān. Another group said: sijjil means: hard. Al-Tabari cited in this regard:

؎ "A blow which the warriors have enjoined upon one another as sijjil"

The verse is from a rhyming ode (qasida nuniyya), where the word is sijjīnan. Another group said: sijjil is a word whose origin is non-Arabic (ghayr muʿarraba); its origin is "sanj" and "jil." It has also been said that its origin is other than this. Its meaning is water and clay. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi and others. This group holds that the stones with which they were pelted were like baked brick, made of clay that had turned to stone (this was explicitly stated by al-Hasan).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This view is plausible, and it is the correct one upon which the majority agree. Another group said: the meaning of sijjil is a stone mixed with clay, that is, stone and clay. The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This could be referred back to the view before it, since baked brick and what resembles it may be described as stone and clay, for it has taken a share of each of the two. It is clay in terms of its origin, and stone in terms of having been hardened.

"Mandud" means: one part upon another, that is, successive. It is an adjective of sijjil. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said, regarding "nadduhu": that it is in the heaven, arranged, one part upon another.

"Musawwama" means: marked with a sign. 'Ikrima and Qatada said: there were white and red marks on them. It is related that each stone bore the name of its owner. This word is from sawwama, meaning to make known. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr: "Mark yourselves, for the angels have marked themselves." It may also be that "musawwama" here means "sent down," and its marking is from its descent.

His saying "and it is not far" refers to the stones. "The wrongdoers" was said to mean the Quraysh. It was also said that it means the general category of everyone characterized by wrongdoing, and this is the more correct view, because it is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "There will occur in my community sinking, transformation, and being pelted with stones." There is also a hadith: "Indeed this community is safe from that." It was said that by "it" (hiya) is meant the cities, and the meaning would be an informing that these lands were near Makkah. The first is clearer. It is related that these lands were between Madina and Syria. Al-Tabari, in naming these cities, mentioned: Say'a, Sa'ada, 'Amaza, Duma, and Sadum, which is the greatest of the villages.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 84–86:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb. He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the balance. Indeed, I see you in prosperity, and indeed I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day."﴾ ﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight with justice, and do not deprive the people of their things, and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing corruption.﴾ ﴿What remains with Allah is better for you, if you are believers. And I am not a watcher over you.﴾

The estimated sense: "And to Madyan We sent their brother Shu'ayb." Scholars differ over the word Madyan. It has been said that it is a place, so the estimate according to this is: "And to the people of Madyan," as in His saying: ﴿and ask the town﴾. It has also been said that this region was in the direction of al-Sham. And it has been said that Madyan is the name of a man, and the tribe was from his descendants, so it was named after him; Madyan is not declinable in both cases (i.e., whether it refers to the place or the man). Al-Naqqash related that Madyan was the biological son of Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is far-fetched. It has also been said that Shu'ayb was Arab, so how can this be reconciled, since the Arabs have no connection to Ibrahim except through Isma'il alone? Shu'ayb's calling them to "the worship of Allah" implies that they were worshipping idols, and this is clear from their words later on. Their disbelief is what made them deserve the punishment, not their sins, for Allah never punished a nation except on account of disbelief; if sin is added to that, it is a follower. By punishment I mean the general annihilation. The grave sin of this nation was that they had colluded to take full measure from those who came to them from outside and to give short measure in their weighing and measuring; so Shu'ayb, by the revelation of Allah the Exalted, forbade them from this. It appears from the book of al-Zajjaj that they had mutually agreed that some of them would cheat others.

As for His saying "with prosperity" (bi-khayr), Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: in cheapness of prices. And "the punishment of the encompassing day" is the arrival of destructive high prices. This interpretation accords with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): «No people diminish the measure and the balance except that provision is lifted from them.» It has also been said that for them His saying "with prosperity" is general, covering all the blessings of Allah the Exalted, and "the punishment of the day" is the destruction that befell them at the end. All that has been said about the word "khayr" is confined to what we have mentioned.

Describing "the day" with "encompassing" (ihata), which is an attribute of punishment, is figurative, since the punishment occurs on the day. It is also possible to describe "the day" as "encompassing" with the estimate: "encompassing its evil," and similar.

He repeated the injunction to them regarding "measure and weight" as emphasis, clarification and admonition, because "and do not diminish" is, in essence, "give full measure." However, the two tend toward one meaning.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

My father, may Allah be pleased with him, related to me that he heard Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Jawhari, on the pulpit in Egypt, exhorting people regarding measure and weight, saying: "Reflect on the fact that when a person raises his hand with the balance, his three fingers extend and the thumb and index finger meet on the top of the balance; the shape of his fingers then forms the likeness of the written letter, so it is as if the balance says: Allah, Allah."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a fine and reminding exhortation. Al-qist (qist) is justice and the like. Al-bakhs is deficiency. Ta'thaw means: you strive in corruption. He repeated "mufsidin" for emphasis. It is said 'atha ya'thu, or 'atha ya'thi, and 'add ya'uddu, and 'aza ya'iadh, meaning: he caused corruption, and similar in meaning. Al-'uththa is the worm that corrupts woolen garments.

As for His saying "baqiyyat Allah": Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said its meaning is: what Allah leaves for you of your wealth after you have fulfilled the measure and the weight is better for you than what you pile up, you yourselves, in a manner not in accordance with its right.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation fitting to the wording of the verse. Mujahid said its meaning is: obedience to Allah. Ibn 'Abbas also said its meaning is: the provision of Allah. All of this is not what the wording of the verse conveys; rather, the meaning in my view is: Allah's preserving (ibqa') of you, if you obey.

Isma'il ibn Ja'far related from the people of Madina a reading with the letter ya' lightened (baqiyyat → baqiyyatu/baqiyya), and this is a dialect. His saying "if you are believers" is a condition for the remainder being better for them; as for with disbelief, there is no good for them in any of the deeds. The answer to this condition is already stated earlier. "Al-hafiz" is the watcher who guards the states of those he observes. The meaning is:

I am only a conveyer (of the message), and the Hafiz, the Reckoner, is the One who recompenses you for your deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 87–88:

(p-5) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb! Does your prayer command you that we abandon what our fathers worshipped, or that we not do with our wealth what we wish? Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided."﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people! Have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord, and He has provided me from Himself with good provision — and I do not intend to oppose you in what I forbid you from. I intend only reform as far as I am able. My success is only through Allah. In Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn back."﴾

The majority of readers recited "أصَلَواتُكَ" (aṣalawātuka, "your prayers") in the plural, but Ibn Wathhab recited "أصَلاتُكَ" (aṣalātuka) in the singular. He also recited in the singular in at-Tawba, "إنَّ صَلاتَكَ" (inna ṣalātaka), and in al-Mu'minun, "عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ" ('alā ṣalātihim), all in the singular. The meaning of "ṣalāh" (prayer) here has been disputed. One group said: they meant the well-known prayers, and it is reported that Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was the most prayerful of the prophets. Al-Hasan said: Allah did not send any prophet without making prayer and zakat obligatory upon him. It was also said: they meant "your recitation" (qirā'atuka). It was said: they meant "your mosques." It was said: they meant "your supplications" (du'ā'uka).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The closest of these opinions are the first and the fourth.

They made "the command" attributed to the one who performs the prayers in a figurative sense, because whoever attains a rank of good or evil is, for the most part, drawn by his ranks to increase in that kind. The meaning is: "Does your being a praying man lead you to go beyond to denouncing our religion and our state?" His state of prayer emboldened him to that, so it was said: "it commands you," as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45].

Their saying: ﴿that we abandon what our fathers worshipped﴾ is an explicit text that they were worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted. The majority of readers recited "نَفْعَلُ" (naf'alu) and "نَشاءُ" (nashā'u) with the nun of the plural in both. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays recited "تَفْعَلُ" (taf'alu) and "تَشاءُ" (tashā'u) with the ta' of address in both. It is also reported from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman: "نَفْعَلُ" with the nun and "تَشاءُ" with the ta', and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. As for the one who recites with the nun in both, then the second "أنْ" (an) is conjoined to "ما" (mā), not to the first "أنْ"; because the meaning becomes: "Does your prayer command you that we do with our wealth what we wish?" This reverses what they intended. As for the one who recites with the ta' in both, then it is valid for the second "أنْ" to be conjoined to the first "أنْ." Some grammarians said: it is also valid to conjoin it to "ما," and the meaning is complete in both cases.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"نَتْرُكَ" (natruka) in the first case comes to mean "we reject," and in the second case comes to mean "we determine." This possibility is, in my view, impossible because of what I have mentioned regarding the variation of "leaving" upon the verbal judgment, or upon an elided genitive. Do you not see that "leaving" in the recitation of the one who recites with the nun in both verbs is merely in the sense of rejecting, without variation? As for the one who recites with the nun in "نَفْعَلُ" and the ta' in "تَشاءُ," then "أنْ" is conjoined to the first, and it is not permissible for it to be conjoined to "ما," because the meaning would also be reversed, so reflect on it.

The apparent meaning of their action to which they pointed is the stinting in measure and weight that was mentioned earlier. It is reported that the reference is to their clipping of the dinar and the dirham, and passing that off with the sound coin by way of deception; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others. It is also reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said: "Clipping dinars and dirhams is among the corruption in the land." He interpreted it in this earlier-mentioned sense. It may also be interpreted as meaning altering the minting dies, by which they intended to consume people's wealth.

It has been disputed regarding their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided.﴾ It was said: their words were originally "Indeed, you are the ignorant, the foolish," and Allah alluded to that with this phrasing. It was said: rather, this is their exact wording, except that they said it by way of mockery; this was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd. It was said: the meaning is: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided in your own estimation." It was said: rather, they said it in earnest and as their genuine belief about him, so they were disparaging him, meaning: he is forbearing and rightly guided, so it is not befitting for you to command us with these commands. This meaning resembles the saying of the Jews of Banu Qurayza when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "O brothers of the apes!" They said: "O Muhammad, we did not know you to be ignorant."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The resemblance between the two matters lies only in the correspondence between the speech of Shu'ayb and his gentleness, and what Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, initiated toward Banu Qurayza.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O my people! Have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence..."﴾ up to the end of the verse. This is a verbal reply, a fine flow of speech, and a gentle invitation. Concerning this verse and similar exchanges of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is the orator of the prophets." The answer to the condition in His saying: ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ is omitted; its estimate is: "Would I go astray as you have gone astray and abandon conveying the message?" and the like of this, which befits this argument. "بَيِّنَةٍ" (bayyinah) may mean "bayān" (clarification) or "bayyin" (clear), and the ta' marbuta entered for emphasis as in "'alāmah." It may also be an adjective of an elided noun, in which case the ta' is the feminine ta'.

As for His saying: ﴿and He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾ he means: pure, free from the corruption you have introduced into your wealth. Then he said to them: I do not intend to do what I have forbidden you from, such as diminishing measure and weight so that I would monopolize wealth for myself. I intend only the reform of all of it. "أُنِيبُ" (unību) means: I return, I repent, and I rely.

His state of prayer emboldened him to that, so it was said: "it commands you," as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, prayer forbids immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45].

Their saying: ﴿that we abandon what our fathers worshipped﴾ is an explicit text that they were worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted. The majority of readers recited "نَفْعَلُ" (naf'alu) and "نَشاءُ" (nashā'u) with the nun of the plural in both. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays recited "تَفْعَلُ" (taf'alu) and "تَشاءُ" (tashā'u) with the ta' of address in both. It is also reported from Abu 'Abd al-Rahman: "نَفْعَلُ" with the nun and "تَشاءُ" with the ta', and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. As for the one who recites with the nun in both, then the second "أنْ" (an) is conjoined to "ما" (mā), not to the first "أنْ"; because the meaning becomes: "Does your prayer command you that we do with our wealth what we wish?" This reverses what they intended. As for the one who recites with the ta' in both, then it is valid for the second "أنْ" to be conjoined to the first "أنْ." Some grammarians said: it is also valid to conjoin it to "ما," and the meaning is complete in both cases.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"نَتْرُكَ" (natruka) in the first case comes to mean "we reject," and in the second case comes to mean "we determine." This possibility is, in my view, impossible because of what I have mentioned regarding the variation of "leaving" upon the verbal judgment, or upon an elided genitive. Do you not see that "leaving" in the recitation of the one who recites with the nun in both verbs is merely in the sense of rejecting, without variation? As for the one who recites with the nun in "نَفْعَلُ" and the ta' in "تَشاءُ," then "أنْ" is conjoined to the first, and it is not permissible for it to be conjoined to "ما," because the meaning would also be reversed, so reflect on it.

The apparent meaning of their action to which they pointed is the stinting in measure and weight that was mentioned earlier. It is reported that the reference is to their clipping of the dinar and the dirham, and passing that off with the sound coin by way of deception; this was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others. It is also reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab that he said: "Clipping dinars and dirhams is among the corruption in the land." He interpreted it in this earlier-mentioned sense. It may also be interpreted as meaning altering the minting dies, by which they intended to consume people's wealth.

It has been disputed regarding their saying: ﴿Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided.﴾ It was said: their words were originally "Indeed, you are the ignorant, the foolish," and Allah alluded to that with this phrasing. It was said: rather, this is their exact wording, except that they said it by way of mockery; this was said by Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd. It was said: the meaning is: "Indeed, you are the forbearing, the rightly guided in your own estimation." It was said: rather, they said it in earnest and as their genuine belief about him, so they were disparaging him, meaning: he is forbearing and rightly guided, so it is not befitting for you to command us with these commands. This meaning resembles the saying of the Jews of Banu Qurayza when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "O brothers of the apes!" They said: "O Muhammad, we did not know you to be ignorant."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The resemblance between the two matters lies only in the correspondence between the speech of Shu'ayb and his gentleness, and what Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, initiated toward Banu Qurayza.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "O my people! Have you considered: if I am upon clear evidence..."﴾ up to the end of the verse. This is a verbal reply, a fine flow of speech, and a gentle invitation. Concerning this verse and similar exchanges of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "That is the orator of the prophets." The answer to the condition in His saying: ﴿if I am upon clear evidence from my Lord﴾ is omitted; its estimate is: "Would I go astray as you have gone astray and abandon conveying the message?" and the like of this, which befits this argument. "بَيِّنَةٍ" (bayyinah) may mean "bayān" (clarification) or "bayyin" (clear), and the ta' marbuta entered for emphasis as in "'alāmah." It may also be an adjective of an elided noun, in which case the ta' is the feminine ta'.

As for His saying: ﴿and He has provided me from Himself with good provision﴾ he means: pure, free from the corruption you have introduced into your wealth. Then he said to them: I do not intend to do what I have forbidden you from, such as diminishing measure and weight so that I would monopolize wealth for myself. I intend only the reform of all of it. "أُنِيبُ" (unību) means: I return, I repent, and I rely.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verse 89–92:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And O my people, let not my opposition bring upon you the like of what befell the people of Noah, or the people of Hud, or the people of Salih. And the people of Lot are not far from you.﴾ ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance. Indeed, my Lord is Merciful and Loving.﴾ ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb, we do not understand much of what you say, and we see you among us as weak. Were it not for your tribe, we would have stoned you, and you are not mighty against us."﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, is my tribe more honored by you than Allah? And you have put Him behind your backs, disregarded. Indeed, my Lord is encompassing of what you do."﴾

﴿Let not ... bring you﴾ (لا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ): its meaning is "let not earn for you," it is said: "jarramahu kadha wa kadha" and "ujarrimuhu" when he caused him to earn, just as it is said "kasaba" and "akhsaba" with the same meaning. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed you struck Abu 'Uyayna a blow, / which caused Fazara, after it, to be angry."

The majority read "yajrimannakum" with a fathah on the ya', while al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read "yujrimannakum" with a dammah on it. "Shiqaqi" means my opposition and my enmity, and "an" is the object of "yajrimannakum." The story of the people of Lot was the closest of the stories in time to the story of the people of Shu'ayb, and it may be intended: "And the dwellings of the people of Lot are not far from you," as if he said: "And the people of Lot are not far from you in distance." This statement includes the citing of the people of Lot as an example for them.

The majority read "mithlu" in the nominative, as the subject of "yusibakum." Mujahid, al-Jahdari, and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "mithla" in the accusative; this is in one of two ways: either "mithla" is the subject, and the fathah on the lam is a fathah of indeclinability because it is attached to something indeclinable, for "mithl" may behave like adverbs in this respect although it is not a pure adverb; or the subject is supposed to be omitted, as the meaning requires, and "mithla" is accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "the befalling of a like."

His saying: ﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord﴾ etc. The discussion of this has already preceded regarding the ordering of this seeking of forgiveness before repentance. "Wadud" means that His actions and His kindness toward His servants, since they are in the utmost of beneficence toward them, are like the act of one who shows affection and loves what he has made.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿They said, "O Shu'ayb"﴾ etc. "Nafqahu" means: we understand. This is like the saying of the Quraysh: ﴿Our hearts are in coverings﴾ [Fussilat: 5]. The meaning of ﴿we do not understand much of what you say﴾ is: we do not understand the soundness of your speech; as for their understanding of its wording and meaning, it is established. It is narrated from Ibn Jubayr and Shurayk al-Qadi regarding their saying "weak" that he was blind. al-Zahrawi related that Himyar call the blind "weak" just as it is said of him "blind." It was also said that he was thin of body.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and no proof stands upon it by the weakness of his sight or body. The apparent meaning of their saying "weak" is that he was weak in ability to defend himself and in power, and that his disbelieving tribe would respect him for this.

"Rahṭ" is a man's clan, and from it comes "al-rahṭa'" because the jerboa takes refuge in it just as a man does with his clan. "Larajamnaka" – it was said its meaning is "with stones," which is the apparent one, and this is what Ibn Zayd said. It was also said its meaning is: "we would have stoned you with abuse," and al-Tabari interpreted it this way. The Arabs also use this, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed I will stone you, so leave me alone for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. Their saying "bi-'azīz" means: one with might, power, and standing in our souls.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, is my tribe…"﴾ etc. "Al-zihriyy" is the thing that is behind the back. A thing may be behind the back in two ways in speech: either by being cast aside, as you say: "I made my speech behind your back and the back of your ear," and from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, let not my need be / behind the back, so that its answer does not fail me."

And either by leaning on it and seeking refuge. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in his supplication: "And I have leaned my back upon You." The majority of interpreters said regarding the meaning of this verse: that "you have taken Allah as a zihriyy—i.e., unregarded—behind the back," in the sense of casting aside; al-Tabari preferred this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is by necessity with an omitted genitive construction.

Some said: the pronoun in His saying "wa-ittakhadhtumuhu" refers to the command of Allah and His law, since the speech implies it. A group said: the meaning is: "Do you see my tribe as more honored by you than Allah, while you take Allah as a support for your backs and a pillar of your hopes?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of the majority is on the basis that the disbelief of the people of Shu'ayb was denial of Allah, the Exalted, and ignorance of Him. This second saying is on the basis that they used to acknowledge the Creator and Provider while believing the idols to be intermediaries and means, and similar. Both of these groups exist among disbelievers. From the same root comes "al-istizhar bil-bayyina" (seeking support by evidence). Ibn Zayd said: "al-zihriyy" is surplus, like the camel-driver who goes out with camels of reserve (zahariyya) which he prepares in case he needs them, and otherwise they are surplus.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is what may be relied upon.

His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾ is a statement that contains within it a threat; its meaning: His knowledge and His power encompass it.
