It was also said its meaning is: "we would have stoned you with abuse," and al-Tabari interpreted it this way. The Arabs also use this, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed I will stone you, so leave me alone for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. Their saying "bi-'azīz" means: one with might, power, and standing in our souls.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿He said, "O my people, is my tribe…"﴾ etc. "Al-zihriyy" is the thing that is behind the back. A thing may be behind the back in two ways in speech: either by being cast aside, as you say: "I made my speech behind your back and the back of your ear," and from it is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, let not my need be / behind the back, so that its answer does not fail me."

And either by leaning on it and seeking refuge. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in his supplication: "And I have leaned my back upon You." The majority of interpreters said regarding the meaning of this verse: that "you have taken Allah as a zihriyy—i.e., unregarded—behind the back," in the sense of casting aside; al-Tabari preferred this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view it is by necessity with an omitted genitive construction.

Some said: the pronoun in His saying "wa-ittakhadhtumuhu" refers to the command of Allah and His law, since the speech implies it. A group said: the meaning is: "Do you see my tribe as more honored by you than Allah, while you take Allah as a support for your backs and a pillar of your hopes?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of the majority is on the basis that the disbelief of the people of Shu'ayb was denial of Allah, the Exalted, and ignorance of Him. This second saying is on the basis that they used to acknowledge the Creator and Provider while believing the idols to be intermediaries and means, and similar. Both of these groups exist among disbelievers. From the same root comes "al-istizhar bil-bayyina" (seeking support by evidence). Ibn Zayd said: "al-zihriyy" is surplus, like the camel-driver who goes out with camels of reserve (zahariyya) which he prepares in case he needs them, and otherwise they are surplus.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is what may be relied upon.

His saying: ﴿Indeed my Lord is encompassing of what you do﴾ is a statement that contains within it a threat; its meaning: His knowledge and His power encompass it.

(p-11) The Exalted and Majestic says:

﴿And O my people, act according to your station; indeed I am acting. You will soon know who will receive a punishment that disgraces him and who is a liar. And watch; indeed I am with you as a watcher.﴾ ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Shu'ayb and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and the Shout seized those who had wronged, so they became prostrate in their homes,﴾ ﴿as though they had never prospered therein. Ah, remoteness for Madyan, just as Thamud were made remote.﴾

﴿عَلى مَكانَتِكُمْ﴾ means "according to your states" (ḥālātikum). This is like your saying: "The standing (makāna) of so-and-so in knowledge is above the standing of so-and-so," where the word is borrowed from places (biqā') to meanings. Al-Ḥasan, Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and ʿĀṣim read "makānatikum" in the plural, while the majority (al-Jumhūr) read it in the singular.

His saying "u'malū" (act) is a threat and a warning, like His saying: ﴿Act as you wish﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 40]. His saying ﴿man ya'tīhi﴾ ("who will come to him") may be that "man" (who) is the object of "taʿlamūna" (you will know), and the second (clause) is conjoined to it. Al-Farrāʾ said: It may also be an interrogative (istifhām) in a position of nominative (raf') by being the subject (mubtada').

As for "al-ṣayḥa" (the Shout), it is the shout of Jibrīl (Gabriel), peace be upon him. Al-judūm (crouching) originally applies to a bird when it strikes the ground with its chest, and then it is used for other than birds when there is a resemblance.

"Let not my people be remote, those who are
The poison of enemies and the calamity of the cuts (of the slaughtered)."

And from it is the saying of Mālik ibn al-Rayb:

"They say: Do not be remote, while they bury me,
And where is the place of remoteness except my place?"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 96–100:

(p-13) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority﴾ ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs. Yet they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not rightly guided.﴾ ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire, and wretched is the watering-place to which they are led.﴾ ﴿And they were followed in this world by a curse, and on the Day of Resurrection too; wretched is the gift that is given.﴾ ﴿That is from the news of the cities which We relate to you; some of them are still standing and some are harvested.﴾

"Ayat" means signs, and "sultan" means proof and clear demonstration in argument. It was said that it is derived from "salit" (a lamp), by which one is illuminated; and it was said that it is because he is empowered (musallat) over every opponent and adversary. "Al-mala'" means the group of men. The meaning is: We sent him to them so that they would believe in Allah, the Exalted, but Pharaoh turned them away, so they followed his command, did not believe, and disbelieved. Then He, blessed and exalted, informed about the command of Pharaoh that it was not rightly guided, i.e., it was not correct in its course and was not free from foolishness.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection﴾, the verse. Allah, exalted is He, informs in this verse about Pharaoh that he will come on the Day of Resurrection together with his people, who were drowned along with him, and he will lead them to the Fire. The past tense in "fa-awradahum" (and he led them) is used in the place of the future because the matter is clear and the difficulty is removed from it. The eloquence of the Arabs in placing the past tense in the position of the future is that the past tense is more indicative of the occurrence and realization of the action. "Al-wurud" in this verse is the arrival of entering, not the arrival of approaching and overlooking something, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when he arrived at the water of Madyan﴾ [al-Qasas: 23]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "In the Qur'an there are four: ﴿And there is none of you but will arrive at it﴾ [Maryam: 71], and His saying: ﴿And We will drive the criminals to Hell as a herd﴾ [Maryam: 86], this one in Maryam, and in al-Anbiya': ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell; you will arrive at it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98]." He said: "All of them are the arrival of entering; then Allah saves those who were mindful of Him." (p-14) "Al-mawrud" is an attribute of the place of "al-wird," on the basis that the implied meaning is: "and wretched is the place of the watering-place to which they are led." It was also said that "al-mawrud" is the subject (mubtada') and the predicate is placed first, meaning: "al-mawrud is wretched as a watering-place."

As for His saying: ﴿in this﴾, it means the abode of this world. "Al-la'na" (the curse) is their being removed from mercy through drowning, annihilation, and an evil reputation lasting through the ages. His saying: ﴿and on the Day of Resurrection﴾ means that they will also be cursed by entering Hell. Mujahid said: "So for them there are two curses." Some people held that the division is that they have a curse in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection they will receive a wretched gift; so there is one curse first and a wretched reward afterward. His saying: ﴿wretched is the gift that is given﴾ means: wretched is the reward that is given to them. In the speech of the Arabs, "rifd" is a gift, and the punishment is here called "rifd" because it is what takes the place of the gift. This is like when you say: "O so-and-so, your goodness to me was only that you struck me," meaning: what took the place of goodness from you was not that. "Al-irfad" is assistance, and from it comes the "rifadat Quraysh," their assistance to the poor pilgrims with the food they used to provide in the season.

As for His saying: ﴿That is from the news of the cities﴾, the verse. "That" refers to what preceded of mention of the punishments that descended upon the peoples mentioned. "Al-anba'" means the reports. "Al-qura" (the cities) may be understood as referring specifically to the cities mentioned in the preceding verses, and it may be understood as referring to cities in general; that is, these reported news related to you are the customs of towns when they disbelieve. On this second interpretation, the contemporary towns enter in it. His saying: ﴿Some of them are still standing and some are harvested﴾ means: some of them are still standing and some are ruined. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas. On the first interpretation, that they are those specific cities, His saying ﴿standing and harvested﴾ means: standing walls and collapsed with no trace left; this is the saying of Qatadah and Ibn Juraij. The verse as a whole contains warning and the striking of an example for those present, from the people of Makkah and others.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 11, verses 101–105:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿We did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves. So the gods they invoked besides Allah availed them nothing whatsoever when the command of your Lord came. And they added nothing to them but ruin.﴾ ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing. Indeed His seizing is painful and severe.﴾ ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for whoever fears the punishment of the Hereafter. That is a Day on which mankind will be gathered, and that is a Day that will be witnessed.﴾ ﴿And We do not delay it except for a limited term.﴾ ﴿On the Day it comes, no soul will speak except by His permission. Among them will be the wretched and the happy.﴾

The meaning: We did not place upon them any punishment that they did not deserve. Rather, they wronged themselves by placing disbelief in the place of faith, and worship in the direction of idols. So those idols did not benefit them, nor did they ward off from them the punishment of Allah when it came.

*Al-tatbīb* (ruin, perdition) means loss. From it is the verse ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish﴾ [al-Masad: 1], and from it is the verse of Jarir:

*ʿArāra min baqiyyati qawmi Lūṭin*
*Alā tabban limā ʿamilū tibāban*

"ʿArāra, a remnant of the people of Lot—
Ah, ruin for what they did, a ruin!"

That is: loss. As for the form in which the idols added to their ruin, it may be conceived in one of two ways: either their hope in them, their trust in them, and their exhaustion in worshipping them occupied their souls, diverted them from considering the Sharīʿa, and hindered them, so that distress and loss followed; or their punishment for disbelief was increased by an added punishment for merely worshipping idols.

[p-16] And His saying, ﴿Such is﴾: the demonstrative refers to what has been mentioned of the events that befell the nations. This is a verse of warning that encompasses the cities of the believers as well, for ﴿wrongdoing﴾ (ẓālima) is more general than "disbelieving" (kāfira). Allah, blessed and exalted is He, may grant respite to some disbelievers, but wrongdoers, in most cases, are hastened to punishment. As for the fact that He grants respite to some of them, in the hadith transmitted through Abu Musa, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Then he recited: ﴿Such is the seizing of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing﴾, to the end of the verse.

Abu Raja al-ʿUṭāridī and ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī read *rabbuka idh akhadha al-qurā* (رَبّكَ إذْ أخَذَ القُرى), whereas the great majority read *idhā akhadha al-qurā* (إذا أخَذَ القُرى). Al-Ṭabarī criticised the reading of ʿĀṣim, and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read it in the same way as ʿĀṣim. Its meaning is sound, but the reading of the community indicates that the threat persists and continues through time, and this is the principle in placing the present tense in the position of the past.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾: the meaning is that in the matter of these cities and what befell them there is a lesson and a sign of guidance for whoever fears the affair of the Hereafter and anticipates that its punishment may reach him, so he looks and reflects. For his looking leads him to faith in Allah, the Exalted. Then Allah magnified the affair of the Day of Resurrection by describing it with what is attached to something foreign to it, because of the connection between them, and by the return of the pronoun to it. The word ﴿mankind﴾ (al-nās) here, according to this, is the object of a passive verb whose subject is not named (*mafʿūl lam yusamma fāʿiluhu*, the grammatical construction "the object of a verb whose agent is unnamed"). It is also permissible for "al-nās" to be in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and "majmūʿ" (gathered) is then the predicate placed first.

[p-17] This verse is information about the gathering. ﴿Witnessed﴾ (mashhūd) is general in its absolute sense: it is witnessed by the first and the last, of humankind, the angels, the jinn, and the animals, according to the view of the majority. Regarding it, that is, the silent animals, there is a difference of opinion. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The witness (*shāhid*) is Muhammad, upon him be prayer and peace, and the witnessed (*mashhūd*) is the Day of Resurrection."

As for His saying, ﴿And We do not delay it﴾, the verse: the meaning is that We do not delay the Day of Resurrection out of inability to do so, but the prior decree has been executed concerning it at a limited term that it neither precedes nor exceeds. The majority read *nuʾakhkhiruhu* (نُؤَخِّرُهُ) with the letter *nūn*, whereas al-Aʿmash read *yuʾakhkhiruhu* (يُؤَخِّرُهُ) with *yāʾ*.

ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamza read ﴿yawma yaʾti﴾ (يَوْمَ يَأْتِ) with the *yāʾ* deleted from *yaʾtī*, both in connected speech and in pausal form. Ibn Kathīr read it with the *yāʾ* retained both in connected speech and at pause. Nāfiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, and al-Kisāʾī retained it in connected speech and deleted it at pause; this was also transmitted from Ibn Kathīr. The *yāʾ* is present in the codex of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, and it was dropped in the Uthmanic codex (*imām*). In the codex of Ibn Masʿūd it reads *yawma yaʾtūna* (يَوْمَ يَأْتُونَ), and al-Aʿmash read it this way. The reason for deleting it at pause is to make it resemble the line-endings (*fawāṣil*). Retaining it in both situations is the original form. The reason for deleting it in connected speech is lightness, as they say: *lā ubāli wa-lā adri* (لا أُبالِ ولا أدْرِ, "I do not care and I do not know"). Al-Ṭabarī recited:

*Kafāka kaffun mā talīqu dirhaman*
*Jūdan wa-ukhrā tuʿṭa bi-al-sayfi al-damā*

"One hand of yours does not deserve a dirham of generosity,
while another gives blood by the sword."

[p-18] And His saying, ﴿no soul will speak﴾, may be a clause in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in *yaʾtī*, which refers back to His saying ﴿that is a Day﴾. It is not permissible for it to refer back to His saying "the Day it comes," because a day that is annexed to a verb cannot be the agent of that verb: the annexed noun is defined by the noun it is annexed to, and the verb is defined by its agent, and it is not in itself a thing intended independently apart from the agent. Their saying "the chief of his people," "the client of his brother," and "the only one of his mother" differs from what does not stand independently, which is why annexation is permissible in those expressions. According to this, "the Day it comes" is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is ﴿among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾. According to this view, there is an omitted returning pronoun in the sentence, its estimated form being: "no soul will speak in it except—." It may also be that His saying ﴿no soul will speak﴾ is a qualifier of His saying "the Day it comes," with the predicate being ﴿among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾. It may also be that His saying ﴿no soul will speak﴾ is a predicate of His saying "the Day it comes." And His saying ﴿that is a Day﴾ is intended to refer to the day before it, namely its night. And His saying "the Day it comes" is intended to refer to a period and a time, not the daylight itself. So it is like what ʿUthmān said: "I have decided not to marry on this day of mine," and like what al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed trustworthiness today among people is scarce."

The meaning of His saying, ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, is a description of the awe of the Day of Resurrection, the bewilderment of the intellect, and the terror of the Resurrection. As for what is reported in the Qur'an of the speech of the people of the Standing Place (*al-mawqif*) in mutual blame, questioning, and disputation, either it occurs with permission, or this exception here applies specifically to speech for the purpose of intercession (*shafāʿa*) or establishing proof (*iqāmat ḥujja*).

And His saying, ﴿among them﴾, refers back to the whole that is contained in His saying ﴿soul﴾, since it is a collective noun intended to denote the plural.

According to this, "the Day it comes" is in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is ﴿among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾. According to this view, there is an omitted returning pronoun in the sentence, its estimated form being: "no soul will speak in it except—." It may also be that His saying ﴿no soul will speak﴾ is a qualifier of His saying "the Day it comes," with the predicate being ﴿among them will be the wretched and the happy﴾. It may also be that His saying ﴿no soul will speak﴾ is a predicate of His saying "the Day it comes." And His saying ﴿that is a Day﴾ is intended to refer to the day before it, namely its night. And His saying "the Day it comes" is intended to refer to a period and a time, not the daylight itself. So it is like what ʿUthmān said: "I have decided not to marry on this day of mine," and like what al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Indeed trustworthiness today among people is scarce."

The meaning of His saying, ﴿no soul will speak except by His permission﴾, is a description of the awe of the Day of Resurrection, the bewilderment of the intellect, and the terror of the Resurrection. As for what is reported in the Qur'an of the speech of the people of the Standing Place (*al-mawqif*) in mutual blame, questioning, and disputation, either it occurs with permission, or this exception here applies specifically to speech for the purpose of intercession (*shafāʿa*) or establishing proof (*iqāmat ḥujja*).

And His saying, ﴿among them﴾, refers back to the whole that is contained in His saying ﴿soul﴾, since it is a collective noun intended to denote the plural.

[p. 19]

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿As for those who are wretched, they will be in the Fire, where for them is groaning and wailing.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills. Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾ ﴿As for those who are blessed, they will be in the Garden, abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your Lord wills, a gift unbroken.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who are wretched﴾. According to some interpretations of the exception at the end of the verse, it refers to everyone who is punished, whether a disbeliever or a sinner. According to others, it refers only to everyone who is made to abide eternally, and this applies only to disbelievers specifically.

Al-zafir is a intense sound specific to one who is grieving, in pain, or being punished, or the like. Al-shahiq is likewise, as when a weeping person cries out in the midst of his sobbing. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: al-zafir is a sharp sound, and al-shahiq is a heavy sound. Abu al-'Aliya said: al-zafir comes from the chest, and al-shahiq from the throat. It was also said the opposite. Qatada said: al-zafir is the first sound of the donkey, and al-shahiq is its last, so the cries of the people of the Fire are like that. It was also said: al-zafir is derived from al-zafr, which means intensity, and al-shahiq is from their saying "a shahiq mountain," meaning tall. Thus, according to this meaning, they are one or close in meaning. The apparent meaning is what Abu al-'Aliya said, for the zafra is that in which the chest and the belly are greatly enlarged, and the shahqa is the final stroke of the sound, which is sometimes accompanied by the pushing out of breath. The dying person may gasp (yashaq), and the one who has fainted may also gasp.

As for His saying: ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾, it was said that its meaning is that Allah, blessed and exalted, will replace the heavens and the earth on the Day of Resurrection, making the earth a place for Hell and the heaven a place for the Garden, and this will be everlasting. So the verse links the eternity of these people with the endurance of those. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Allah created the heavens and the earth from the light of the Throne, and then He will return them there in the Hereafter, so for them there is then lasting permanence. It was also said: the meaning of His saying ﴿for as long as the heavens and the earth endure﴾ is an expression for [p. 20] eternity, in the manner Arabs are accustomed to. For it is from the eloquent speech of the Arabs that when they wish to express the eternity of something, they say: "I will not do such and such for the duration of the age, as long as the dove coos, and as long as the heavens and the earth endure," and similar expressions by which they mean length without end. So Allah, exalted, made them understand the eternal abiding of the disbelievers by this, even though He has informed that the heavens and the earth will cease.

As for His saying: ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾, it was said regarding it: this is in the manner of the exception which the Law has encouraged to be used in every speech, and it is like His saying, exalted: ﴿You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security﴾ [al-Fath: 27], an exception concerning something obligatory. This exception is in the sense of a condition, as if he said: "if Allah wills." Therefore it does not need to be described as connected (muttasil) or disconnected (munqati'). This is supported by His saying: ﴿a gift unbroken﴾. It was also said: it is an exception from the length of the period, according to what has been narrated, that Hell will be ruined, its people will be annihilated, and its gates will be closed. Thus, according to this, they will abide until their affair comes to this.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an unsound opinion. What has been narrated and transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud and others is only the lowest level of Hell, which is specific to the sinful among the believers, and which is called Jahannam. The whole was named by it metaphorically.

It was also said: what is excepted is only what Allah, exalted, shows kindness to among the sinful believers, by bringing them out of the Fire after a period. Thus His saying, exalted, ﴿except as your Lord wills﴾ means: for some people. This is the view of Qatada, al-Dahhak, Abu Sinan, and others. According to this, His saying ﴿As for those who are wretched﴾ is general, covering disbelievers and sinners as we have previously mentioned, and the exception applies to ﴿abiding﴾. It was also said: "illa" here means "wa" (and), so the meaning of the verse is: "and what Allah wills in addition to that." Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

Every brother who parts from his brother,
By the life of your father, except the two Farqads.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This verse may validly be cited as evidence for our belief in the annihilation of the two Farqads and the rest of the world. But if its speaker was one of the materialist (dahriyya) Arabs, then there is no proof in it, since he holds that it is everlasting, and so he kept "illa" in its original sense.

It was also said: "illa" in this verse means "siwa" (other than), and the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), as you say: "I have two thousand dirhams with you, except the thousand that I lent you," meaning: other than that. So it is as if He said: "abiding therein for as long as the heavens and the earth endure, other than what Allah wills in addition to that." This interpretation is supported by His saying afterwards: ﴿a gift unbroken﴾. This is the view of al-Farra', for he takes the disjunctive exception as "siwa," while Sibawayh takes it as "lakin" (but). It was also said: "other than what He has prepared for them of the various kinds of punishment that are unknown, such as the zamharir (extreme cold) and the like." It was also said: it is an exception from the duration of the heavens and the earth, meaning the period that passed for them in the life of this world. It was also said: it refers to the barzakh (intermediate state) between this world and the Hereafter. It was also said: it refers to the intervals between them in entering the Fire, since their entry is in groups after groups. It was also said: the exception is from His saying ﴿in the Fire﴾, as if He said: "except what your Lord wills of delay from that." This view was narrated by Abu Nadra from Jabir, or from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. Then He informed, drawing attention to the power of Allah, exalted, with His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is the Doer of what He intends.﴾

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, read ﴿sa'idu﴾ with a fatha on the sin, and it is an intransitive verb. There is no proof in their saying "mas'ud," because it is a passive participle of as'ada with the augment removed, just as one says "mahbub" from ahabba, and "majnun" from ajannahu Allah. It is also mentioned that al-Farra' related that the Hudhayl tribe say "sa'adahu Allah," meaning "as'adahu" (made him fortunate). Nor does the interpretation of the one who said regarding that one, that the exception is from His saying ﴿in the Fire﴾, apply here either.

As for His saying ﴿a gift unbroken﴾, it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). Al-majdhudh means "cut off," and al-jadhdh means "cutting," and likewise al-jadd, and likewise al-hazz.

And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been judged between them. And indeed, they are in disquieting doubt concerning it.﴾ ﴿And indeed, to all [of them] your Lord will surely pay in full [the due for] their deeds. Indeed, He is Acquainted with what they do.﴾

Rather, it is from the eloquence of speech, in clarifying the misguidance of the disbelievers, that it is phrased in this expression: their state is too clear to be doubted. Al-mirya (المِرْيَة) means doubt. The word ﴿these﴾ refers to the idolatrous disbelievers of the Arabs. Then He said: ﴿They worship only as their fathers worshipped before.﴾ The meaning: they are imitators (مُقَلِّدُون), having neither proof nor argument. Their worship is only an imitation of their fathers, not from insight. The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded, you and those who turned back with you, and do not transgress. Indeed, He is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And do not incline toward those who have wronged, lest the Fire touch you, and you will not have, other than Allah, any protectors; then you would not be helped.﴾ ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and in some hours of the night. Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

The Prophet's ﷺ being commanded to steadfastness, while he himself was upon it, is nothing but a command to continuity and firmness. This is like when you order a person to walk, eat, and the like while he is already engaged in it. The address in this verse is to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and to those companions who turned in repentance from disbelief, and to the rest of his community in meaning. It is narrated that some scholars saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, it has reached us from you that you said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey-haired.' Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds. That is a reminder for those who remember.﴾ ﴿And be patient, for indeed Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

The Prophet's ﷺ being commanded to steadfastness, while he himself was upon it, is nothing but a command to continuity and firmness. This is like when you order a person to walk, eat, and the like while he is already engaged in it. The address in this verse is to the Prophet (peace be upon him) and to those companions who turned in repentance from disbelief, and to the rest of his community in meaning. It is narrated that some scholars saw the Prophet ﷺ in a dream and said to him: "O Messenger of Allah, it has reached us from you that you said: 'Hud and its sisters have made me grey-haired.' What is it in Hud that has made you grey?" He said to him: "His Exalted saying: ﴿So be steadfast as you have been commanded﴾."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The well-known interpretation of the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "Hud and its sisters have made me grey-haired," is that it refers to what is in them of what befell the earlier nations, so his concern for this community lest it suffer the like of that greyed him (peace be upon him).

His saying ﴿commanded﴾ is an address of honour. His saying "and whoever" is conjoined to the pronoun in His saying ﴿so be steadfast﴾, and this is acceptable without emphasis because of the length of the speech with His saying ﴿as you have been commanded﴾. And ﴿do not transgress﴾ means: do not exceed the limits of Allah the Exalted. Transgression (tughyan) is exceeding the limit, and from it is His saying ﴿When the water overflowed﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11], and His saying about Pharaoh: "Indeed he transgressed." It has been said regarding this verse that its meaning is: do not let blessings make you transgress, and this is close to the first meaning. The majority read "taʿmalūna" (what you do) with a ta' (second person), while al-Hasan and al-A'mash read "yaʿmalūna" with a ya' from below (third person).

The majority read "wa-lā tarkanū" with a fatha on the kaf, while Talha ibn Musarrif, Qatada, al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli, and Abu 'Amr, as transmitted from him by Harun, read it with a damma, and this is a dialect; it is said rakina yarkanu and rakana yarkunu. Its meaning is to settle upon a thing and be content with it. Abu al-'Aliya said: (p-28) "Ruku' is contentment." Ibn Zayd said: "Ruku' is submission."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ruku' applies to both little and much of this meaning, and the prohibition here follows from the meaning of ruku' as inclination toward them by associating with them, down to the least degree of refraining from changing their ways while having the ability to do so. And "those who have wronged" here are the disbelievers, and this is the explicit text for the exegetes, and in meaning it includes the people of sins.

The majority read "fa-tamassakum"; Yahya ibn Wthththab, 'Alqama, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif, and Hamza, as transmitted from him, read "fa-timassakum" with a kasra on the ta', and this is a dialect of giving the three vowel-markers a kasra except for the ya' of the third-person masculine, and it has come in the ya' as "yījal" and "yībā"; this has been explained by the fact that the ya' following the first has pulled it toward a kasra.

As for His exalted saying: "Establish the prayer..." the verse: No one has differed that the prayer in this verse refers to the obligatory prayers. They differed regarding "the two ends of the day and the zulaf of the night." It was said: the first end is the dawn, and the second is the noon and afternoon, and the zulaf are the sunset and night prayers; this was said by Mujahid and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi. And it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the sunset and night prayers: "They are the two zulfas of the night." It was also said: the first end is the dawn, and the second is the afternoon; this was said by al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Dahhak. The zulaf are sunset and night, and the noon prayer is not in this verse according to this view but is in other verses. It was said: the two ends are dawn and sunset; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas and also al-Hasan, and the zulaf is the night prayer, and noon and afternoon are not in the verse. It was said: the two ends are noon and afternoon, and the zulaf are sunset, night, and dawn.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems this speaker considered the audible recitation. The first of these sayings is, in my view, the best. Al-Tabari preferred that the two ends are dawn and sunset, and that this is the apparent meaning, but the generality of the five prayers through the verse is more fitting.

The majority read "zulafan" with a fatha on the lam. Talha ibn Musarrif, Ibn Muhaysin, 'Isa, Ibn Ishaq, and Abu Ja'far read "zulufan" with a damma on the lam, as if it were a singular noun. Mujahid read "zulfan" with a sukun on the lam, and he also read "zulfa" on the pattern of "fu'la"; this is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin. The zulaf are the hours close to one another, and from it is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

A wayfarer whom weariness and what it dried out have carried,
Folding the nights zulafan then zulafa,
Until the crescent's half became bent.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove misdeeds﴾, the majority of the exegetes from the Companions and Successors held that "the good deeds" refers to the five prayers, and to this verse 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, referred when performing ablution while sitting on seats, and this is also the interpretation of Malik. Mujahid said: the good deeds are a man's saying: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is only by way of example regarding good deeds, and because the five prayers are the greatest of deeds. What appears is that the wording of the verse is general regarding good deeds but specific regarding misdeeds, by his peace and blessings be upon him saying: "As long as the major sins are avoided." It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning a man from the Ansar, it was said: he is Abu al-Yusr ibn 'Amr, and it was said: his name was 'Abbad, who was alone with a woman, kissed her, and enjoyed her short of intercourse. Then he came to 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and complained to him, and he said: "Allah has covered you, so cover yourself." The man was distressed, so he came to Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and complained to him, and he said to him the like of what 'Umar said. The man was distressed, so he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and prayed with him, then informed him and said: "Decide concerning me as you wish." The Messenger ﷺ said: "Perhaps she is the wife of a warrior in the way of Allah." He said: "Yes." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ rebuked him and said: "I do not know." Then this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him, recited it to him, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: "O Messenger of Allah, is it specific to him?" He said: "Rather, it is for people in general."

It is also narrated that this verse had been revealed before that, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ applied it to that man. It is narrated that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said what is related from Mu'adh.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Friday to Friday, the five prayers, and Ramadan to Ramadan are expiation for what is between them, if the major sins are avoided." The People of the Sunna differed regarding the interpretation of this condition in his saying "if the major sins are avoided." Most of them said: it is a condition within the whole promise, meaning: if the major sins are avoided, the mentioned acts of worship are expiation for sins; but if they are not avoided, the acts of worship do not expiate any of the minor sins. Another group said: the meaning of "if they are avoided" is that these are the ones which worship does not remove; the condition was stated so that the generality of "what is between them" would be valid with its condition, and if they are not avoided, worship does not remove them, but it removes the minor sins.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

I say this, and it is what the hadith about sins falling out with the drops of water (p-31) and others requires, and all of that is conditional upon repentance from those minor sins and not persisting in them. This is the explicit view of the skilled jurists of usul. According to the first interpretation, this would be restricted to those who avoid major sins only.

His saying "that" refers to the prayers, and He described them as "a reminder," meaning: they are a cause of remembrance and a place of remembrance. It is possible that "that" refers to the statement that good deeds remove misdeeds, so this reminder urges toward good deeds. It is also possible that the reference is to all the commands and prohibitions mentioned earlier in this surah, and this is al-Tabari's explanation.

Then He commanded him to be patient.

These verses came in one pattern: Allah the Exalted informed him that He will fully repay all creatures for their deeds, the wrongdoer and the good-doer. Then He commanded him to steadfastness, and the believers with him. Then He commanded him to establish the prayers and promised a reward for that. Then He commanded him to be patient in conveying and in hardships for the sake of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, then He promised with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not allow the reward of the good-doers to be lost.﴾

**Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 11, verses 116–117:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿Why were there not, among the generations before you, people of virtue who would forbid corruption on the earth, except a few of those whom We saved from among them? But those who did wrong pursued the luxury they had been given, and they were criminals.﴾ ﴿Your Lord would never destroy the towns unjustly while their people were reforming.﴾

"Fa-lawla" (why not, if only) is the one used for urging (tahdid), but here it carries the sense of grief and regret that should befall humankind over these nations which did not find guidance. This is like His saying: ﴿Alas for the servants!﴾ [Ya-Sin: 30]. "Qurun" (generations) before you are the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud and those previously mentioned. A "qarn" (generation) among people is a group of contemporaries over a long period, most of which—according to what people have estimated—is one hundred years; it is said eighty, and it is said other than that, down to thirty years. The first view is more preponderant, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Consider your night this, for at the end of a hundred years from it, none of those who are today upon the face of the earth will remain." Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he means that it sweeps away that generation.

"Baqiyyah" (remnant) here is meant to refer to insight, intellect, resolve and steadfastness in religion. It is called "baqiyyah" because the laws, states and the like have their strength at their beginning and then continue to weaken; so whoever remains firm in a time of weakness is a remnant of the first era. A group read "baqiyyah" with the yaa lightened, which reduces the form fa'iliyah to fa'ilah. Abu Ja'far and Shayba read "buqyah" with a damma on the ba and a sukun on the qaf, on the pattern fu'lah.

"Corruption on the earth" is disbelief and what accompanies it of disobedience. This verse contains a warning to the community of Muhammad ﷺ and an exhortation to change the evil and forbid corruption. Then Allah the Exalted made an exception of the people whom He saved along with their prophets, and they were few in comparison to their communities. "Qalilan" (few) is in the accusative as an exception; according to Sibawayh it is a disjunctive (munqati') exception, and the statement, in his view, is affirmative; others regard it as negative in terms of its meaning, since there were no people of virtue among them.

The majority of people read "wa-ittaba'a" with the verb built for the active subject. Ja'far ibn Muhammad read "wa-utbi'a" with it built for the passive object, and it is related from Abu 'Amr. "Ma utrifu fihi" means: the consequence of what they were given comfort with—with the verb built for the passive object. "Mutraf" means a person given luxury whose affluence distracted him from the truth until he perished. From this is the poet's saying:

"You present the heads of the affluent, the obstructers, * to the Commander of the Faithful, the one who is questioned."

(p-33) He means: the one who is asked; it is said "madahu" when he asked him.

His saying, the Exalted, "bi-zulm" (with injustice) may mean: with injustice from Him towards them—exalted is He above that. Al-Tabari said: it may also mean: with shirk from them while they were reforming in their deeds and conduct, and in the justice of some of them towards others; that is, there must be disobedience accompanying their disbelief.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak. Its proponent only went in the direction of what has been said: "Allah the Exalted gives respite to states in disbelief, but does not give them respite in injustice and oppression." Were it reversed, it would have been more apt; that is, Allah would not punish a nation for their wrongdoing in their disobediences while they were reforming in faith. The first possibility in our arrangement is more correct, God willing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 118–119:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if your Lord had willed, He would have made mankind one community, but they will not cease to differ﴾ ﴿except those on whom your Lord has mercy. And for that He created them. And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and mankind, all together."﴾

The meaning: He would have made them one community of believers, said Qatadah, so that no disbelief would occur among them and no punishment (muthla) would befall them. But Mighty and Majestic He did not will that; so they will not cease to differ in religions, opinions and creeds (milal). This is the interpretation of the majority (al-jumhur). Al-Hasan, 'Ata', Mujahid and others said: those excepted and shown mercy are the believers, among whom there is no difference. A group said: they will not cease to differ regarding happiness and misery, and this meaning is close to the first, since it is the fruit of religions and of differing about them; and the difference, on this interpretation, includes the believers, since they oppose the disbelievers. Al-Hasan also said: they will not cease to differ regarding wealth and poverty.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a statement whose meaning is far from the meaning of the verse.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, made an exception from the pronoun in "yazaluna" (they will not cease) for those whom He has shown mercy among mankind, by guiding them to faith and granting them success in it.

As for His statement: ﴿And for that He created them﴾, the interpreters differed concerning it. One group said: "for the witnessing of the Day witnessed" mentioned earlier, He created them. Another group said: "that" (dhalika) refers to His earlier statement: ﴿So among them is the wretched and the happy﴾ [Hud: 105], meaning: for this He created them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two meanings, although they are correct, this distant return of the reference is not good. Ashhab reported from Malik that he said: "that" refers to there being a group in Paradise and a group in the Blaze.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

So the reference "that" comes to both matters together: the difference and the mercy. Ibn 'Abbas said this and al-Tabari chose it, and on this reading the pronoun in "khalaqahum" (He created them) applies to both categories. Mujahid and Qatadah said: "that" refers to the mercy contained in His statement ﴿except those on whom He has mercy﴾, meaning: and for mercy He created those who receive mercy. Al-Hasan said: "that" refers to the difference mentioned in His statement ﴿and they will not cease to differ﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This may be objected to by asking: how did He create them for difference? And is difference itself the purpose of their creation? The proper resolution is to say: the rule of the Shari'ah is that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, created one kind for happiness and another kind for misery, then facilitated for each what it was created for, and this is explicit in the authentic hadith. He then made disagreement over the religion concerning the truth the sign of wretchedness, and upon it is the attachment of punishment. So his statement here, "and for that He created them", may be understood as: for the fruit of difference and what results from it of wretchedness.

It is also permissible to take the lam in His statement "wa-li-dhalika" as the lam of consequence (lam al-sayrura), meaning: He created them so that their affair would end up in that, even though He did not intend difference by them. The meaning of His statement ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56] is: that I might command them to worship, and make it obligatory upon them; so He expressed this by the fruit of the command and its requirement.

As for His statement ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled﴾, meaning: His decree has taken effect and His command has become binding. The lam in "la-amla'anna" is the lam of oath, since "the word" (al-kalima) contains an oath. "Al-Jinn" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form; it derives from ajanna, meaning he concealed. The ha' in "al-jinnah" is for emphasis (lil-mubalagha), though "al-jinn" may apply to a single individual, and "al-jinnah" is its plural.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 11, verses 120–123:

The words of the Most High:

﴿And We relate to you the news of the messengers, by which We strengthen your heart. And in this [surah] there has come to you the truth, and an admonition and a reminder for the believers.﴾ ﴿Say to those who do not believe: "Act according to your position; indeed, we are acting."﴾ ﴿And wait; indeed, we are waiting.﴾ ﴿To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and to Him the whole matter is returned. So worship Him and rely upon Him. And your Lord is not unaware of what you do.﴾

His saying "وَكُلًّا" (wa-kullan) is a fronted object (مَفْعُولٌ مُقَدَّمٌ) of "نَقُصُّ" (naqussu). It was also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial (حال, ḥāl) construction, and it was said that it is in the accusative as an absolute object (مَصْدَر, maṣdar).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These two views are weak.

(p. 36) "مَا" (mā) is a substitute (بَدَل) for "وَكُلًّا". "﴿نُثَبِّتُ بِهِ فُؤادَكَ﴾" means: We comfort you in what you encounter, and We make for you an example in those prophets who came before you. As for His saying "﴿فِي هَذِهِ﴾" (fī hādhihi), al-Hasan said it refers to the abode of this world, while Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to the surah and the verses in it that mention the stories of the nations. This is the view of the majority.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The reason the surah is specifically described as "the truth" (الحَقّ) — although the whole Qur'an is truth — is that this implies a meaning of threat to the disbelievers and an alert to the observer. That is: there has come to you in this surah the truth that befell the wrongdoing nations. This is like the saying used in times of hardship, "the truth has come" (جاءَ الحَقُّ), although truth may come in other than hardship and in other than one way, and "the truth has come" is not used for that. Then He also described what the surah contains as an admonition and a reminder for the believers. This supports that the word "the truth" is specifically concerned with the threat it contains for the disbelievers.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And say to those who do not believe﴾, to the end of the verse. This is a verse of threat; that is: act according to your states in which you are, of your disbelief. The majority read here "مَكانَتِكُمْ" (makānatikum) as a singular form indicating a plural. The wording of this verse is suitable for a truce, and it is also suitable to be said as a pure threat while war is ongoing.

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿To Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, to the end of the verse. This is a verse of glorification and of exclusivity in that which no creature has any share of, namely the knowledge of the unseen, and of clarifying that good and evil, the great and the small of things, are directed by the rulings of their Owner.
